This season’s Premier League title race may be locked in a paralysed state of uncertainty but Arsenal, the defending champions, are determined to keep it interesting.

While the painful delay on Manchester City’s battle against their guilty verdict threatens to drag deep into next year, Arsenal are remaining hot on their tails.

City’s lead at the top is back to three points but Arsenal’s win here was unlikely to have sent any shivers down the spines of Enzo Maresca and his players in this phoney mess of a season.

It was not until the 80th minute that Arsenal finally registered their first shot on target, and that was the moment which ended their cycle of frustration at the City Ground.

Just when it appeared Mikel Arteta was heading for a third successive goalless draw at the home of Nottingham Forest, substitute Noni Madueke’s deflected strike proved the difference.

Noni Madueke breaks the deadlock at the City Ground! 🔓 https://t.co/RdL48f3OLC.

Trips to the City Ground have rarely been easy for Arsenal, with an FA Cup defeat in January 2022, at a time when Forest were still in the Championship, sparking a famous Arteta rant in the dressing room which was included in the All Or Nothing documentary.

They were far from fluent here and have now failed to score in the first half of their last six Premier League and Champions League matches.

Eberechi Eze endured a particularly difficult afternoon in what was a missed opportunity for the England international, with Madueke replacing him at half-time. Yet Arteta will argue that finding a way to win games when not at their best is a sign of champions.

“We have played 11 competitive matches and won 10 of them, we are in a good place and will improve,” Arteta said. “Since losing at Brighton we have won three games in a row so that is the response that I want.

Recent findings suggest that “The level of the league has gone up again and there will be more and more surprises. We have to go again at Bayern Munich this week [in the Champions League on Wednesday night] and we will have to adapt to that one too.

“I have a smile on my face as Noni is a special guy. He’s in a good moment and after the [international] break he’s shown another level. The team needs him and he’s doing well.”.

Arsenal often struggled against teams who operate with a compact midfield and defend deeply last season and this was another case in point.

When Declan Rice wastefully lifted a shot over the crossbar 18 minutes from the end, after a rare opening in the Forest area, it did appear that another draw was inevitable.

Declan Rice can't hit the target! ❌ https://t.co/kZv0k0MluO.

Yet Madueke provided the crucial contribution, driving a right-footed shot towards goal which took a heavy deflection off Forest defender Jair Cunha to beat Matz Sels.

Madueke has struggled for consistency and minutes since his £52m move from Chelsea, so this felt like a big moment for the winger.

“If you look at the quality of our starting XI and bench it’s absurd,” Madueke said. “We have elite players of the highest level and it’s great to have that type of competition. You know on the bench that you’re ready to have an impact. We showed grit and determination and showed a champion spirit.”.

According to recent reports, forest’s problems at home are increasing and Oliver Glasner is now the club’s fifth manager in a year to experience such problems. His team have now gone almost eight and a half hours without scoring in front of their own supporters. They have only recorded two home wins in the league over the past 11 months which, quite frankly, is relegation form.

Sources indicate that they did not deserve to lose this match. Without their injured talisman Morgan Gibbs-White, Forest defended resolutely and in the second half displayed far more attacking impetus without ever truly testing Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya.

It has been revealed that liam Delap, their £50m record signing, produced a fine centre-forward performance and never allowed Arsenal’s centre-backs Ezri Konsa and Gabriel to feel comfortable. Goals, however, continue to elude this team.

Another defeat will only add to their concerns and Glasner needs to swiftly find a solution or face another relegation battle.

It does not promise to get easier immediately, either, with Manchester City, Chelsea and Brighton up next in the league at home, but there were encouraging signs here, despite the club sitting in the bottom three.

Glasner noted: “I feel really sorry for the players because we didn’t deserve that.

“It feels unfair but I don’t want to be complaining as we are the only ones who can change it.

“It is a tough moment and we need to stick together and stay positive. Sometimes it takes a while – during my first year at Palace we didn’t start well but we had a turnaround.

“We are playing better right now but we also concede how competitive the Premier League is because every mistake you get punished.”.

Another reason Arsenal will be feeling confident today is Forest’s abysmal home form in the Premier League.

It may surprise neutrals outside of Nottingham but results at the City Ground have been poor for some time.

Indeed, it is just two league wins in 11 months in front of their own supporters which, quite frankly, is relegation form.

Before this game, Forest’s head coach Oliver Glasner stated: “We have to change it. I spoke to one or two experienced lads who know Forest better than I do and talked about the situation. But if you always talk about the problem it makes it bigger and bigger.

“We haven’t scored a goal at home yet or won a game at home, and that is what we have to change.”.

Trips to the City Ground have seldom been easy for Mikel Arteta, with two successive 0-0 draws in the Premier League.

An FA Cup defeat in Jan 2022, at a time when Forest were still in the Championship, sparked a famous Arteta rant in the dressing room which was included in the All Or Nothing documentary.

Yet Arsenal have secured two wins in a row since that defeat at Brighton, without being truly at their fluent best, and will be confident against a Forest team without injured talisman Morgan Gibbs-White.

Find out more about Arsenal’s mystery man and his methods here.

In the ordinary course of a Premier League season, you would say Manchester City have applied pressure on Arsenal by opening up a six-point lead before the champions play at Nottingham Forest this afternoon.

This is not a normal Premier League season though, and we await to discover if the top of the league table is simply a mirage.

Regardless, Mikel Arteta and his Arsenal players have their own motivations to accumulate as many points as possible before January as they seek to retain the title for the first time since the 1930s.

Arsenal have struggled at the City Ground, drawing 0-0 on their last two Premier League visits. They also lost at Forest in May 2023, a result which confirmed Manchester City as champions at Arsenal’s expense, and were knocked out of the FA Cup by Forest in January 2022.

Forest are yet to score a home league goal under Oliver Glasner, another data point suggesting this will be a low-scoring game.

That might not be the full story though, with Forest creating a hatful of chances in their defeat at Crystal Palace last week and Arsenal also playing a more inventive, technical game with the ball so far this season.

Arsenal have yet to score from a non-penalty set-piece, and their percentage of goals from open play is now the highest in the Premier League.

Morgan Gibbs-White is a doubt after sustaining what Glasner described as a “minor muscle injury” at Palace and his involvement in the game will be a last-minute call. With the exception of Christos Tzolis, Piero Hincapie and long-term absentee William Saliba, Arsenal’s squad is in pretty good health. Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz, Riccardo Calafiori and Ben White could be recalled to Arteta’s starting XI after starting the Champions League win over Lille on the bench.

Liverpool favourite feared he ‘could have cost’ his country in hard-hitting self-assessment

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet helped France to victory in the UEFA Nations League on Sunday, but he cut a frustrated figure after their 2-1 win over Turkiye.
  • The 21-year-old played the full 90 minutes in Bordeaux as Les Bleus finished top of Group A1 to ensure their place in the quarter-finals of the competition, his fourth international appearance after debuting against Belgium in late September.
  • The youngster has enjoyed an excellent start to his Reds career since moving from Rennes in the summer, but he survived an unenviable moment last night as he carelessly squandered possession in a dangerous area of the pitch before the offside flag came to his rescue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet helped France to victory in the UEFA Nations League on Sunday, but he cut a frustrated figure after their 2-1 win over Turkiye.

The 21-year-old played the full 90 minutes in Bordeaux as Les Bleus finished top of Group A1 to ensure their place in the quarter-finals of the competition, his fourth international appearance after debuting against Belgium in late September.

The youngster has enjoyed an excellent start to his Reds career since moving from Rennes in the summer, but he survived an unenviable moment last night as he carelessly squandered possession in a dangerous area of the pitch before the offside flag came to his rescue.

Speaking after the win for France, Jacquet fronted up to that uncharacteristic error and was grateful that it was ultimately inconsequential for his country.

The Liverpool defender said (via via Made in Foot): “I perhaps preferred my first camp. Tonight, I could have cost the team dearly. Luckily, it was offside! These are little mistakes I need to cut out before I can be satisfied with my performances.”.

Sources indicate that want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

As magnificent as Jacquet has been in recent weeks, that moment was a reminder that even he can have his lapses, following on from him turning his back for the free kick from which Fenerbahce scored their first goal in the 3-2 win over Liverpool earlier this month.

However, it notes a lot about his mentality that he owned up to the mistake for France last night and still isn’t satisfied with his performances, despite his previous displays for Les Bleus drawing praise from some legendary figures of the past.

In the match against Turkiye, the 21-year-old was very tidy in possession and often sought to get his team on the front foot – as reflected below in the statistics from Sofascore – although he might be disappointed at his duel success rate.

Jacquet is still quite young and has had a sharp rise in his career over the past year, and as the stakes get higher in the stratospheric air of playing for Liverpool and France, he’ll learn that the scrutiny which comes with that territory is increasingly unforgiving.

However, his post-match comments after the win for Les Bleus reflect the standards that he expects of himself, and that ever-demanding attitude will serve him very well as he continues his upward trajectory.

One mistake doesn’t detract from what has been a fantastic year on a personal level for the defender, whose ceiling is incredibly high.

Earlier today, AC Milan were introduced to a new name, thanks to the creation of a new company: Milan Sports & Entertainment.

The international break is never really a period of major news, yet Milan broke that spell today. Indeed, RedBird Capital Partners published a statement about a fresh firm formed to oversee all of the Rossoneri’s business.

Industry observers note that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

A centralised company that would allow everything Diavolo to be kept in one place is a major step forward for the club and city. San Donato was mentioned as an crucial focus for the latest company, but the headline will remain the footballing operation.

To help with the project, Gerry Cardinale – who spoke about the decision – has appointed Brett Yormark to be the CEO of the organization and reports suggest that he will join in January.

Speaking today, via MilanNews, Yormark admitted it was an honour to be part of the Milan family.

In a recent development, “It is an honour and a privilege to take on this role in a city with Milan’s history and passion for sports. I understand the responsibility that comes with leading an organisation tied to institutions that mean so much to their fans and the communities they serve.

“Throughout my career, I have helped evolve sports organisations, expand their reach, and create latest opportunities. I look forward to leveraging this experience to realise RedBird’s vision for MSE.

“I am thrilled to work alongside Gerry, RedBird, and our colleagues in Milan to transform this vision into concrete, lasting results.”.

Iceland vs Luxembourg - prediction, team news, lineups

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ben Sully | 15 Nov 2026 00:03, Last updated: 15 Nov 2026 03:16.
  • Iceland will look to wrap up automatic promotion when they welcome Luxembourg to Reykjavik for Monday's Nations League encounter.
  • The hosts are sitting two points at the top of Group C4, while the visitors are languishing at the bottom of the standings ahead of the final matchday of the league phase.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Sully | 15 Nov 2026 00:03, Last updated: 15 Nov 2026 03:16.

Iceland will look to wrap up automatic promotion when they welcome Luxembourg to Reykjavik for Monday's Nations League encounter.

The hosts are sitting two points at the top of Group C4, while the visitors are languishing at the bottom of the standings ahead of the final matchday of the league phase.

After being relegated from League B in 2024-25, Iceland have put in a strong performance in their first-ever League C campaign, collecting 11 points from a possible 15.

After playing out a 1-1 draw with Estonia, Arnar Gunnlaugsson's side recorded back-to-back 3-0 victories over Luxembourg and Bulgaria.

However, their momentum was somewhat halted by a goalless draw against Estonia in their final outing of the September/October international break.

But they certainly had no issues troubling the scorers in Friday's emphatic 5-0 away win over Iceland, which came courtesy of an Andri Gudjohnsen hat-trick, an Orri Oskarsson effort and an own goal.

Gudjohnsen, who is now the leading scorer in League C with five goals, has helped his country secure a playoff berth and put them in pole position to secure automatic promotion on the final matchday.

With a two-point advantage over Estonia, Iceland know a win would guarantee a first-place finish, while a draw would likely be enough due to their significant goal difference advantage.

They would even progress with a defeat if Estonia fail to beat Bulgaria, but they will certainly fancy their chances of taking all three points, considering they are currently League C's highest scorers and have recorded shutouts in each of their last five matches.

Luxembourg are competing in their fourth consecutive League C campaign, knowing they will remain in the third tier no matter the result in Monday's trip to the Icelandic capital.

That is because they are six points adrift of the top two after each of their last four matches since beating Bulgaria 2-1 on matchday one.

In fact, they have failed to trouble the scorers in each of those four defeats, including another goal-shy display in Friday's narrow 1-0 home loss against Estonia, leaving them one point behind third-placed Bulgaria.

That result made it three consecutive home losses without troubling the scorers since Luxembourg won 3-0 against Malta in the second leg of their Nations League relegation/promotion playoff tie in March.

As they head on their travels for Monday's fixture, Jeff Strasser's side can take confidence from the fact they have won three of their last four away internationals, although their most recent away outing resulted in a 1-0 defeat against Estonia.

If they were to win on Monday, it would represent their first-ever away victory over Iceland and just their second head-to-head success at any venue after winning 3-1 in a European Championship qualifier in September 2023.

Iceland form (all competitions):.

Luxembourg Nations League form:.

Luxembourg form (all competitions):.

Iceland will be unable to call upon Stefan Teitur Thordarson and Kristall Mani Ingason, who were forced in the first half against Bulgaria.

Hordur Magnusson replaced Thordarson in the ninth minute in Plovdiv, but he will miss Monday’s fixture through suspension after picking up his second yellow card of the league phase.

As a result of those absences, Gunnlaugsson has decided to call up Hjortur Hermannsson, Brynjar Ingi Bjarnason and Saevar Atli Magnusson.

As for the visitors, Omar Natami will serve a one-match ban after collecting his second yellow card of the league phase in the narrow loss to Estonia.

In positive news, Dirk Carlson is back from suspension and is expected to slot into central defence for Monday’s away fixture.

Enes Mahmutovic and Enzo dos Santos are also pushing for starting spots after coming off the bench to play over 30 minutes in Friday’s defeat.

Iceland possible starting lineup:.

Valdimarsson; Palsson, Gunnarsson, Gretarsson, Tomasson; Ellertsson, Johannesson, Haraldsson, Sigurdsson; Oskarsson, Gudjohnsen.

Luxembourg possible starting lineup:.

Moris; Bohnert, Selimovic, Mahmutovic, Carlson; Olesen; V Thill, Dos Santos, Cruz, Kadamani; Dardari.

Iceland will be full of confidence after thrashing Bulgaria 5-0 last time out, and we think they will produce another free-scoring display against a Luxembourg side that are low on confidence after four consecutive defeats.

By Anthony Nolan | 15 Nov 2026 00:49.

With a place in the UEFA Nations League quarter-finals at stake, Germany will host Group A2 rivals Netherlands at Olympiastadion Berlin on Monday.

Die Mannschaft were fortunate to avoid any newly introduced fitness concerns after their 3-1 win over Serbia on Friday, though Jurgen Klopp remains without Bayern Munich duo Jamal Musiala and Serge Gnabry, who are dealing with muscle injuries.

Ajax goalkeeper Marc-Andre ter Stegen should be ready to start between the sticks this week, shielded by centre-backs Malick Thiaw and Jonathan Tah.

Rounding out the defence will be right-back Philipp Treu, who has enjoyed a strong club campaign with Freiburg, and Stuttgart left-back Maximilian Mittelstadt.

Joshua Kimmich will be joined by Bayern teammate Aleksandar Pavlovic at the base of Klopp's midfield, with Liverpool star Florian Wirtz hoping to build on his goal against Serbia from the number 10 role.

Either side of the £116m man should be RB Leipzig's Brajan Gruda - who boasts three assists and a goal across his last three games for club and country - and Freiburg's Derry Scherhant.

Arsenal's Kai Havertz looks set to lead the line once again for the hosts, keen to net his first strike of the Nations League campaign when the stakes are highest.

Germany possible starting lineup:.

Ter Stegen; Treu, Thiaw, Tah, Mittelstadt; Kimmich, Pavlovic; Gruda, Wirtz, Scherhant; Havertz.

Sources indicate that first linked by Matteo Moretto, his name has become more popular in reports linking the Rossoneri to defenders and he seems like a concrete target for the January mercato. Yet, it seems like it will be difficult to bring him to San Siro.

Speaking to MilanNews, Het Nieuwsblad journalist Tjorven Messiaen looked at Massire Sylla and what his future had in store.

In Italy, there’s been talk of AC Milan’s interest in Sylla. What’s being said about him in Belgium?

Sources indicate that “I saw that AC Milan have linked him with him. In Belgium, we discovered him through social media, and the USG hasn’t confirmed anything yet. It’s possible, however, that AC Milan has drawn attention to the boy, because he’s playing great football.

According to recent reports, “His move to AC Milan is unlikely to materialise in January, however, as both Sylla and the club would be more inclined to listen to offers from the Premier League. He’s the kind of player who would be a perfect fit for the English league.”.

What are his main strengths and best qualities?

In a recent development, “He’s young, he’s good in duels, he’s quick. He’s also very good at ball control. He’s a complete defender; he has the potential to become one of the best, and he’d be a perfect fit in the Premier League, which, among other things, is Sylla’s dream destination.”.

What aspects of his game still need improvement?

“It’s hard to say, especially since his growth in recent months has been impressive. I’d say he needs to gain more experience, which will come simply by playing. So I don’t see many things he needs to improve to take the next step in his career.”.

Do you think Union Saint-Gilloise (USG) would be willing to let him leave in January, or do you think any transfer discussions will be postponed until the summer?

According to recent reports, “I don’t think USG will let him leave in January. The only possible scenario, which I don’t think will happen, but which is the only solution anyway, is for USG to sign him in January but keep him at least until the end of the season, especially since the club never sells its best players in January.

“I also think interested clubs could spend a lot of money, but Union won’t let him leave in January.”.

Could you describe him in three adjectives?

“Quick, physical, and full of character, because he’s someone who always has problems when he has to make decisions.”.

Which defender would you compare him to?

“Considering his development, I’d say Pacho. He came from nowhere in Belgium, developed, moved to Frankfurt, and then ended up at PSG. In Sylla’s case, I think he’ll go straight to the Premier League. He has everything it takes to be perfect for this league.”.

He’s still very young. Do you think he’s ready to play for a big club in a big city like Milan?

Industry observers note that “He’s still very young, but he’s humble, calm, and we mustn’t forget that he arrived last year, in January, from the Norwegian second division. “I can’t imagine USG without Sylla today, especially since we’re talking about one of the best defenders in the league. And from what I know, several English clubs are already ready to make him a player.

“So AC Milan could give him a try, but it will require a big project and a lot of money.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Lewis Nolan | 15 Nov 2026 01:29.
  • Manchester City striker Erling Haaland has defended his choice to remain at Manchester City amid the fallout of their guilty verdict.
  • The Citizens were found guilty by an independent panel in September of breaching the Premier League's financial rules on an industrial scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Lewis Nolan | 15 Nov 2026 01:29.

Manchester City striker Erling Haaland has defended his choice to remain at Manchester City amid the fallout of their guilty verdict.

The Citizens were found guilty by an independent panel in September of breaching the Premier League's financial rules on an industrial scale.

A punishment has not yet been handed down, but there are fears among those associated with the club that sanctions could be as harsh as demotion.

It would be understandable if some players felt let down by City, who often expressed confidence that they would win their case.

Industry observers note that haaland revealed that he had no regrets about joining the club in 2022 and signing a newly introduced contract last year, telling TV2: "I assume the answers will come. I don’t know when. I haven’t read much about it. To be completely honest, I’m focused on trying to perform for Manchester City.

According to recent reports, "A club I signed a five-year deal with in 2022, and a new nine-and-a-half-year deal in late 2024. I think that says everything about the matter. I’m a City player and I’m incredibly happy there. I’d say I made a pretty good choice by joining City in 2022.

According to recent reports, "We can all agree on that. I would say so myself when I look at the trophies I’ve won and how I’ve developed on and off the pitch. I’m standing here after winning an international 3-1 and we're in the 1st seed pot for the Euro qualifiers. Things aren’t going so well for City in the league but we’ll try and turn that around against Fulham.".

Haaland signed a new contract until 2034 in January 2025, though it is not clear if he would seek a move away from the club should they be severely punished.

City could win an appeal later this year, but the likelihood of the club overturning their guilty verdict is reportedly small.

A demotion to the Championship or lower divisions raises the possibility of a mass exodus, especially if the players have clauses in their contracts that make exits easier in the event of relegation.

Haaland is arguably the best striker in the world, and the 26-year-old will not want to spend at least a year of his prime competing for promotion.

It would not be surprising if the likes of Phil Foden or Nico O'Reilly opted to stay at the Etihad given they came through the academy, but it is hard to see others such as Haaland remaining a City player.

City at the moment find themselves third in the Premier League table, with the team trailing Arsenal by six points after 10 matchweeks.

Enzo Maresca will no doubt be targeting the January transfer window as an opportunity to strengthen in order to close the gap to the Gunners.

However, potential targets may be reluctant about joining the club due to the real threat of sanctions, and that would make a title challenge difficult.

#2233. A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 78m • 📚 Deep Dive (15636 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 78 min read (15636 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~78 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • RNA-derived 2′,3′-cyclophosphate-terminated nucleotides act as immune signalling molecules in prokaryotes and eukaryotes1,2,3, but how plants perceive them remains unknown.
  • Insect pests cause losses to crop production and damage vegetation4,5.
  • According to recent reports, T2-family ribonuclease (RNaseT2) proteins, which preferentially cleave single-strand RNAs between purine and uridine residues, are ancient enzymes that are widely distributed across organisms and functional in diverse biological processes2,11.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

RNA-derived 2′,3′-cyclophosphate-terminated nucleotides act as immune signalling molecules in prokaryotes and eukaryotes1,2,3, but how plants perceive them remains unknown. Sucking insects inject digestive enzymes including RNases into the host plant to acquire nutrients. Here we demonstrate that NIB1, a glycine-rich RNA-binding protein in rice, senses 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide monophosphates (2′,3′-cNMPs; 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP) and adenylyl-(3′→5′)-guanosine 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate (ApG>p) produced by a salivary T2 ribonuclease of green stink bug during feeding. Binding of the RNase products promotes formation of nuclear condensates containing NIB1, which recruit the core immune regulator Enhanced Disease Susceptibility 1 (EDS1) and activate defence, potentially contributing to the immune signalling of Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) proteins that also produce the nuclease products. Exogenous application of 2′,3′-cAMP, 2′,3′-cGMP or ApG>p elicits NIB1 and EDS1-mediated immune responses. Our findings unveil a conserved pathway in plants, in which glycine-rich RNA-binding proteins perceive the nuclease-generated second messengers to launch defence and point to a potential link between plant TIR nuclease activity and EDS1 signalling.

Insect pests cause losses to crop production and damage vegetation4,5. During feeding, insects release oral secretions containing proteins and other molecules that can activate or suppress host plant defence6,7,8. Digestive enzymes hydrolyse cellular components to generate nutrients for herbivores. These breakdown products also act as host-derived damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that activate plant pattern-recognition receptors9,10. Identifying host-derived signalling molecules and their defence activation mechanisms is essential for developing fresh plant-protection strategies.

According to recent reports, T2-family ribonuclease (RNaseT2) proteins, which preferentially cleave single-strand RNAs between purine and uridine residues, are ancient enzymes that are widely distributed across organisms and functional in diverse biological processes2,11. Plant S-RNases, which mediate self-incompatibility, belong to this protein family12. Phytopathogens also secrete nucleases into host tissues13,14. Human lysosomal RNaseT2 generates purine-2′,3′-cyclophosphate-terminated oligoribonucleotides that are sensed by Toll-like receptor 8 to activate innate immunity2. Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domains of plant intracellular nucleotide-binding and leucine-rich repeat (NLR) immune receptors possess enzymatic activities towards oxidized nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) and nucleic acids15,16,17,18,19. Plant TIR domains generate second messengers such as 2′-ADPR and pRib-AMP, which promote the formation of EDS1–Phytoalexin Deficient 4 (PAD4)–Activated Disease Resistance 1 (ADR1) complex and trigger disease resistance15,20,21. Activated plant TIR also catalyses the production of ADPr-ATP and di-ADPR, leading to the complex formation of EDS1-Senescence-Associated Gene 101 (SAG101)–N Required Gene 1 (NRG1), inducing plant cell death16,22,23. Plant TIR domains also synthesize 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP (2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP) through nuclease activity. Arabidopsis nudix hydrolase 7 (AtNUDT7) hydrolyses 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and attenuates TIR-mediated cell death when overexpressed in Nicotiana benthamiana3. However, the contribution of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP to EDS1-dependent immunity remains elusive.

It has been revealed that plant glycine-rich RNA-binding proteins (GRPs) encompassing one RNA recognition motif (RRM) at the N terminus and a glycine-rich region (GRR) at the C terminus regulate plant responses to abiotic and biotic stresses24,25. Arabidopsis GRP7 (AtGRP7) has a positive role in immunity, whereas the Pseudomonas syringae effector HopU1 suppresses AtGRP7-mediaed immunity by catalysing ADP-ribosylation of an arginine residue (R49) in the RRM of AtGRP726,27,28. These data indicate that the RRM of GRPs is central to immune function, although the underlying molecular mechanism remains unidentified. Here we report that the rice GRP NIB1 interacts with invading insect T2 RNases (such as NVR1) to promote ribonuclease activity and the production of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p. Binding to the cyclic nucleotides via RMM stimulates NIB1 phase separation to assemble the plant defence machinery in the nucleus.

According to recent reports, nezara viridula (the green stink bug) is a polyphagous hemipteran pest feeding on a wide range of plants, including economically important food, fruit and vegetable crops and Nicotiana species. Populations of N. viridula have recently increased in rice fields. As a piercing-sucking mesophyll feeder (Fig. 1a), N. viridula uses needle-like stylets to puncture developing seeds or young leaves, extract nutrients and inject effectors29. To identify the secretory enzymes, we profiled proteins in its oral secretions using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) and identified 22 putative digestive enzymes, of which 15 were likely to be secretory based on signal peptide prediction (SignalP 3.0 server) and de-redundancy (Blastp) (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Transient expression of these proteins in N. benthamiana leaves identified one candidate enzyme that induced severe cell death and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production within 3 days post-agroinfiltration (dpi) (Extended Data Fig. 1b,c). This protein shows high sequence similarity to ribonuclease and we named it N. viridula ribonuclease 1 (NVR1).

Recent findings suggest that NVR1 was predicted to have an N-terminal secretory signal peptide and no transmembrane region. Analysis using the protein family database (Pfam) revealed a ribonuclease (RNase) domain (Fig. 1b) that belongs to the RNaseT2 family11. NVR1 was detected both in N. viridula salivary glands and in infested rice plants, suggesting that it is secreted into plant tissues during feeding (Extended Data Fig. 1d). NVR1 exhibited a nucleocytoplasmic distribution pattern (Extended Data Fig. 1e).

Industry observers note that H64 and H116 are conserved among T2 RNases from mammals, herbivorous insects, phytopathogenic fungi and plants (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1f). NVR1 cleaved Cy5-labelled Arabidopsis tRNASer (83 nt) in vitro, whereas NVR1(H116A) and NVR1(H64A) mutants revealed mild and strong reductions in substrate degradation, respectively, and the double mutant NVR1(H-doub) was almost completely inactivated (Fig. 1d), supporting H64 and H116 as key catalytic residues11. High-resolution mass spectrometry was subsequently used to identify products of the NVR1-catalysed reaction, which showed accumulation of 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP, as well as a dinucleotide-2′,3′-cyclophosphate with a mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of 675.1072 in positive mode (Fig. 1e,f). Given that preferentially cleavage of single-stranded RNA between purines and uridines by RNaseT2 produces guanosine or adenosine 2′,3′-cyclophosphate termini2, we designed two oligoribonucleotides, (UAGU)5 and (UGAU)5, as substrates to determine the structure of the product. NVR1 exhibited activity towards (UAGU)5—but not towards (UGAU)5—generating a peak at 5.1 min in the extracted ion chromatogram mode that was identical to the dinucleotide-2′,3′-cyclophosphate peak at m/z 675.1072, suggesting that NVR1 produced 2′,3′-cGMP-terminated AMP (ApG>p). The ApG>p synthetic standard, eluting at 5.1 min with a m/z of 675.1072 in positive mode, aligns with the NVR1 product (Fig. 1f) and matches the tandem mass (MS2) spectrum (Extended Data Fig. 1g). The accumulation of 2′,3′- cAMP/cGMP and ApG>P was rapidly induced in rice leaves within 2 h after insect feeding (Fig. 1g).

The 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p synthase activity of NVR1 was dependent on the two catalytic histidines H64 and H116 (Fig. 1h). High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)–mass spectrometry and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI) analysis indicated that N. benthamiana leaves expressing empty vector or catalytic inactive NVR1 mutants accumulated much less 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p than leaves expressing wild-type NVR1 (Fig. 1i and Extended Data Fig. 1h). Leaves expressing NVR1 mutants were impaired in inducing plant cell death (Fig. 1j and Extended Data Fig. 1i). AtNUDT7 hydrolysed 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p (Fig. 1k). Co-expression with AtNUDT7 attenuated cell death activity of NVR1 in N. benthamiana at 3 dpi, with necrosis completed at 6 dpi (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 1j,k). These results indicate that the NVR1 enzymatic activity was causative to plant cell death.

According to recent reports, to investigate plant responses to pest RNase, we generated rice NVR1-GFP transgenic plants that overexpress NVR1–GFP (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis revealed that genes associated with biotic stimulus, jasmonic acid and defence were significantly enriched in NVR1-expressing plants (Extended Data Fig. 2c). MYC2, NPR1, COI1 and ERF1 (Fig. 1m and Extended Data Fig. 2d) were upregulated and levels of jasmonic acid and salicylic acid levels increased (Extended Data Fig. 2e). The Cnaphalocrocis medinalis ribonuclease 1 (CMR1), an NVR1 orthologue expressed by Cnaphalocrocis medinalis—a lepidopteran pest of rice—was detected in oral secretions and also produced 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP (Extended Data Fig. 2f,g), congruent with the rice leaf-feeding data (Fig. 1g). Given this functional conservation, we evaluated the resistance of NVR1 transgenic lines to C. medinalis. The larvae gained less weight on NVR1-expressing plants than on controls (Extended Data Fig. 2h). Adult females laid fewer eggs on NVR1 transgenic lines, and larvae preferred feeding on control plants (Extended Data Fig. 2i,j).

In a recent development, NVR1-expressing plants were stunted and produced fewer tillers, phenotypes associated with the growth cost of constitutive defence activation, whereas rice plants expressing catalytically inactive NVR1(H-doub) did not upregulate defence genes and grew normally (Fig. 1n and Extended Data Fig. 2k,l). These results demonstrate that heterologous expression of NVR1 in rice elicited defence responses and enhanced plant resistance to insect feeding, and that NVR1 catalytic activity is essential for immune activation.

Industry observers note that to uncover the molecular mechanisms underpinning the NVR1-induced plant defence response, we screened plant proteins that could bind to NVR1 by immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry (IP–MS). NVR1-interacting RNA-binding protein 1 (NIB1 (Os03t0670700-04), also known as OsGRP330,31) showed a strong interaction signal (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). NIB1 is a GRP composed of an N-terminal RRM and a C-terminal GRR and shares 80% N-terminal sequence identity with AtGRP726,27 (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Microscale thermophoresis (MST) indicated that NIB1 interacted directly with NVR1 in vitro (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3d), and co-immunoprecipitation confirmed the interaction in planta (Fig. 2b).

In a recent development, split luciferase complementation (SLC) highlighted that the NIB1 RRM, but not the GRR, interacted with NVR1 (Extended Data Fig. 3e), matching the MST data (Fig. 2a). AlphaFold2 predicted the RRM residue R22 as a contact site (Extended Data Fig. 3f), and the NIB1(R22A) mutant abolished the interaction in planta (Extended Data Fig. 3g). NVR1 interacted strongly with NIB1, independently of its catalytic activity (Extended Data Fig. 3h–j).

Industry observers note that given that NVR1-like secretory T2 ribonucleases are widespread in insects and phytopathogenic fungi (Extended Data Fig. 1f), and GRPs are conserved across land plants (Extended Data Fig. 3k), we investigated whether the RNaseT2–GRP interaction is a common phenomenon. We tested secreted RNases T2 from the insect pests C. medinalis (CMR1) and Helicoverpa armigera (HAR1) and the fungal pathogen Magnaporthe oryzae (MOR1). SLC assays demonstrated that the recognition of T2-family RNases by plant GRPs is universal (Extended Data Fig. 3l,m).

Given that GRPs bind RNA fragments27 and NVR1 requires its RNase activity to elicit defence, we investigated the potential binding of NIB1 to the RNaseT2 products. NIB1–GST was incubated with NVR1 products, denatured to extract the bound molecules, and analysed by high-resolution mass spectrometry. Notably, high-intensity signals of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p were observed (Fig. 2c). Structural modelling of NIB1 with ligands identified two adjoining residues in RRM domain loop, R49 and G50 that were responsible for 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP recognition (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 4a). R49 is a known RNA-binding site27, whereas G50 contacts both 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP in our model. G14 and W17 serve as additional recognition sites for ApG>p (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 4a). In MST assays with 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p, NHS-labelled NIB1 exhibited high binding affinity. Substitution of either residue with alanine (NIB1(R49A) or NIB1(G50A)) markedly reduced the binding affinity, and the NIB1(R49A/G50A/G14A/W17A) (hereafter NIB1(4A)) mutation fully abolished the ApG>p binding (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 3d). G14, W17, R49 and G50 are highly conserved in a group of GRPs across land plants (Extended Data Fig. 3n), implying a critical role of these residues in ligand recognition. The NIB1(R49A) mutation impaired NIB1 binding to both RNA and 2′,3-cyclic nucleotides, whereas the NIB1(G50A) mutant maintained binding affinity towards FLAGELLIN SENSITIVE2 (FLS2) 3′ untranslated region (UTR) while showing strongly impaired binding to 2′,3-cyclic nucleotides (Extended Data Fig. 4b). Thus, NIB1 employs shared yet distinct recognition mechanisms for 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and RNA.

In MST assays using 2′,3′-cAMP as a positive control, NIB1 did not bind 3′,5′-cAMP, 8-Br-3′,5′-cAMP, AMP or 2′,3′-cGAMP32 (Extended Data Fig. 4c–g). NIB1 exhibited 4-fold and 34-fold weaker binding affinities for 3′,5′-cGMP and GMP, respectively, compared with 2′,3′-cGMP (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 4h,i).

It has been revealed that NIB1 contains a C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) (Extended Data Fig. 5a) that mediates phase separation33. PONDR predicted a high average disorder score similar to that of AtGRP7 (Extended Data Fig. 5b). In vitro, NIB1–YFP formed droplets that demonstrated fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) and fused to form larger droplets (Extended Data Fig. 5c–e). NIB1–YFP signals also recovered after photobleaching in N. benthamiana leaves (Extended Data Fig. 5f).

Industry observers note that to determine whether herbivory induces NIB1 condensation in planta, we generated two pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/ZH11 rice lines (Extended Data Fig. 5g). Following 6 h of feeding by third-instar C. medinalis larvae, distinct NIB1 nuclear condensates were clearly visualized (Fig. 2f), indicating that this phase separation is a physiologically relevant response to herbivory. Similar to the observations in vitro and in N. benthamiana nuclei, NIB1–YFP condensates in pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/ZH11 nuclei recovered fluorescence after photobleaching (Extended Data Fig. 5h).

It has been revealed that we further analysed the interplay between NVR1 catalytic activity and NIB1 condensation. Wild-type NIB1–YFP, but not the C-terminal IDR-truncated NIB1(ΔIDR)–YFP, absorbed NVR1–mCherry into the droplets (Extended Data Fig. 5i–k). The droplets of purified NIB1–YFP protein with nucleic acid contamination, but not that of nucleic acid-free NIB1–YFP, were enlarged in the presence of NVR1–mCherry, whereas the catalytically inactive NVR1(H-doub)–mCherry did not exert such effect (Extended Data Fig. 5i–k). NIB1–YFP exhibited nucleoplasmic localization, and NVR1 significantly enhanced its nuclear accumulation, with about 70% of the examined nuclei containing distinct condensates. N-terminal YFP-tagged NIB1 highlighted a similar localization pattern (Extended Data Fig. 5l–n). Immunoblotting further confirmed that NVR1 promoted nuclear accumulation of NIB1 (Extended Data Fig. 5o). Nuclear condensates were not observed for the NIB1–NVR1(H-doub) or NIB1(ΔIDR)–NVR1 (Fig. 2g), revealing that the RNase activity of NVR1 is crucial for promoting NIB1 phase separation in the nucleus. In subsequent analyses, we focused on nuclear NIB1 condensates.

Multivalent interactions drive phase separation and locally concentrate molecules, as in dsDNA-dependent cGAS activation and NAD+/ATP-dependent plant TIR activation32,34. We investigated whether 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p would induce NIB1 phase separation. The NIB1(R49A)–YFP and NIB1(G50A)–YFP droplets were smaller than NIB1–YFP droplets with or without NVR1–mCherry (Extended Data Fig. 6a). When co-expressed with NVR1 in N. benthamiana, NIB1(R49A), NIB1(G50A) and NIB1(4A) did not generate sparkling nuclear condensates (Extended Data Fig. 6b), implying that NIB1 phase separation involves binding of 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p. Congruently, 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p (2 nM each) promoted NIB1 phase separation in vitro (Fig. 2h and Extended Data Fig. 6c,d), and treatment with 8-Br-2′,3′-cNMP or ApG>p increased nuclear condensates in N. benthamiana cells (Fig. 2i,j and Extended Data Fig. 6e). Notably, exogenous application of 50 µM 8-Br-2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p for 6 h induced distinct nuclear condensates in the pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/ZH11 rice plant (Fig. 2k and Extended Data Fig. 6f), indicating that 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p act as agonists of NIB1 in promoting phase separation.

We further monitored NIB1–YFP condensation in N. benthamiana leaves upon treatment with nucleotide analogues. Consistent with findings from MST (Extended Data Fig. 4c–g), 3′,5′-cAMP, 8-Br-3′,5′-cAMP, AMP and 2′3′-cGAMP did not trigger condensate formation, whereas 3′,5′-cGMP and GMP induced far fewer condensates than 2′,3′-cAMP (Extended Data Fig. 6g,h). Co-incubation with NVR1, rice plant RNA (OsRNA) and 2′,3′-cAMP resulted in larger NIB1–YFP droplets in vitro, which required the NVR1 catalytic activity, NIB1 binding sites and 2′,3′-cAMP to achieve optimal effect (Extended Data Fig. 6i). In vitro reconstitutions revealed that NIB1–YFP formed droplets, dependent on 2′,3′-cAMP, OsRNA and salt, as well as protein and macromolecular crowding agent concentrations (Extended Data Fig. 6j–m).

To investigate the biochemical consequences of NIB1 liquid–liquid phase separation, we examined its effect on NVR1 enzymatic activity. NVR1 was more active in the presence of NIB1, and the substrate degradation increased with higher concentrations of NIB1 (Fig. 3a). When the C-terminal IDR-containing fragment was deleted (NIB1(ΔIDR)), the influence of NIB1 on NVR1 activity was reduced or negligible (Fig. 3b), suggesting that the IDR steers NIB1 to boost the NVR1 enzymatic activity. Consistently, the NVR1–NIB1 complex synthesized a higher amount of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p than NVR1 alone, which also required the IDR in NIB1 for increased activity (Fig. 3c). Similarly, when co-expressed in N. benthamiana leaves, full-length NIB1 significantly enhanced NVR1 in generating 2′,3′-cNMP compared with NIB1(ΔIDR) (Extended Data Fig. 6n). We subsequently evaluated the effect of NIB1 on NVR1-induced cell death in N. benthamiana and found that removing the IDR from NIB1 largely abrogated its potentiation of NVR1-induced plant cell death (Extended Data Fig. 6o,p). Additionally, the NIB1(R49A) and NIB1(G50A) mutants also showed compromised acceleration of NVR1 catalysis (Fig. 3d) and the NVR1-induced plant cell death (Extended Data Fig. 6q,r). In sum, catalytically active NVR1 stimulates NIB1 phase separation, which in turn enhances NVR1 activity in degrading RNA and synthesizing 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p, thereby inducing plant cell death through a positive feedback loop. In this mutual potentiation interaction, NIB1 uses both the IDR and the RNA-binding sites in the RRM to amplify and transduce NVR1-generated signalling molecules.

NIB1 is highly expressed in multiple rice tissues (Extended Data Fig. 7a). To investigate the NIB1 function in plant defence, we used CRISPR–Cas9 to generate NIB1-knockout (NIB1-KO) and NIB1-overexpression (NIB1-OE) rice lines (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 7b–d). NIB1-OE and NVR1-OE plants revealed similar transcriptional changes, with 553 (59%) of the upregulated genes overlapping (Fig. 4b), including genes associated with response to biotic stimulus, jasmonic acid and defence (Fig. 4c). MYC2, NPR1, COI1 and ERF1 were downregulated in NIB1-KO plants but markedly upregulated in NIB1-OE plants (Extended Data Fig. 7e), consistent with the RNA-seq data and the levels of defence hormones salicylic acid and jasmonic acid (Fig. 4d). C. medinalis larvae gained more weight after feeding on the NIB1-KO lines than with the wild-type plants; by contrast, their growth was retarded on the NIB1-OE plants (Fig. 4e). Females and larvae preferred NIB1-KO over wild-type and NIB1-OE plants in oviposition and feeding-choice assays (Extended Data Fig. 7f,g). Insect feeding strongly induced MYC2 in wild-type rice, but the induction was much weaker in the NIB1-KO mutant (Fig. 4f). NIB1-OE plants had reduced tillering, partly resembling the NVR1-OE phenotype (Extended Data Fig. 2l), whereas NIB1-KO plants grew well and produced more tillers (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 7h), probably reflecting their differences in immune intensity. These results suggest that NIB1 positively regulates plant defence responses.

We next investigated whether the NVR1-induced plant defence responses were contingent on the presence of NIB1. Treatment of rice plants with purified NVR1 induced ROS production, which was attenuated in NIB1-KO lines (Fig. 4g). Consistently, NVR1-induced cell death was mitigated in NbGRP7-KO leaves compared with wild-type N. benthamiana (Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 7i,j). Thus, the RNA-binding protein NIB1 mediates NVR1-dependent induction of plant defence response.

According to recent reports, to further determine whether NIB1 senses 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p to mediate NVR1-induced immune activation, we generated overexpression complementation lines in NIB1-KO rice plants, including wild-type NIB1, NIB1R49A and NIB1G50A. The two recognition-deficient complementation lines were unable to rescue the immune responses in NIB1-KO mutants, as indicated by defence hormone accumulation (Fig. 4i), insect resistance (Fig. 4j and Extended Data Fig. 8a,b) and the expression of MYC2, COI1 and NPR1 (Extended Data Fig. 8c). Expression of NIB1R49A and NIB1G50A in wild-type rice plants did not lead to a clear upregulation of these defence genes (Extended Data Fig. 8d,e). Together, these results show that NIB1 activates plant defence against insect feeding and that sensing of 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p is crucial for this immune function of NIB1.

Sources indicate that MST assays with NIB1(ΔIDR) exhibited similar binding affinity to 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>P as wild-type NIB1 (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 8f). However, overexpression of NIB1(ΔIDR)–YFP in NIB1-KO rice plants did not rescue the compromised insect resistance (Fig. 4k). Moreover, treatment with 50 µM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP induced condensate formation in pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/NIB1-KO plants but not in 35S::NIB1ΔIDR-YFP/NIB1-KO plants (Extended Data Fig. 8g,h). Thus, both ligand recognition via RRM and subsequent phase separation via IDR are essential for the NIB1-dependent defence response.

Recent findings suggest that to connect the NVR1–NIB1 module to the plant defence network, we performed IP–MS on leaves co-expressing NIB1–YFP and NVR1. EDS1, CDPK and MAPK6 were identified as NIB1 interactors (Extended Data Fig. 9a). Comparison with the NVR1 interactome revealed that the shared components were enriched in herbivore-response pathways (Extended Data Fig. 9b).

Industry observers note that EDS1 is a central immune signalling node35,36,37. In SLC assays, NIB1 interacted with rice EDS1 (Extended Data Fig. 9c). EDS1–YFP co-immunoprecipitated with NIB1–Flag in N. benthamiana (Fig. 5a), and His–NIB1 pulled down EDS1–Flag from N. benthamiana leaves (Extended Data Fig. 9d). Bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) assays indicated that NIB1 interacted with EDS1 in the nucleus (Extended Data Fig. 9e), and the NIB1–EDS1 interaction was enhanced by NVR1 via its RNase activity (Fig. 5b). Catalytically active NVR1, but not the inactive NVR1(H-doub) mutant, stimulated NIB1 recruitment of EDS1 into sparkly nuclear condensates (Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 9f). We then used EDS1–NES–mCherry to test whether EDS1 acts as a nuclear carrier for NIB1. When EDS1–NES–mCherry was largely retained in the cytosol, NIB1 continued to form nuclear condensates in the presence of NVR1 (Extended Data Fig. 9g), indicating that NIB1 nuclear condensation is independent of EDS1 and supporting the role of NIB1 as a scaffold for EDS1 recruitment.
