Right, NIB1 and EDS1 partition coefficients with empty vector, NVR1 or NVR1(H-doub). mCh, mCherry. d, Salicylic acid and jasmonic acid contents in ZH11 and eds1 leaves. e, MYC2 expression in CR-eds1 leaves with or without 6 h of C. medinalis feeding (ZH11 set to 1). f, Decreased resistance in eds1 plants, evaluated by C. medinalis larvae weight after 3 days of feeding. g, RT–qPCR of PR1 and MYC2 in ZH11 leaves, NIB1-OE ZH11 leaves and NIB1-OE CR-eds1 leaves. h, PR1 and MYC2 expression in wild-type, NIB1-KO and CR-eds1 leaves 6 h after treatment with water, 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP, ApG>p or 8-Br-AMP (50 μM each). i, NbPR1 and NbMYC2 expression in wild-type, NbGRP7 and epss leaves 6 h after treatment with water or 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP. j,k, Spraying 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP enhanced plant insect resistance in the laboratory (j) and the paddy field (k), as indicated by growth of C. medinalis third-instar larvae fed with water- or 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP-treated ZH11 plants. l, A proposed model of GRP in the plant defence response to insect oral secretory RNaseT2. Data are mean ± s.d. n = 3 biologically independent samples (d,e,g–i); n = 6 (b) or 8 (c, middle) nuclei; n = 20 condensates (c, right); n = 11 (f) or 12 (j,k) larvae. Results in a represent three independent experiments; experiments in j,k were repeated twice. Statistical differences were analysed by two-tailed t-test (d–f,j,k); one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (b,c,g); or two-way ANOVA with the two-stage linear step-up procedure of Benjamini, Krieger and Yekutieli (h,i). Scale bars, 10 μm (b) and 5 μm (c).

Sources indicate that the rice CR-eds1 mutant generated by CRISPR–Cas9 accumulated lower levels of jasmonic acid and salicylic acid (Fig. 5d) and expressed lower levels of COI1, NPR1 and ERF1 (Extended Data Fig. 9h–j). The induction of MYC2 expression in response to insect feeding was minimal in the rice CR-eds1 mutant (Fig. 5e). CR-eds1 plants were more vulnerable to C. medinalis (Fig. 5f and Extended Data Fig. 9k,l), demonstrating a vital role of rice EDS1 in insect resistance.

The immune activation phenotype of NIB1 overexpression was highly attenuated in the rice eds1-KO mutant and NIB1-triggered induction of defence genes PR1, MYC2, COI1, NPR1 and ERF1 was diminished in CR-eds1 rice plants (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 9m,n). Treatment with 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p induced the expression of PR1 and MYC2 in rice leaves, but this induction was compromised in NIB1-KO and CR-eds1 plants (Fig. 5h). Similarly, 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP treatment upregulated NbPR1 and NbMYC2 expression in wild-type N. benthamiana but not in NbGRP7-KO or N. benthamiana epss (eds1a, pad4, sag101a, sag101b) mutants (Fig. 5i). RNA-seq analyses of N. benthamiana wild-type, NbGRP7-KO and N. benthamiana epss leaves treated with 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP showed that the differential gene expression observed in wild-type N. benthamiana was largely absent in NbGRP7-KO and N. benthamiana epss mutants (Extended Data Fig. 9o,p). The upregulated genes were predominantly enriched in defence pathways (Extended Data Fig. 9q). These data demonstrate that EDS1 and NIB1 are important signalling components for the immune function of 2′,3′-cAMP.

Herbivore-induced endogenous 2′,3′-cAMP concentration reached around 21 μM in rice (Fig. 1g), comparable to the 50 μM concentration used in our assays. Treating N. benthamiana leaves with 21 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP for 6 h upregulated NbPR1 and NbMYC2 to similar levels as the 50 µM 2′,3′-cAMP treatment. Thus, the herbivore-induced endogenous accumulation of 2′,3′-cAMP is physiologically sufficient to elicit defence responses (Extended Data Fig. 9r). Exogenous application of 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP via spray significantly enhanced plant resistance against herbivory under both laboratory and paddy field conditions (Fig. 5j,k and Extended Data Fig. 9s).

Given that plant TIR proteins function as 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP synthases3, we tested whether the TIR-induced immunity also involves NIB1 or the orthologous GRP by expressing the TIR domain of Arabidopsis RPS4 (RPS4TIR) in NbGRP7-KO lines. Arabidopsis RPS4TIR-induced cell death in NbGRP7-KO leaves indicated slight attenuation at 36 h post-infiltration (hpi) but became obvious and complete by 56 hpi (Extended Data Fig. 10a–c). The cell death triggered by the rice TIR-only protein OsTIR was also slightly attenuated in the NbGRP7/NbGRP8-KO mutants when observed at 40 hpi (Extended Data Fig. 10d–g), with obvious cell death and completion at 68 hpi (Extended Data Fig. 10h). These results suggested a general role of GRP in sensing the 2′,3′-cyclophosphate-terminated mono- and dinucleotides. In sum, our results show that GRPs sense the nuclease products of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p, contributing to the activation of the EDS1-dependent signalling pathway (Fig. 5l).

Sources indicate that plants express many cell-surface and intracellular immune receptors to perceive alien molecules and activate defence38,39. Here we found that the rice GRP NIB1 interacts with invading RNaseT2 and senses 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p to induce plant defence. The presence of NVR1 orthologues in oral secretions of the piercing-sucking pest Apolygus lucorum (ALR1; data not shown) and chewing insect C. medinalis suggests that T2-family ribonuclease effectors are conserved across divergent feeding types and may be a broadly deployed strategy in plant–insect interactions. Given the involvement of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP in abiotic stresses40,41,42,43, it is worth further investigating the role of GRPs in leveraging biotic and abiotic stresses. Whether and how plants discriminate between different sources of second messengers are also notable questions to address.

Condensates or membraneless compartments are engaged in a variety of plant developmental and stress response processes44,45,46,47. NIB1, as a sensor, perceives 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p and forms nuclear condensates that recruit the core immune regulator EDS135,36,37 and activate downstream signalling pathways, highlighting protein phase separation as a mechanism in response to second messengers. Our study focuses on the immune function of nuclear NIB1, whereas the biological roles of its cytoplasmic condensates deserve future investigation. Exogenous spraying of these RNA degradation-derived signalling molecules triggered plant defence responses, highlighting their application potential as immune activators. Our study opens a door for exploring the engagement of RNase products in plant defence, adaptation and development.

Industry observers note that plant TIR-catalysed and NAD+-derived products induces formation of EDS1–SAG101–NRG1 and EDS1–PAD4–ADR1 heterotrimers, as well as oligomerization of ADR1 and NRG1 as calcium channels at the plasma membrane, to confer immunity. The link between TIR nuclease-derived 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and EDS1 remains unclear, and the nuclear function of EDS1 in TIR-mediated immunity is unknown. Our unpublished data show that 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP does not contribute to the EDS1–SAG101–NRG1 or EDS1–PAD4–ADR1 heterotrimer formation, consistent with the proposed role of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP in amplifying rather than initiating TIR signalling3. In bacteria, 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP have been shown to modulate activities of transcription factors48. 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP-induced NIB1 condensate in the nucleus recruits EDS1 to trigger defence, potentially via transcriptional modulation, providing a possible explanation for the biological relevance of plant TIR nuclease activity. Plant TIR-only proteins but not TIR–NLR receptors possess nuclease activity—thus, TIR nuclease activity and 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP are likely to be involved in TIR-only-mediated basal immunity but not TIR–NLR-mediated effector-triggered immunity3,49, consistent with the weak contribution of GRPs towards TIR-induced cell death phenotypes in N. benthamiana. The T2 RNase NVR1 produces ApG>p, and the nuclease product spectrum of plant TIR-only proteins awaits further studies. Future studies could investigate whether other GRPs are also involved in perceiving such nuclease products and their interactions. Detailed analyses of NIB1 condensate components will add valuable knowledge to understanding this nuclease-based defence pathway.

Sources indicate that phytophagous insects, especially mesophyll feeders, generate various small molecules from biopolymers by injecting digestive enzymes into plant tissues, in addition to mechanical injury. Detection of DAMPs is essential for plants to activate defence programmes. Although the wide-scale cultivation of transgenic crops expressing Bacillus thuringiensis insecticidal proteins has effectively controlled the lepidopteran chewing insects in the field, heteropteran mesophyll feeders such as the mirid bug A. lucorum (Miridae) and the green stink bug N. viridula (Pentatomidae), are less sensitive to these proteins and are emerging as a threat to agriculture50. Our findings show that plant GRP is a sensor of the invading RNase products and orchestrates immune responses to activate an EDS1-dependent signalling pathway, providing a potential target for advanced plant protection technologies.

Rice plants (Oryza sativa L. subsp. japonica cv. ZH11) grown in experimental fields in Shanghai or Hainan, or under controlled greenhouse conditions, were used for stable transformation and CRISPR–Cas9-mediated gene knockout. To generate overexpression lines, the cDNAs of NVR1 and NIB1 (transcript ID: Os03t0670700-04) were introduced into the pCAMBIA1300 vector under the control of the CaMV 35S promoter, or as indicated. DNA sequences were analysed using SnapGene 6.0.2. Following transformation, more than ten independent overexpression lines were obtained for both NVR1 and NIB1. The NIB1-KO rice mutants, as well as N. benthamiana NbGRP7-KO plants, were generated by WIMI Biotechnology. NbGRP7/NbGRP8-KO lines were generated by Wuhan BioRun Biosciences. For transient expression assays, leaves from 4-week-old N. benthamiana plants grown in a greenhouse at 22 °C under long-day conditions (16 h light:8 h dark) with a photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD) of 112.81 μmol m−2 s−1.

N. viridula was collected from the Hangzhou farm, Zhejiang Academy of Agricultural Sciences, and reared on kidney beans and corn in a growth chamber at ~28 °C. C. medinalis was at first collected from the experimental farm in Songjiang, Shanghai, China in 2022. To maintain genetic homogeneity and sensitivity, the insects were continuously laboratory-reared for more than 15 generations without pesticide exposure. Larvae were reared on fresh wheat seedlings, and adults were supplied with a 15% honey solution. The colony was maintained under strictly controlled conditions at 26 °C with 12 h light:12 h dark photoperiod.

N. viridula saliva was collected using a Parafilm sachet feeding assay. Following a 24-h starvation period, 20 adult N. viridula were supplied with 1 ml of 2.5% sucrose solution encapsulated within Parafilm membranes. After 24 h of feeding, the saliva-containing sucrose solution was collected and concentrated using Amicon Ultra-0.5 centrifugal filter devices (Millipore). Salivary proteins were mixed with 4× SDS loading buffer, denatured at 95 °C for 10 min, and separated by SDS–PAGE. The salivary proteome was subsequently analysed via LC–MS/MS (Novogene) (Supplementary Table 1).

The constructed vectors were introduced into A. tumefaciens strain GV3101 (pSoup-p19). After cultivation in medium at 30 °C overnight, the bacteria were collected and resuspended in infiltration buffer (10 mM MgCl2, 10 mM MES, 150 μM acetosyringone, pH 5.8), and incubated at room temperature for 2–3 h. The bacterial suspensions were adjusted to OD600 = 0.6 and infiltrated to the leaves of 4-week N. benthamiana with needleless syringe. For co-expression, equal volumes of Agrobacterium suspensions (adjusted to an OD600 of 1.0) carrying the respective constructs were mixed for co-infiltration.

According to recent reports, the protein coding sequences for His- and GST-tagged proteins were cloned into pColdTF/pET-28a and pGEX-4T vectors, respectively, and expressed in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) pLysS cells. Cultures were grown in LB medium at 37 °C to OD600 of 0.5, followed by induction with 0.5 mM IPTG at 15 °C for 16 h. Cells were collected, lysed by sonification in lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, pH 8.0) and centrifuged at 20,000g for 30 min at 4 °C. For His-tagged proteins, the supernatant was loaded onto Ni-NTA resin, washed with a wash buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 10 mM imidazole, pH 8.0), and subsequently eluted with an elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole, pH 8.0). For the purification of GST-tagged proteins, the supernatant was incubated with Glutathione Sepharose 4B resin, washed with lysis buffer (140 mM NaCl, 27 mM KCl, 10 mM Na2HPO4, 1.8 mM KH2PO4), and eluted with the same buffer supplemented with 10 mM reduced glutathione. To obtain nucleic acid-free NIB1–YFP, recombinant protein-expressing E. coli cells were collected and resuspended in cold TBS (20 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, pH 7.6) at 9 ml per gram of wet cells. TieChui E. coli Lysis Buffer (ACE Biotechnology) was added at one-ninth of the suspension volume, followed by incubation at 4 °C for 10 min to lyse the cells and digest bacterial DNA and RNA. After centrifugation at 20,000g at 4 °C, the clarified supernatant was subjected to affinity purification.

It has been revealed that to investigate potential protein–protein interactions, coding sequences were cloned into JW772-35S-cLUC or JW771-35S-nLUC. The constructs were introduced into Agrobacterium GV3101 (pSoup-p19), and the bacterial cultures were co-infiltrated into N. benthamiana leaves as described above. After 48 h of transformation, fluorescence was detected and imaged using the Tanon Chemi Dog 5200T Imaging System to visualize protein interactions.

The interacting protein candidates were co-expressed in N. benthamiana leaves for 48 h. The leaves were collected, homogenized in liquid nitrogen and suspended in IP lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, 20% glycerol, 0.5% NP-40, 1×protease inhibitor cocktail). The mixture was centrifuged at 14,000g for 10 min. The supernatant was incubated with GFP magnetic beads for 2 h at 4 °C and then washed 5 times in IP lysis buffer. Beads were boiled at 95 °C in 50 μl 4× SDS loading buffer for 10 min and analysed by immunoblotting. Measurements were repeatedly taken from separate lysates to confirm repeatability.

Sources indicate that for immunoblotting, proteins were separated by 4–20% SDS–PAGE and transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes. After blocking with 5% (w/v) non-fat milk, the membranes were incubated with the following primary antibodies: mouse anti-DDK (Flag) monoclonal antibody (ZSGB-BIO, TA-05, clone OTI11C3, lot no. 230021225; 1:2,000), mouse anti-His monoclonal antibody (OriGene, TA150088, clone OTI2B5; 1:5,000), mouse anti-plant actin monoclonal antibody (ABclonal, AC009, clone AMC0496, lot no. 9100009001; 1:5,000), horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated rabbit anti-Myc-tag monoclonal antibody (ABclonal, AE102, clone ARC5004-12-HRP, lot no. 3523030201; 1:5,000), rabbit anti-GFP-tag polyclonal antibody (ABclonal, AE011, clone N/A, lot no. 3560104011, RRID: AB_2771922; 1:2,000), rabbit anti-β-actin monoclonal antibody (ABclonal, AC026, clone ARC5115-01; 1:10,000), rabbit anti-histone H3 monoclonal antibody (HUABIO, ET1701-64, clone JJ090-07, lot no. H641565025; 1:5,000), rabbit anti-PEPC polyclonal antibody (Agrisera, AS09 458, lot no. 2410; 1:2,000), or a custom rabbit anti-NVR1 polyclonal antibody generated for this study by ABclonal Technology (1:500). For unconjugated primary antibodies, the membranes were subsequently incubated, as appropriate, with HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) (ZSGB-BIO, ZB-2305, lot no. 219760308; 1:10,000) or HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (H+L) (ZSGB-BIO, ZB-2301, lot no. 242521208; 1:10,000). Chemiluminescent signals were detected using ECL reagents and imaged with a Tanon 5200T Imaging System.

The YFP-tagged protein was immunoprecipitated using GFP magnetic beads at 4 °C for 2 h. After washing the beads 5 times with IP lysis buffer, the bead-bound proteins were treated with 10 mM TCEP and 50 mM CAA (in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate) at 95 °C for 10 min.

Samples were prepared via a filter-aided sample preparation method using Vivacon 500 filters (10,000 MWCO; Sartorius), sequentially washed with 8 M urea and 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, and digested overnight with 1 μg of trypsin (Promega). Following desalting with Pierce C18 Spin Tips (Thermo Fisher Scientific), peptides were dried by centrifugation at 10 °C, reconstituted in 0.1% formic acid, and subjected to LC–MS/MS analysis.

According to recent reports, LC–MS/MS analysis was performed using a timsTOF Pro 2 mass spectrometer coupled to a nanoElute liquid chromatography system (Bruker Daltonics). In brief, 200 ng of peptides were separated on a reversed-phase analytical column (25 cm × 75 µm internal diameter, IonOpticks) over a 60-min gradient at a flow rate of 300 nl min−1 and a column temperature of 50 °C. The mobile phases consisted of buffer A (0.1% formic acid in water) and buffer B (0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile). The gradient elution profile was set as follows: an increase to 22% buffer B from 0 to 45 min, up to 37% buffer B from 45 to 50 min, and a final step at 80% buffer B from 50 to 60 min. The mass spectrometer was operated in DDA-PASEF mode with the following parameters: capillary voltage, 1,500 V; dry gas flow, 3.0 l min−1; and drying temperature, 180 °C. The collision energy was linearly ramped as a function of ion mobility.

The raw LC–MS/MS data were searched against the N. benthamiana protein sequence database (Nbe_v1.1_pep.fa.gz), downloaded from NbenBase (https://nbenthamiana.jp/downloads), using MSFragger within FragPipe v22.0. Trypsin was specified as the digestion enzyme, allowing up to two missed cleavages. Precursor and fragment ion mass tolerances were set to 10 ppm and 0.02 Da, respectively. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine (+57.021 Da) was set as a fixed modification, whereas methionine oxidation (+15.995 Da) was included as a variable modification. Peptide and protein identifications were filtered to a 1% false discovery rate using a target-decoy strategy (Supplementary Tables 3, 6 and 7).

According to recent reports, his–TF and His–TF–NIB1 were incubated with 15 μl of Ni-NTA resin for 1 h at 4 °C. Protein extracts from leaves expressing EDS1–Flag were added to each resin and incubated overnight at 4 °C. The resin was washed 6 times with IP lysis buffer, resuspended in 50 μl of 4× SDS loading buffer and heated at 95 °C for 10 min. Bound proteins were analysed by immunoblotting.

Target coding sequences were cloned into pCAMBIA1300S-cYFP or pCAMBIA1300S-nYFP. Following co-expression of the fusion proteins in N. benthamiana leaves for 2 days, YFP signals were acquired by 20× water immersion objective through Leica TCS SP8 STED 3X.

MST was used to determine the protein–protein interactions and the binding affinities of NIB1 and its mutated versions to the indicated small molecules or RNA, protein labelling was performed in strict accordance with the manufacturer’s protocol. In brief, the purified recombinant proteins (NIB1–GST, NIB1(R49A)–GST, NIB1(G50A)–GST and NIB1(4A)–GST) at a concentration of 10 μM were labelled with NT–647–NHS using the Monolith Protein Labeling Kit RED-NHS 2nd Generation (NanoTemper Technologies). The labelled NIB1–GST and its mutants were adjusted to 50 nM in PBST buffer (PBS, with 0.05% Tween-20) and 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p (5 μM to 0.000153 μM) were added separately. For characterizing the interaction between NVR1 and NIB1 (NIB1RRM and NIB1GRR), 10 μM NVR1–TF was labelled and adjusted to 40 nM in PBST buffer. Subsequently, NIB1–GST, NIB1RRM–GST and NIB1GRR–GST (2.5 μM to 0.0000763 μM) were added separately. For protein–RNA interaction, the Cy5-labelled FLS2 3′-UTR served as the target and adjusted to 20 nM. NIB1–GST and the mutant fusions (10 μM to 0.000306 μM) were incubated with target. To access the interaction between NIB1(ΔIDR) and 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>P, the labelled NIB1(ΔIDR) was used as target and adjusted to 50 nM. The target protein was independently mixed with 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>P (10 μM to 0.000306 μM). Furthermore, to test the binding affinity of NIB1–GST with 3′,5′-cAMP, 3′,5′-cGMP, 8-Br-3′,5′-cAMP, AMP, GMP and the unrelated cyclic dinucleotides 2′,3′-cGAMP, 50 nM labelled NIB1–GST was used as target and independently mixed with the indicated compounds (15 μM to 0.000458 μM). A Microscale Thermophoresis Monolith NT.115 instrument (NanoTemper Technologies). was used to measure binding reactions at 25 °C, 40% MST power and 20% LED power. Measurements were repeatedly taken repeatedly from separate protein preparations to confirm repeatability. The curve was fitted using the MO.AffinityAnalysis_x86_2.3.0.7385, and the dissociation constant (Kd) value was determined.

It has been revealed that NIB1–YFP fusion protein and its various mutants were purified by Ni-NTA resin. NIB1–YFP droplets with 10% PEG 8000, or as specifically indicated, were observed by Leica TSC SP8 STED 3× 100× oil immersion objective. The droplets were bleached by 100% intensity 488 nm laser and the recovery was recorded every 3 s 290 ms for 50 frames in FRAP. Fusion of NIB1 droplets was recorded through time-lapse photography. Droplet diameters were measured from microscopy images using Fiji (ImageJ, version 1.54f).

Target proteins fused with fluorescent protein (YFP or mCherry) were co-expressed in N. benthamiana leaves. Condensates in leaves were observed by Leica TSC SP8 STED 3X (Leica) 40 × oil immersion objective. To prevent fluorescence bleed-through during imaging, all images were acquired using the sequential scanning mode on a Leica TCS SP8 confocal microscope. YFP was excited with a 488 nm laser and detected at 498–540 nm, and mCherry was independently excited with a 561 nm laser and detected at 600–630 nm. The images of condensates were analysed using Fiji (ImageJ, version 1.54f). Line profile analysis was performed to evaluate co-localization of the proteins. To quantify the partition coefficient of the EDS1–mCherry into NIB1–YFP condensates with or without NVR1, regions of interest of equivalent size were analysed. The partition coefficient (Kp) was defined as the ratio of intracondensate EDS1 fluorescence intensity to that of the extracondensate background.

The Cy5-labelled AttRNAser (83 nt) used as substrate for NVR1 digestion was obtained through in vitro transcription using T7 RiboMAX Express RNAi System. A reaction mixture containing 0.5 mM Cy5-UTP and 1 mM synthesized AttRNAser DNA template (sequence listed in Supplementary Table 13) were incubated at 37 °C for 30 min. The template DNAs were then removed by 0.5 μl RNase-Free DNase (Promega) at 37 °C for 30 min. In the RNase activity assay, 2 μM Cy5-AttRNAser was incubated with 0.02 μM NVR1 in buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 5 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 1 mM ATP, 0.5 μl RNase Inhibitor at 25 °C for 20 min. The reaction was stopped by 400 μl stop solution (40 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5 and 500 mM NaCl). Then RNAs were purified with PCIA solution (phenol:chloroform:isopentyl alcohol, 25:24:1) and the RNA pellet was resuspended in 1× TBE urea loading buffer. The RNA was then separated using 16% urea polyacrylamide gels at 150 V for 90 min and subsequently detected with a Amersham Typhoon 5.

Cy5-labelled FLS2 3′-UTR were synthesized in vitro using the HyperScribe T7 High Yield Cy5 RNA Labeling Kit (APExBIO) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. In brief, the 3′-UTR sequence of FLS2, as previously described44, was amplified using a forward primer containing a T7 promoter sequence (TAATACGACTCACTATAGGGGAAGTTTAGCAGCAAAGC) and a reverse primer (GTTCATCAAAACCAAATTTC). One microgram of DNA template containing a T7 promoter was combined in a 20 μl reaction volume. The reaction mixture consisted of 2 μl of 10× Reaction Buffer, 2 μl of T7 RNA Polymerase Mix, 2 mM each of ATP, GTP, and CTP, 1.5 mM UTP and 0.5 mM Cy5-UTP. The reaction was thoroughly mixed and incubated at 37 °C for 2 h. Following transcription, the DNA template was digested by adding 1 μl of DNase I and incubating at 37 °C for 15 min. The synthesized Cy5-labelled RNA was subsequently purified via phenol/chloroform extraction and ethanol precipitation. To evaluate the labelling efficiency, the absorbance of the purified RNA was measured at 260 nm and the Cy5 maximum excitation wavelength using NanoDrop.

Recent findings suggest that cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions were extracted according to the manufacturer’s manual instructions of Minute Cytoplasmic and Nuclear Extraction Kit for Cells. In brief, leaves (0.1 g, co-expressing NIB1–YFP and EDS1–mCherry with or without NVR1 for 48 h) were homogenized in cytoplasmic extraction buffer. Following centrifugation (14,000g, 5 min, 4 °C), the cytoplasmic supernatant was collected. The pellet was lysed in nuclear extraction buffer through repeated cycle of vortexing and ice incubation, and then centrifuged through a pre-chilled filter cartridge (14,000g, 30 s) to collect the nuclear extract. Histone H3 and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC) served as nuclear and cytoplasmic markers, respectively, to confirm successful fractionation.

Leaves were incubated in DAB solution (1 mg ml−1 DAB, 0.05% Tween-20, 10 mM Na2HPO4, pH 5.8) for 4–5 h in the dark. Bleaching buffer (ethanol:acetate:glycerol, 3:1:1) was added to displace DAB stain, and the sample was heated to 90–95 °C 3–5 times until the chlorophyll was removed completely. The samples were immersed in 50% glycerol for imaging.

Sources indicate that RNaseT2 proteins were filtrated from the genomes of plants (Gossypium hirsutum, Nicotiana tobacum, O. sativa), fungi (Fusarium graminearum, M. oryzae), insects (N. viridula, A. lucorum, Nilaparvata lugens, Aphis gossypii, C. medinalis, H. armigera) and mammals (Homo sapiens and Rattus norvegicus) using PF00445 HMM search or NCBI blastp. The GRPs (GRPIVa) encoded in genomes of 18 plant species of 14 families (Physcomitrella patens, Adiantum capillus, Cycas revoluta, Picea abies, Nymphaea colorata, O. sativa, Zea mays, Sorghum bicolor, Brachypodium distachyon, G. hirsutum, Arabidopsis thaliana, Vitis vinifera, Carica papaya, Cucumis sativus, Glycine max, Solanum lycopersicum, Solanum tuberosum and Populus trichocarpa) were filtrated under the condition of only one PF00076 domain. The genomes were obtained from Phytozome (https://phytozome-next.jgi.doe.gov/) or NCBI (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/), and insect proteomes were obtained from the NCBI Protein database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/protein/). All filtrated proteins in these two classes were aligned by MUSCLE 5.1, trimmed using trimAl 1.2. The phylogenetic tree was constructed by using IQ-TREE 2.2.0 and annotated by Evolview v3. Conservation diagram of amino acid residues was shown using Jalview 2.11.2.5.

Sources indicate that total RNA was extracted from leaves of ~4-week-old wild-type O. sativa ZH11 and transgenic lines, as indicated. Leaves of four-week-old tobacco (N. benthamiana) were infiltrated with 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP for 6 h, followed by RNA extraction. RNA-seq was performed by Personalbio. Clean reads were aligned to the O. sativa reference genome (GCF_001433935.1_IRGSP-1.0_genomic.fna; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCF_001433935.1/) or the N. benthamiana reference genome (Niben.genome.v1.0.1; https://solgenomics.net/ftp/genomes/Nicotiana_benthamiana/assemblies/) using HISAT2. Differential gene expression analysis was subsequently performed using DESeq, with differentially expressed genes identified based on the thresholds of |log2(fold change)| > 1 and P < 0.05. GO enrichment and volcano plots were generated using R v4.3.2 in RStudio 2023.09.1. The differentially expressed genes and corresponding GO enrichment results are provided in Supplementary Tables 2, 4, 5, 8–12.

Sources indicate that the third-instar C. medinalis larvae were placed on leaves of the 12-day-old rice seedlings of the indicated lines. Larval weight was recorded after the feeding for three days. Oviposition selection assay was conducted in nylon mesh cages (90 × 70 × 90 cm). Three one-month-old, uniform rice plants per genotype were grouped and arranged triangularly to prevent positional bias. 15 pairs of newly emerged moths were mated for 48 h. Subsequently, males were removed, and the 15 mated females were released into the cage centre with a 15% honey solution. After 24 h of oviposition at 26 °C (12 h:12 h light:dark photoperiod), the total number of eggs laid on the three plants of each genotype was summed. The assay was repeated with three independent cages. Oviposition preference was quantified by the oviposition index: OI = (T − C)/(T + C), where T and C are the number of eggs in the mutants and wild type, respectively. The deviation of the oviposition index against 0 was tested using a one-sample Student’s t-test.

Sources indicate that for larval feeding preference, leaf segments (3 cm) from 3 plant lines were arranged equidistantly in a circle within a Petri dish. Ten third-instar larvae (pre-starved for 2 h) were introduced to the centre. After 1 h of selection in darkness, the number of larvae settled on each plant was recorded. The selection rate was calculated as Ntarget/Ntotal selection × 100%, where Ntarget and Ntotal selection represent the number of larvae on a specific plant and the total number of larvae making a definitive choice, respectively.

For field test, wild-type ZH11 seeds were sown in soil, and 35-day-old plants were transplanted into six 1 m × 1 m field plots. Each plot was surrounded by two rows of rice plants serving as buffer rows, and all six plots were maintained within mesh enclosure. Four weeks after transplantation, the plots were arranged in an alternating pattern and sprayed with either water or 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP. Following treatment, 20 mated female C. medinalis moths were released at the centre of the enclosure. Once rolled-leaf shelters became visible, the number of shelters was counted. Insects and plant positions were randomized in laboratory assays, field treatments followed an alternating design, and outcomes were assessed blind to genotype or treatment.

Sources indicate that leaves tissue of 4-week-old rice plants were ground into powder with liquid nitrogen and resuspended in 500 μl ethyl acetate. Following vortex for 1 min and centrifugation at 14,000g for 10 min at 4°C, the supernatant was transferred and dried in vacuum concentrator and resuspended in 30 μl 30% (v/v) methanol. The samples were centrifuged at 14,000g for 15 min and the supernatant was applied to the LC–MS/MS on a QTRAP 6500+ mass spectrometer (AB SCIEX) for analysis. Salicylic acid samples were diluted to 1/100 with 30% (v/v) methanol.

Leaf sheath segments of 2 mm were excised from 2-week-old rice seedlings and pre-incubated overnight in sterile distilled water. The samples were then treated with water or purified recombinant His–NVR1 protein in buffer containing 20 μM luminol and 10 μg ml−1 HRP. Luminescence was recorded at 1-min intervals for 100 min with Varioskan Flash multireader (Thermo Fisher Scientific).

NVR1 (1 μM) and the rRNA substrate (2 μg) were incubated in a 20-μl reaction mixture at 25 °C for 25 min. The reaction was stopped by adding methanol, and the mixture was centrifuged at 12,000g for 10 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was collected and analysed by liquid chromatography–high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC–HRMS) using a Q Exactive quadrupole-Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometer coupled to a Dionex Ultimate 3000 RSLC (HPG) ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography system. The injection volume was 1 μl. The samples were separated on an ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3 column with a particle size of 1.8 μm. The mobile phase were water (A) and methanol (B), each containing ammonium formate (2 mM). The gradient elution was set as follows: 0–6.5 min, 2% methanol; 6.5–8.5 min, 20% methanol; 8.5–11 min, 98% methanol; 11.1–15.0 min, 2% methanol. The flow rate was consistently set to 0.40 ml min−1, and the column temperature was precisely maintained at 40 °C. Detection was performed in positive-ion mode using a heated electrospray ionization source. LC–HRMS data were analysed using Thermo Scientific Xcalibur 4.1.50.

In a recent development, extraction of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP was performed as described3. Leaf tissue was ground into powder with liquid nitrogen. Samples were resuspended in 600 μl 4% acetate containing 1 mM IBMX and vortexed for 2 min. The supernatant was extracted twice with 800 μl chloroform. The samples were dried through vacuum spinning and resuspended in 50 μl sterile water.

It has been revealed that the dissolved samples were subjected to analysis by LC–MS/MS on a QTRAP 6500+ mass spectrometer (AB SCIEX) coupled to an Agilent 1290 LC system. Chromatographic separation was achieved using a Waters XSelect HSS T3 column with a particle size of 2.5 μm and dimensions of 100 mm × 3.0 mm. Sample of 1 μl was injected. The mobile phase consisted of water (A) and methanol (B), both containing 2 mM ammonium formate. The gradient elution method was used as follows: 0–2.5 min, 2% B; 2.5–3.0 min, 2–70% B; 3.0–5.0 min, 70–99% B; 5.0–7.0 min, 99% B; 7.1–10 min, 2% B. The flow rate was set at 0.4 ml min−1, and the column temperature was maintained at 40 °C. Metabolites were detected using electrospray ionization in negative ion mode with multiple reaction monitoring. The mass spectrometer parameters were as follows: −4,500 V of capillary voltage, 500 °C of source temperature, 50 psi of ion source gas 1 (GS1) and gas 2 (GS2), and 35 psi of curtain gas. Data acquisition and analysis were performed using Analyst 1.6.3 software (AB SCIEX).

Step 1. To a stirred solution of 2′,3′-O-isopropylideneguanosine (1.0 eq) in anhydrous tetrahydrofuran (THF) at 0 °C under an inert atmosphere, trimethylsilyl chloride (TMSCl) (1.0 eq) was introduced, followed by the dropwise addition of pyridine (2.5 eq). The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 2 h. Next, isobutyryl chloride (1.0 eq) was added dropwise at 0–5 °C, and the mixture was stirred at room temperature for an additional 1 h. After quenching and extraction, the crude product was obtained and purified by C18 flash chromatography. The final product was characterized by LC–MS and 1H NMR spectroscopy for structural confirmation. Step 2. To a stirred solution of the Step 1 product (1.0 eq) and starting compound 2 (1.0 eq, CAS: 104992-55-4) in dichloromethane (DCM) at 0 °C, 5-(benzylthio)-1H-tetrazole (5-BTT) (1.0 eq) was added. The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 3 h. Reaction solution washed water and brine, the DCM solution was concentrated under vacuum, the crude by C18 flash purification. Confirmed by LC–MS, 1H NMR and 31P NMR. Step 3. To a stirred solution of iodine (1.0 eq) in a THF:water:pyridine mixture (10:5:1, v/v/v), the Step 2 product was added at room temperature. The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 1 h, followed by the addition of 10% sodium sulfite solution until the colour disappeared. The reaction mixture was then concentrated under vacuum, and the residue was extracted with ethyl acetate. The organic layer was dried over anhydrous Na2SO4, filtered, and concentrated under vacuum. The crude product was used directly in the next step without further purification. Confirmed by LC–MS and 31P NMR. Step 4. To a stirred solution of the Step 3 product (1.0 eq) in DCM, trifluoroacetic acid was added at room temperature. The reaction mixture was stirred at 45 °C for 4 h. After completion, the solution was concentrated under vacuum. Due to the product’s high water solubility, the residue was purified directly by C18 flash chromatography. Confirmed by LC–MS, 1H NMR and 31P NMR. Step 5. To a stirred solution of the Step 4 product (1.0 eq) in acetonitrile, N-methylmorpholine (1.0 eq), 2-methoxy-1-ethanesulfonyl chloride (2.0 eq), trimetaphosphate tri-tetrabutylammonium salt (1.0 eq), 1H-4(5)-nitroimidazole (0.1 eq), and DBU (3.0 eq) were added sequentially under nitrogen protection. The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature until completion. MgCl2 (2.0 eq) was then added, and the mixture was stirred at room temperature. After completion, the solvent was concentrated under vacuum, and water was added to the residue to adjust the pH to 3–4. The mixture was extracted with ethyl acetate, washed, dried, and concentrated to obtain the crude product, which was further purified by preparative HPLC and lyophilization. Confirmed by LC–MS, 1H NMR and 31P NMR. Step 6. To a stirred solution of the Step 5 product (1.0 e) in THF, HF (6.0 eq) was added at room temperature. The reaction mixture was stirred at 50 °C until completion. Triethylamine was then added to the residue to adjust the pH to 6–7, and the mixture was concentrated under reduced pressure to obtain the crude product. The crude product was purified by preparative HPLC and lyophilization. Confirmed by LC–MS, 1H NMR and 31P NMR. Step 7. To a stirred solution of the Step 6 product (1.0 eq) in methanol (10 volumes), NH3/methanol (10.0 eq) was added at 0 °C. The reaction mixture was stirred at 0 °C for 6 h until completion. The methanol solution was then concentrated under vacuum and the residue was purified by preparative HPLC followed by lyophilization. Confirmed by LC–MS, 1H NMR and 31P NMR.

In a recent development, NIB1–GST was incubated with 10 μl of glutathione agarose resin at 4 °C for 2 h. Empty vector (encoding TF tag) or NVR1 products were added to the resin for an overnight incubation at 4 °C. Then the resin was treated with 100 μl of 80% acetonitrile and 5% formic acid and incubated at 25 °C for 30 min before proceeding with liquid chromatography analysis.

According to recent reports, the 12-day-old rice seedlings were sprayed with 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP, 8-Br-2′,3′-cGMP or ApG>p for 6 h, with water and 8-Br-AMP as controls. After treatment, RNA was extracted, and the expression levels of defence genes were analysed by RT–qPCR. Leaves of 4-week-old N. benthamiana plants were infiltrated with 50 μM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP for 6 h, and gene expression was analysed by RT–qPCR.

AlphaFold2 was used to predict the structure of the NVR1–NIB1 complex. The 3D structures of 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP were obtained from PubChem (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/), and ApG>p was modelled using ChemBioDraw Ultra 14.0. The ligands were optimized using density functional theory (DFT) in Gaussian 16 and prepared for docking with NIB1 using AutoDockTools 1.5.7. Molecular docking was performed using AutoDock 4.2.6 with ligand-specific grid boxes at a spacing of 0.375 Å. Grid dimensions were adjusted to 46 × 50 × 50 for 2′,3′-cAMP, 50 × 56 × 56 for 2′,3′-cGMP and 100 × 100 × 100 for ApG>p. The Lamarckian genetic algorithm was applied with 50 runs, a population size of 150 and 2.5 × 106 energy evaluations. The lowest-energy poses were analysed using PyMOL 2.5.5 and LigPlot+ 2.2.8.

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9 (GraphPad Software). Comparisons between two groups were performed using unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests. For comparisons among multiple groups, one-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s or Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test was used, as appropriate. Two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test or the two-stage linear step-up procedure of Benjamini, Krieger and Yekutieli was performed, as indicated in the figure legends. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05, with a false discovery rate of 5% for analyses using the Benjamini–Krieger–Yekutieli procedure. For violin plots, width indicates data density, lines show the median and quartiles, and dots represent individual values. Details of the statistical tests are provided in the corresponding figure legends.

Greece vs Serbia - prediction, team news, lineups

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Anthony Nolan | 15 Nov 2026 02:13, Last updated: 15 Nov 2026 05:04.
  • Under pressure in League A of the UEFA Nations League, Greece will welcome Serbia to Panthessaliko Stadium for their final Group A2 showdown on Monday.
  • The Azure and White are battling for a place in the quarter-finals, while the Eagles are competing to earn a place in the League A/B playoffs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Anthony Nolan | 15 Nov 2026 02:13, Last updated: 15 Nov 2026 05:04.

Under pressure in League A of the UEFA Nations League, Greece will welcome Serbia to Panthessaliko Stadium for their final Group A2 showdown on Monday.

The Azure and White are battling for a place in the quarter-finals, while the Eagles are competing to earn a place in the League A/B playoffs.

Ivan Jovanovic's Greece kicked off their Nations League campaign in excellent fashion, but have been on a slow descent as the group has progressed.

The Azure and White beat Monday's opponents 2-1 in their opener on September 24, before claiming an impressive 1-0 victory over Germany three days later.

However, that success in Augsburg was Jovanovic's side's last taste of triumph, even if following it up with a pair of home draws against the Netherlands and Die Mannschaft was commendable.

On Friday, Greece were thrashed 7-0 by Xavi's Oranje, a defeat that was not only humiliating but has put their path to the quarter-finals in jeopardy.

Monday's hosts are at the moment second in Group A2, level on eight points with Germany, and must match their result while hoping Jurgen Klopp's team drop points on home soil in order to finish in the top two.

Meanwhile, Veljko Paunovic's Serbia have endured a disastrous Nations League term and are now fighting to avoid automatic demotion to League B, the fate awaiting the two lowest-ranked fourth-placed teams in League A.

The Eagles have lost all five of their matches so far, and are doomed to finish bottom of the group as a result, but they can still make the playoffs if they can rank higher than Turkey from Group A1 and the Czech Republic or Croatia from Group A3.

Paunovic's side are at the moment level on zero points with both Turkey and the Czech Republic, while boasting a three-superior goal-difference to those nations and a four-goal advantage over Croatia, who have three points.

Fans looking for a reason to be hopeful ahead of Monday's showdown could lean on the fact that Serbia were able to score in four of their defeats, three of which were by just one goal.

On the other hand, the Eagles were beaten 3-1 by Germany on Friday, falling two goals behind with just 14 minutes on the clock before having two players sent off in the second half.

That latest disappointment means the visitors have conceded 11 times in just five games - a rate of 2.2 per match - and their leaky defence could be exploited by a motivated Greece.

Greece are expected to be without midfielder Dimitrios Kourbelis due to an ankle injury, though Nectarios Triantis and Athanasios Androutsos should be on hand to start in the centre of the park.

Out wide, Arsenal's Christos Tzolis and Borussia Dortmund starboy Konstantinos Karetsas will be hoping to support a strike partnership of Vangelis Pavlidis and Fotis Ioannidis up top.

As for Serbia, they are missing Rangers midfielder Vanja Dragojevic and PAOK winger Andrija Zivkovic, both of whom are suspended after being sent off against Germany.

Filling the gaps, manager Paunovic could opt for Stefan Dzodic to be joined by Lazar Samardzic and Sergej Milinkovic-Savic in midfield.

Further forward, Mihajlo Cvetkovic is likely to partner captain and record appearance holder Dusan Tadic in attack, desperate to fire his team into the playoffs.

Greece possible starting lineup:.

Tzolakis; Rota, Mavropanos, Retsos, Tsimikas; Karetsas, Triantis, Androutsos, Tzolis; Pavlidis, Ioannidis.

Serbia possible starting lineup:.

V Milinkovic-Savic; Nedeljkovic, Gudelj, Milenkovic, Babic, Sukacev; Samardzic, Dzodic, S Milinkovic-Savic; Cvetkovic, Tadic.

Greece may have been hammered 7-0 by the Netherlands last time out, but that defeat came as a shock, and with a place in the quarter-finals at stake, the hosts will be motivated to bounce back.

Serbia have struggled throughout this term's Nations League, and it would be surprising to see them avoid a sixth consecutive defeat on Monday.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 17:31 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:01 EST, 14 November 2026.
  • Sebastien Pocognoli has backed Ben Gannon-Doak to find his killer instinct in the final third and establish himself as Scotland’s main man.
  • The Bournemouth youngster had an up-and-down evening in Friday’s 2-1 Nations League win over North Macedonia, getting into numerous promising positions on the right flank and winning the penalty – dispatched by John McGinn – which decided the game.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 17:31 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:01 EST, 14 November 2026.

Sebastien Pocognoli has backed Ben Gannon-Doak to find his killer instinct in the final third and establish himself as Scotland’s main man.

The Bournemouth youngster had an up-and-down evening in Friday’s 2-1 Nations League win over North Macedonia, getting into numerous promising positions on the right flank and winning the penalty – dispatched by John McGinn – which decided the game.

But, as has been the case throughout his Scotland career, the 21-year-old’s final ball in key moments left a lot to be desired.

Pocognoli is under no illusions that Gannon-Doak still has plenty to improve on, but insists that it won’t be long before things start to click for the talented youngster.

‘As long as he is high on the pitch and is creating one v ones I am happy,’ said the Belgian. ‘With Ben, we know that he is at a young age and needs to work on specific things.

‘On Friday, he had great opportunities. We know that he needs to improve on the end product, but he created a penalty and against Slovenia and North Macedonia away he created a number of unbelievable one v ones.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli greets Ben Gannon-Doak as he is substituted at Hampden.

‘He did that last night as well. We know he can be good if we dominate the game and he can get in good positions if we control the ball. I am happy with his performance.

‘He is a young lad, just 21. Okay, he has become more mature than he was, but I believe in one moment he will have a click about decision making.

‘I believe if he is playing every game he can make many decisions. He will know that in the next game he will have to do it again.

‘If he knows that he only has to play a game every two weeks, sometimes he can think, “This is my moment”.

‘It is a process. He will become older and at some point will become relaxed in his decision making, but at this very young age what he is producing is very good.

In a recent development, ‘I say exactly the same thing to him after training on the pitch. I say, “Ben, this is the next step”. He knows that and it is vital he knows that.’.

Scotland conclude their Nations League campaign in Switzerland on Monday knowing that only a victory against the group winners will be enough if they are to have any chance of leapfrogging Slovenia – currently one point better off ahead of their trip to North Macedonia – into second spot.

Pocognoli admits Gannon-Doak's end product has to improve after another frustrating show.

Should that happen, Scotland would have a crack at earning promotion to League A via a play-off in March, and also crucially guarantee their place as a Pot 2 side for the upcoming Euro 2028 qualifying draw.

According to recent reports, ‘We are still alive in this competition,’ mentioned Pocognoli, who celebrated his first win at Hampden on Friday at the third time of asking. ‘We know we have to do more than this competition. This competition is about trying to build something.

‘But it is nice to have that possibility on Monday to try to create something against one of the top 20 teams in the world.

‘We need to try to be brave. Switzerland have already qualified so let’s go there and be smart because they are a good team.

It has been revealed that ‘It is part of the process to play away against a top team. That is not something we have done yet. The approach will be different and, for me as a coach, it is a game with a lot of responsibility.’.

#2217. Arsenal: Viktor Gyokeres overtakes Cristiano Ronaldo, extends all-time Nations League goals record

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (465 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

Arsenal: Viktor Gyokeres overtakes Cristiano Ronaldo, extends all-time Nations League goals record

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (465 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ben Knapton | 15 Nov 2026 07:35.
  • Arsenal striker Viktor Gyokeres extended an extraordinary UEFA Nations League goals record and surpassed Cristiano Ronaldo in Sweden's 3-2 victory over Bosnia-Herzegovina on Saturday evening.
  • The 28-year-old has experienced a frustrating start to the 2026-27 season with Arsenal, scoring just two goals in 14 appearances, while also providing three assists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 15 Nov 2026 07:35.

Arsenal striker Viktor Gyokeres extended an extraordinary UEFA Nations League goals record and surpassed Cristiano Ronaldo in Sweden's 3-2 victory over Bosnia-Herzegovina on Saturday evening.

The 28-year-old has experienced a frustrating start to the 2026-27 season with Arsenal, scoring just two goals in 14 appearances, while also providing three assists.

Gyokeres has started just one Premier League game to boot, having fallen behind Kai Havertz in the strikers' pecking order, but he remains indispensable for the Sweden national team.

Gyokeres and strike partner Alexander Isak led the line for Graham Potter's men against Bosnia, whom Sweden drew first blood against through Daniel Svensson with just five minutes gone.

Gyokeres doubled his nation's lead from the penalty spot shortly afterwards, before rifling home from 12 yards yet again on the stroke of half time, and Sweden survived a fightback attempt from their visitors to make it four wins from five.

By making the net bulge at the Strawberry Arena, Gyokeres scored for the eighth Nations League game running, becoming the first player in the history of the competition to achieve that feat.

According to recent reports, viktor Gyökeres has now scored in eight consecutive Nations League games for Sweden ?? 8 games played, 12 goals ? https://t.co/jOt5Hc5U6o.

The 28-year-old already held the record for the most consecutive Nations League games scored in, as no other player has struck in more than six straight matches.

However, Gyokeres has now extended his unparalleled achievement; his closest challenger is England captain Harry Kane, who has scored in six consecutive Nations League matches and could make it seven on the spin when the Three Lions face Spain on Sunday.

Gyokeres's record run began in October 2024, when he netted once in a 3-0 win over Serbia, and the ex-Sporting Lisbon man also bagged against Slovakia and Azerbaijan in that year's tournament, scoring four against the latter.

Gyokeres now boasts six goals from five Nations League games in 2026-27, scoring in previous matches against Romania, Bosnia, Poland and Romania again before his Saturday double.

Not only did Gyokeres's brace on Saturday extend his successive scoring streak; the Arsenal forward has now overtaken Cristiano Ronaldo in the all-time Nations League scoring charts.

Ronaldo managed 15 Nations League goals for Portugal, but Gyokeres has now found the net 16 times in the competition, the second-most in the competition's history.

The Sweden star now only trails Erling Haaland in the list, as the Manchester City marksman has scored 23 Nations League goals for Norway after his strike in Saturday's victory over Wales.

Sweden have now moved onto 13 points from five games in League B Group 4, thus guaranteeing promotion to League A ahead of their last game against Poland on Tuesday.

Vinicius Junior matches previous 46-game Brazil goal tally in 12 matches

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (753 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Naim Beneddra | 15 Nov 2026 07:55.
  • Real Madrid forward Vinicius Junior has matched his goalscoring tally from his previous 46 Brazil appearances in just 12 international matches, completing a remarkable reversal in fortunes while enduring one of his most difficult periods at club level.
  • The 26-year-old scored twice during Brazil's 3-2 friendly defeat to Japan in Singapore on Saturday, producing two outstanding finishes to temporarily rescue Carlo Ancelotti's side from a two-goal deficit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Naim Beneddra | 15 Nov 2026 07:55.

Real Madrid forward Vinicius Junior has matched his goalscoring tally from his previous 46 Brazil appearances in just 12 international matches, completing a remarkable reversal in fortunes while enduring one of his most difficult periods at club level.

The 26-year-old scored twice during Brazil's 3-2 friendly defeat to Japan in Singapore on Saturday, producing two outstanding finishes to temporarily rescue Carlo Ancelotti's side from a two-goal deficit.

Despite the result, Vinicius extended an impressive international scoring run that stands in stark contrast to his struggles under Jose Mourinho at Real Madrid this season. The winger has now registered eight goals and three assists across his last 12 appearances for the Selecao.

Remarkably, he had scored just eight times in his previous 46 international matches, a record that frequently attracted criticism given his outstanding performances for Madrid.

The latest brace takes his overall international tally to 16 goals in 58 appearances, with Brazil increasingly becoming the environment in which he produces his best football.

For much of his international career, Vinicius struggled to reproduce the performances that established him among the world's leading attacking players.

His difficulties were particularly evident at the 2024 Copa America, when he failed to consistently influence Brazil's campaign despite arriving after another outstanding season with Real Madrid.

The situation has changed considerably in recent months.

Vinicius responded to criticism following Brazil's disappointing performance against France in March and has since developed into one of the team's most reliable attacking outlets.

He scored in all three group-stage matches at the 2026 World Cup, helping Brazil finish ahead of Morocco before their elimination against Norway in the last 16.

Although he failed to find the net in that defeat, his performances during the tournament provided further evidence of his growing importance to Ancelotti.

Saturday's friendly against Japan offered another demonstration.

With Brazil trailing 2-0 following early goals from Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura, Vinicius pulled one back in the 33rd minute, collecting a pass from Newcastle United midfielder Bruno Guimaraes before firing an unstoppable effort into the top corner.

The Real Madrid attacker was less convincing in other phases of the encounter, losing possession on several occasions and struggling to make an impact against Japan's organised defence.

However, he produced another moment of individual brilliance in the 75th minute.

Receiving possession following a short corner, Vinicius cut inside Yukinari Sugawara and unleashed a powerful strike that struck both posts before crossing the line.

His equaliser appeared to have earned Brazil a draw, only for Coventry City's Tatsuhiro Sakamoto to score the winner in stoppage time.

The defeat left Ancelotti with questions to answer about Brazil's defensive organisation, but Vinicius's finishing provided another encouraging sign ahead of the team's final international fixture of 2026.

The transformation in Vinicius's international performances is particularly striking given his current situation at the Santiago Bernabeu.

The Brazilian has managed just one goal and three assists in 12 appearances for Real Madrid this season, struggling to establish any consistency under Mourinho.

His problems intensified after he received a four-match domestic suspension following his red card against Villarreal in October.

Madrid subsequently won all four La Liga matches during his absence, while summer signing Yan Diomande took advantage of the opportunity to establish himself as an alternative on the left flank.

The emergence of the Ivory Coast international has raised questions about Vinicius's previously unquestioned place in the starting lineup.

However, Mourinho has publicly backed the Brazilian to rediscover his best form, insisting that the club will continue supporting him through a difficult period.

The Portuguese manager has also acknowledged that performances, rather than reputation, must determine selection decisions.

Madrid's attacking hierarchy has become increasingly competitive, with Kylian Mbappe maintaining an exceptional goalscoring rate and Diomande providing greater defensive involvement on the left.

That contrast was highlighted when Marc Cucurella defended Vinicius against comparisons with Diomande earlier this month.

Vinicius's latest performances for Brazil offer an encouraging reminder of the qualities that made him a decisive figure in two Champions League triumphs.

His eight international goals across 12 matches represent an average of one every 1.5 appearances, compared with one every 5.75 games during his previous 46 outings.

He will have an opportunity to extend that sequence when Brazil face Singapore on Tuesday, November 17.

Four days later, Madrid return to La Liga action against Celta Vigo, when Mourinho will have to decide whether Vinicius's renewed international confidence merits an immediate return to the starting lineup.

Cardinale indicates MSE will give Milan ‘financial muscle’ and reiterates: “I will never sell”

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1299 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sempremilan

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gerry Cardinale has commented on the launch of AC Milan’s new holding firm, Milan Sports & Entertainment (MSE), stating that he will never sell the club.
  • According to recent reports, yesterday, it was confirmed that RedBird had rolled out the upcoming holding company to ‘consolidate RedBird’s Milan-based investments in sports, infrastructure, and entertainment’.
  • Brett Yormark has been appointed as the CEO of MSE after impressing as the Commissioner of the Big 12 Conference (college sports), labelling it ‘an honour’ to get the position.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gerry Cardinale has commented on the launch of AC Milan’s new holding firm, Milan Sports & Entertainment (MSE), stating that he will never sell the club.

According to recent reports, yesterday, it was confirmed that RedBird had rolled out the upcoming holding company to ‘consolidate RedBird’s Milan-based investments in sports, infrastructure, and entertainment’. From the new stadium to the NBA Europa project, there are substantial plans for the company.

Brett Yormark has been appointed as the CEO of MSE after impressing as the Commissioner of the Big 12 Conference (college sports), labelling it ‘an honour’ to get the position. It doesn’t mean that we will see less of Cardinale though, quite the opposite.

In an interview with Gazzetta dello Sport this morning, Cardinale outlined exactly what he wants to achieve with MSE and explained why he will never sell the club. Silvio Berlusconi 2.0, as he calls it, with the goal of taking Milan back to the very top.

Cardinale, what benefits will AC Milan gain from the holding tech giant?

“The driving force behind deals like this is to provide AC Milan with the financial muscle needed to compete in the transfer market and secure the best players in the world.

“I will transform the club’s financial profile with the resources that will come from the stadium, the San Donato Arena, and the other activities we are working on with NBA Europe.

“I’m doing everything I can to ensure that, when we want a player, no one can tell me, ‘You can’t sign him because you can’t afford him.’ At the moment, only Premier League clubs are able to invest such sums and secure top players.

“If I want to bring AC Milan back to the top of European competition, not just in Italy, we need to figure out how to compete with the world’s top clubs.”.

This project confirms that your commitment to Milan is long-term….

“Yes. I will never sell AC Milan. Never. And this is a project to get them back to winning ways. I’m not willing to tolerate it taking a long time to achieve this. I want to do it as soon as possible. We’ll see how quickly….

Recent findings suggest that “My goal is to consistently win Scudetti and, of course, return to the Champions League. Milan Sports & Entertainment represents the foundation to make all this possible.”.

The connection with Milan deserves a separate mention: RedBird and the city are now even more connected….

“This is the legacy we will leave in Milan. The stadium, obviously, represents a huge legacy that will transform our financial profile, but then there’s also the San Donato development project and the rest.

It has been revealed that “If we want AC Milan to become great again, we need to close the revenue gap with the Premier League clubs. When I bought the club four years ago, I used the expression ‘Berlusconi 2.0’ and no one understood what I meant. Now perhaps we are starting to see it.”.

Sources indicate that “Everyone thought I was making an arrogant, self-centred comparison between me and Berlusconi, but that wasn’t my point. What I was trying to explain was that, just as Berlusconi transformed AC Milan and Serie A, we want to be able, through our ownership, to lead the club into a new era.

It has been revealed that “We need to do it in the same way Berlusconi did, albeit in a modern way. I’m used to working a certain way because that’s how I do things, at the highest levels worldwide and in America.”.

Could your “recipe” also be valid for Serie A?

“Of course, even for Serie A. In my opinion, it wouldn’t have been a good deal to sell 30% of the league’s international TV rights when JP Morgan made that offer. That’s not how Serie A can return to the top of Europe.

“It needs to be done through business planning and by creating every opportunity to generate new revenue. Like we will do with Milan Sports & Entertainment.

Recent findings suggest that “We will be the first to build a stadium since 2011, and that’s a huge achievement. I started working on it when I bought AC Milan, and finally… the right time has arrived.”.

Do you think others will follow you on this path?

Recent findings suggest that “No. Some may do it, others may not. We know what it takes to innovate and change. To avoid continuing to practice Einstein’s definition of insanity, according to which everyone wants a different outcome, but doesn’t want to do anything different to get it.”.

How long do you think it will take to complete the other projects that will be part of the new holding tech giant?

“I think the NBA is negotiating with the Euroleague, but one way or another, if they can’t reach an agreement, NBA Europe will still launch. Perhaps the first batch of fresh franchises for Europe will be confirmed at the end of the year or in early 2027.

“We will see when that happens… We own the land in San Donato, and if I’m granted the Milan franchise, I will be able to start construction fairly swiftly because we already have planning permission for a 20,000-seat arena.

“We will also continue to explore opportunities and hold discussions within the tennis world and to organise a tournament in Milan. Finally, we are already making progress in building and launching a hospitality and facility management tech giant.”.

Does your strategy include organising and managing hospitality services for other clubs’ stadiums as well, not just the newly introduced San Siro?

In a recent development, “Yes, the model is the organization I created in 2009, called Legends Hospitality. I created it with the Upcoming York Yankees and the Dallas Cowboys. Now that company is worth several billion dollars.

Sources indicate that “We not only sell premium seats, suites, merchandise, and hospitality, food, and beverage services for Yankee Stadium and Cowboys Stadium, but also for other clubs. I would like to adopt the same model here, probably in partnership with another club.”.

Not many football clubs in the world have established an organisation like the one you are leading….

Recent findings suggest that “Exactly. My ambition is to compete with the best clubs in the world. I want to do so thanks to my global vision of the world of sports and entertainment.

“There aren’t many multi-sports platforms in the world that also own some of their own facilities, and we want to add AC Milan to that list. To compete with them and then be better.”.

It has been revealed that in an effort to generate new revenue, are you also considering a tour for AC Milan next summer? Will that still be Australia or the United States?

It has been revealed that “We have already discussed it with Amorim, and I will just tell you that if we play friendlies abroad, they will be in the United States next summer. If we do… We haven’t decided yet, and the decision will be up to Ruben.

Sources indicate that “It will depend on what’s best for the team: playing friendlies abroad must add value to the group, not bring in a couple of million for the club. Those extra two million will no longer be our goal, as they were under the previous management. That won’t happen again under this ownership.

In a recent development, “Everything we organise in terms of friendlies will be carefully considered with our coach. Every move. And we won’t participate in tours organised by others. We put our players first. We want to help them prepare well to win. That’s our goal, and we aim to achieve it as soon as possible.”.

Rio Ngumoha dazzles on coming-of-age night in Europe

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There will be many more Champions League nights for Rio Ngumoha, although the 18-year-old will always remember this career landmark when his teenage skill plunged the opposition into fearful indecision and decided the game.
  • This young man has not yet played 40 senior games but there is no doubting the quality.
  • Ngumoha created the second Liverpool goal for Ronald Araújo and then the third for Mac Allister with the game’s best moment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There will be many more Champions League nights for Rio Ngumoha, although the 18-year-old will always remember this career landmark when his teenage skill plunged the opposition into fearful indecision and decided the game.

This young man has not yet played 40 senior games but there is no doubting the quality. Alexis Mac Allister scored twice, Liverpool came from two goals behind, and it all ended with a panic that meant they came close to chucking it away again. But what everyone could agree on from this strange match of fluctuating fortunes was that Ngumoha looks like one of the best young players in Europe. He is also a bona fide two-sided winger, winning this game for Liverpool from the right wing rather than his conventional left-wing role.

Ngumoha created the second Liverpool goal for Ronald Araújo and then the third for Mac Allister with the game’s best moment. That was an electrifying run into a group of converging yellow shirts in which he beat two men and still retained the composure to pick out Mac Allister in the area. Even as the Argentine ran to the Kop to celebrate, that stand was chanting the name of the teenager from east London. Ngumoha was one of three academy boys in Andoni Iraola’s XI, along with Lewis Koumas and Trey Nyoni, and all had an impact.

Magic from Rio Ngumoha 🤩🪄 Alexis Mac Allister puts Liverpool ahead with his second goal of the night ⚽️ https://t.co/3FTNWOUYhl.

In a recent development, iraola noted later that Ngumoha had taken care of the defensive work too against Sergi Cardona, an attacking left-back who scored his team’s second goal. From an attacking point of view, Iraola agreed, Ngumoha had periods of the game when he looked unstoppable. “If we can put Rio in situations one-v-one, he makes plays, [and] he produces things,” Iraola noted. “The assist for Alexis is a lovely play. He could go down for a penalty but he decides to continue which is a great decision. Also endurance-wise he is able to play more minutes.”.

In a recent development, he becomes the youngest Liverpool player in Champions League history to register an assist in the competition. For Iraola it will be hard to leave Ngumoha out of the game against in-form Brighton and Hove Albion on Sunday. “I believe in myself to do it,” Ngumoha said to Amazon Prime TV. “The more chances we get, the more it makes the opposition worry. I just keep going and be ruthless.”.

According to recent reports, iraola would later bring on the three £100m attackers whom he had left on the bench, with Sunday’s game in mind. Florian Wirtz, a half-time arrival, scored the fourth and Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak would later come on. Hard to call how it might go at home to Brighton. Liverpool’s defending was erratic at times, but their comeback was impressive.

The floodgates are opening ⚽️ Florian Wirtz scores his first goal of the season for Liverpool 🇩🇪 https://t.co/5HP72tA3bE.

Iraola made major changes at half-time, substituting Araújo and playing without a conventional right-back for the second half. It was brave and changed the momentum of the game, pushing his team higher up the pitch in what looked like a man-to-man marking arrangement. It enabled Iraola’s players to deny Villarreal the space and possession they had enjoyed in the first half when they had taken a two-goal lead – chiefly because of the mistakes of the home team. However much that was destabilising for Liverpool, by half-time they were level.

“They are so good on the ball,” Iraola remarked of Villarreal afterwards. Indeed, Villarreal’s manager Iñigo Pérez, a former Athletic team-mate of the Liverpool manager, was a coach whom Iraola sought to appoint at Bournemouth. “People probably don’t rate them [Villarreal],” Iraola said, “but after Barça they are probably the best in La Liga. They have 61 per cent of possession. Probably they have not had the results they deserve. If you are not really aggressive, you are not going to get the ball.

“We didn’t take as much risk. We were struggling because it is not a team that you can just press a bit. Either you go all the way or you will struggle without the ball.” Once Liverpool had done so, he remarked, his team had “won a lot of duels”. He was right in that respect. With the space squeezed, it was the power of Liverpool’s midfield that was telling.

Virgil van Dijk gave the first goal to Villarreal’s small No 9 Georges Mikautadze who had looked up to that point like he was hopelessly mismatched against the Liverpool captain and Jérémy Jacquet. Van Dijk’s misjudged header back to Alisson let in the striker, who did well to gather the ball and then hit it early. The second Villarreal goal at the midpoint of the first half was a mistake from Kostas Tsimikas, who failed to step up and played both Mikautadze and Cardona onside from Nathan Saliba’s ball. Either might have tucked it in but it was the left-back Cardona who took it on.

A moment to forget for Virgil van Dijk 😨 Georges Mikautadze takes full advantage to give Villarreal the lead at Anfield 🟡⚽️ https://t.co/3JTl00UwYa.

The pace of the game was slow and Villarreal were in control until the later stages of the half. Koumas and Cody Gakpo created a chance and from the corner that resulted Mac Allister headed in Tsimikas’s cross. Liverpool were up and running. Ngumoha’s cross from the left was unwisely left by Cardona for Araújo to score and the game was level.

Out of nowhere 😳 Ronald Araújo sneaks in to grab Liverpool's equaliser on the stroke of half-time 🇺🇾 https://t.co/Qrn8PmB2bJ.

According to recent reports, then came Ngumoha’s big second half, creating the third for Mac Allister. The teenager went past Cardona and the substitute Juan Foyth in a couple of strides. Wirtz dispatched the fourth from Gakpo’s ball.

Recent findings suggest that even so there was still time for Liverpool to show that they had sacrificed some defensive stability. The absence of a right-back cost them when substitute Tani Oluwaseyi ran into that area of the pitch to score Villarreal’s third late on. The third win of Liverpool’s Champions League season puts them second in the 36-team super-table, and behind defending champions Paris St-Germain only on goal difference.

In a recent development, liverpool are also seeing a new star emerge. Ngumoha might be the most expensive academy signing in the game’s modern history but alongside the £100m men he looks like a risk that was worth taking.

We have noted all night about momentum, and talking about how they Liverpool will play against Brighton at the weekend, I’ll be amazed if Rio [Ngumoha] doesn’t start because of the momentum that he has got from this game.

You see the fans, you see how everyone got a lift by him and that’s what they need at the weekend, they need someone to lift them.

It has been revealed that they are flying. Their confidence is through the roof. A similar style to Villarreal. They are second in everything after Barcelona. It has been a good game to prepare and we will use it.

I am really happy with Rio. He is trying to improve everything and we are trying to correct things. He played a lot on the left and know he is playing a lot on the right and he has adapted really well. We encourage him always. Even defensively as well he is improving. He has become a more complete player – and we must not forget he is 18!

Rio Ngumoha was magnificent tonight. Such a threat, and he dedicated himself to his tasks. On the ball this kid has so much potential, and I say kid, but he’s a young man. He has so much quality and it’s stuff that you can’t teach to be honest.

Sources indicate that what he does with the ball at his feet, that is God given ability, and his hard work on the training pitch, doing things day in and day out, and being ruthless, is what he stated in his interview, and I like that. He wants to be decisive, and I love that about him.

I’m not tall but I love going in the box. I really like it. They know I like to attack the near post. I scored in the World Cup as well. It was a good header. The second goal, Rio, was amazing. I talk with him about cutting it back on the floor.

In a recent development, it’s not something I really practice. My dad is a bit smaller than me but he was quite good in the air so maybe it’s something I got from him.

Last year was a really difficult year for all of us. It was clear I was not at the level and I am the first one to say. Something wasn’t right in the group and this manager changed it. The way we play is different, I don’t like to compare. I’m feeling good.

In a recent development, A lot of things happened today. They were much better than us in the first half and we were much better in the second half. When we’ve been under pressure, we answered well. When we relaxed, we made mistakes. You cannot relax against very good opposition. I value the win.

According to recent reports, we have to know that if we don’t go to the limit, it will be difficult. We are facing very good teams. It’s good to come back but we’ve started losing too many goals this season.

Florian Wirtz has scored or assisted in three consecutive games for the first time in his Liverpool career: 🅰️ vs LASK 🅰️ vs Brentford ⚽️ vs Villarreal https://t.co/woLWk2SGGL.

It has been revealed that it was a top performance from the boys. We were two goals down but the mentality was always there. We knew we were going to win.

Industry observers note that it’s up there with one of the best I’ve played. I enjoyed myself and the team helped me a lot.

Whenever I get the ball and there’s an opportunity to go one v one or two v one, I believe in myself. I’ll just keep going and be ruthless.

Rio Ngumoha talking to Gabriel Clarke on Amazon Prime: “Definitely one of the best games I played. I enjoyed it. Whenever I get the ball and go one v one, the more it makes the opposition worried.”.

When he was reminded that he was the youngest Englishman to provide an assist in the Champions League, he said: “Records are amazing to break.”.

Industry observers note that and on playing on the right instead of the left wing: “It’s helped me a lot in training. Slowly I’m getting better on the right.”.

Sources indicate that and to hear the crowd chanting his name: “This stadium, we have the best fans. To hear my name being chanted is a dream.”.

PSG’s 4-2 win over Barcelona tonight also puts them on nine points. Aston Villa, Arsenal, Real Madrid, Sporting and Real Betis are the teams playing tomorrow night with the opportunity to maintain a 100 per cent record.

According to recent reports, nine points from a possible nine for Liverpool in the Champions League, but they made hard work of it. Some dysfunction was probably to be expected after Iraola decided to start without Mac Allister, Isak, Wirtz and Barcola, but their defensive structure was unzipped far too easily at times.

According to recent reports, on the other hand, they dragged themselves off the canvas and the night belonged to Rio Ngumoha. He looked dangerous every time he received the ball, set up the third goal, and received a standing ovation when he was substituted. Liverpool need to put that contract in front of him sharpish.

Still time for another hairy moment at the back for Liverpool, but Perez’ shot from the edge of the area is blocked and that will surely be that.

Pape Gueye floats a cross straight down the throat of Alisson. A wasted opportunity for Villarreal. But still a couple of minutes to play.

Polo shirt and slacks for the young Spanish coach.
