Industry observers note that A very interesting team selection from Andoni Iraola. Liverpool’s head coach had indicated at his pre-match press conference that he was going to go as strong as possible, as his side seek to secure their third straight Champions League win. But the very fact Iraola has chosen to put Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola on the bench indicates he has one eye on Sunday’s demanding assignment against Brighton at Anfield.

Sources indicate that iraola will be delighted to have Cody Gakpo fit again and Lewis Koumas certainly deserves another opportunity to lead the line. But after victory’s against Atletico Madrid and LASK, Liverpool have given themselves some breathing space and it is understandable if Iraola, who has bemoaned the lack of time he has to train his squad, is already plotting Brighton’s downfall.

Recent findings suggest that your Reds to take on Villarreal in the #UCL! 🔴💫 https://t.co/tlQNFZVMBv.

Industry observers note that the club known as the “Yellow Submarine” made themselves some fans in the red half of Merseyside by denying Everton a place in the Champions League proper in 2005/06. Everton lost 4-2 on aggregate, and there was controversy in the second leg in Spain when Pierluigi Collina disallowed a Duncan Ferguson header that could have taken the tie to extra time. Everton had finished fourth, one place above Liverpool, the previous season, but Liverpool’s triumph in Istanbul assured them of a qualification place too. Unlike Everton, they prevailed.

Speaking of which, Rafael Benitez is at Anfield this evening.

Dominic King takes stock of Andoni Iraola’s first 10 games in charge of Liverpool and, despite some teething problems, he believes there are reasons to be optimistic. The demands Iraola is putting on Liverpool’s midfielders are an interesting tactical wrinkle, with Dom writing: “Liverpool’s formation will always be written as 4-2-3-1, but the reality is that Iraola’s team do not play in four clear tactical lines. He asks specific jobs of his midfielders, deploying them detailed instructions, and it is going to require some patience before performances become consistent.”.

A precious victory at Brentford, Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak among the goals and a couple of improved showings from Florian Wirtz mean things now look a little brighter for Liverpool.

They are strong favourites to make it nine points from nine in the Champions League by beating Villarreal at Anfield this evening, the Spanish club they vanquished in the 2022 semi-finals under Jürgen Klopp.

In a recent development, liverpool drew Atletico Madrid at home (already ticked off) and Inter Milan away as their two pot-one fixtures, which is about as kind as you can expect. A top-two finish in the league phase is a realistic aspiration for Andoni Iraola’s team, and something would need to go badly awry for them to miss out on the top eight.

Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Isak returned from injury to strengthen Liverpool at Brentford, although Szoboszlai has been lost for a few weeks following another hamstring complication.

Villarreal have punched well above their weight in Europe for the past few decades, reaching two European Cup semi-finals (beaten by Arsenal in 2006 as well as Liverpool in 2022) and winning the Europa League under Unai Emery in 2021.

According to recent reports, they have been mediocre in La Liga so far this season though, 12th after nine games on nine points and with a goal difference of zero. Their Champions League performances have been promising though, losing by the odd goal in a frantic finish at Borussia Dortmund and beating Napoli 3-1 at home. Villarreal’s best player is probably Senegalese central midfielder Pape Gueye, and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pépé is also in their ranks. Gueye, despite his position, is their joint-top scorer in all competitions with three goals.

According to recent reports, iraola will be up against his close friend and former Athletic Bilbao team-mate Inigo Perez who is now in charge at Villarreal. Perez was also Iraola’s assistant at Rayo Vallecano, the job which earned the Basque his move to Bournemouth. Perez guided Rayo Vallecano to the Uefa Conference League final last season.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ben Knapton | 15 Nov 2026 07:58.
  • Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes reportedly wants to see how new manager Mauricio Pochettino fares in the hotseat before committing himself to a new contract.
  • The 32-year-old's current deal expires at the end of the season, although the Red Devils have the option to activate a 12-month extension until the summer of 2028.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 15 Nov 2026 07:58.

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes reportedly wants to see how new manager Mauricio Pochettino fares in the hotseat before committing himself to a new contract.

The 32-year-old's current deal expires at the end of the season, although the Red Devils have the option to activate a 12-month extension until the summer of 2028.

Man United are keen to tie the Portugal international down for longer, but Fernandes reportedly rejected a second contract offer from the club last week.

The former Sporting Lisbon man has supposedly been left dissatisfied with the contract terms offered to him so far, both in terms of renewal length and the financial package.

However, according to The Sun, Fernandes is also hesitant to sign on the dotted line until new head coach Pochettino proves himself, having been left 'disillusioned' with the Red Devils' start to the season so far.

Pochettino has been confirmed as Man United's newly introduced manager on a three-year contract following the sacking of Michael Carrick, who won just one of his first 10 Premier League matches of the season.

Man United's dire start - their worst to a top-flight campaign since 1986 - has left them in 18th place in the Premier League table, just one point above basement side Crystal Palace in the relegation zone.

While Man United are supposedly confident that Fernandes wants to commit his future to the club, the Portugal international wants to see the hierarchy give Pochettino proper backing in the transfer market.

Fernandes and other Red Devils players allegedly believe that they have been 'set up to fail' by INEOS this season, and while the captain admires Pochettino's qualities as a head coach, he and others have been left 'bemused' with the decision-making from higher up.

Man United's failure to sign a new left-back in particular was seen as 'inexcusable', and has caused a 'disconnect' between the playing squad and Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox.

Fernandes broke the single-season assist record in the Premier League last term with 21 helpers, and he boasts six goals and three assists from 14 games in all tournaments this season.

However, the 32-year-old's overall form has been disappointing, as he has managed just one goal and one assist from his last seven Premier League appearances.

Sports Mole has identified four clubs Fernandes could join if he decides against signing a fresh Man United contract, amid reported interest from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Serie A.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
  • Published: 17:42 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:03 EST, 14 November 2026.
  • Amid the clamour for a change at the helm following another poor showing at a major tournament, it was easy to lose sight of the reality of the situation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 17:42 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:03 EST, 14 November 2026.

Amid the clamour for a change at the helm following another poor showing at a major tournament, it was easy to lose sight of the reality of the situation.

In a recent development, steve Clarke didn’t crash and burn in the US because a raft of world-class talents failed to turn up on the biggest stage. It happened primarily because a limited squad was unable to outperform two top-ten nations in Brazil and Morocco who could call upon infinitely superior footballers.

Sources indicate that sebastian Pocognoli has since arrived on the scene having earned a stellar reputation from his title success with Union Saint-Gilloise and his less feted spell at Monaco. But he has not come armed with a magic wand.

In opening the door to a string of fresh faces and advocating the more attacking approach which so many craved, the turbulence he’s experienced to date should only have been expected.

Limited by both the standard of players who are eligible for Scotland and the time he has to work with them, only the blissfully naïve would have seen his appointment as a quick fix.

While there were some positives to be taken from the game with North Macedonia – primarily the result – it’s likely the nation will have to endure more short-term pain for long-term gain.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli greets his players after a satisfactory evening at Hampden.

This was always going to take time, perhaps, in the view of John McGinn, more than many may have imagined.

‘The manager’s got a great reputation, a good record at both places he’s been,’ said the Aston Villa captain. ‘The most important thing now in football is individuals don’t win you games. It’s unity, teamwork and everyone being on the same page.

‘You see how successful clubs and successful countries do it. And we want to be one of them.

‘It’s not going to happen overnight. There’s a lot to learn but we did create big chances against North Macedonia where we could have scored three, four or five and it could be a different story.

‘But this isn’t something that gets fixed in March or even next September. It will start to build over the next 18 months.’.

If that predicted time frame might raise an eyebrow or two, McGinn makes no apology for it. Call it managing expectations from the midfielder if you please. But without a degree of patience from the Tartan Army, he feels Pocognoli’s ideas won’t take root.

‘I understand it’s frustrating,’ he added. ‘It’s freezing and you want to see four, five, six goals, but the balance has got to be there.

McGinn sends his penalty home to give Scotland a deserved lead against North Macedonia.

‘They’re entitled to their opinion, but there’s got to be a mixture of patience.

It has been revealed that ‘The supporters are entitled to say whatever they like. But just as long as they hurl anything they want to shout at the experienced boys and just let the young ones flourish and try and settle into the team.’.

Give credit where it’s due. With Clarke accused of causing stagnation by selecting the same old faces, Pocognoli has capped five players for the first time while recalling the likes of Oli McBurnie.

The sages in the stands can’t have it both ways. If the squad was going to evolve, it was never going to be a smooth ride.

According to recent reports, ‘I think the young players are starting to show more now,’ McGinn stressed. ‘Luke Graham on Friday night, I thought he was brilliant. It’s not easy playing in the middle of a back three. He’s been waiting for his chance and the manager’s shown that if you deserve your chance you’re going to get put in there.

‘We’ve got so many players that can step up and they will. We just need to show that belief and take it to the pitch.’.

It has been revealed that even in victory, McGinn doesn’t dispute that there is significant scope for improvement. He’s convinced, however, that this will all come good in the end.

McGinn insists it's vital the entire Scotland squad buy into the methods of manager Pocognoli.

‘We need to play slightly better,’ he stated. ‘We know that, but we’re going through a period which I’ve been used to at club level, a lot of changes, a lot of detail that we need to try and remember and get used to.

Recent findings suggest that ‘And it’s about sticking at it. We’re keen to play a style of football that’s not easy but is going to get bums off seats. It’s notable that everyone believes in it because if one person drops off or doesn’t believe in it, that’s when it all starts to fall apart.’.

Friday was another memorable night on a personal level for McGinn. Having broken the tension with the opener only to see North Macedonia level, he held his nerve to put Scotland back from the penalty spot.

The brace put him on 24 international goals, now within six of Denis Law and Kenny Dalglish. But all of that is for another day.

Recent findings suggest that ‘It feels a bit strange, but at the minute that’s gone to the back burner,’ he stressed. ‘I had a wee chat with Scott (McTominay) about the penalties. I was designated penalty taker but, to be fair, he’s not missed one I don’t think in his career.

‘So, we had a wee chat and I think we both mentioned the most vital thing was just no matter who hit it, hit the back of the net.’.

McGinn is eyeing three points against Switzerland in St Gallen to close the campaign on a high.

Sources indicate that tomorrow, the equation is clear. To finish second in the Nations League group and secure a place in pot two for the Euro draw, Scotland must beat the Swiss and hope that Slovenia don’t beat North Macedonia.

Even if everything clicks for Pocognoli’s side, it will be the tallest of orders.

According to recent reports, ‘Difficult,’ stated McGinn. ‘I know they drew on Friday night (with Slovenia) but they’ve got a couple of players back that they were missing last time.

According to recent reports, ‘It is a tough one but we want to be competing against these teams away from home. It’s not going to be perfect for a while, but we’ll stick at it.’.

Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 123 min read (24656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~123 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that breast cancer, the most diagnosed cancer among women, is stratified by gene expression patterns into luminal and basal-like subtypes, and the latter is associated with worse prognosis1,2,3.
  • It has been revealed that gene expression profiles classify breast cancers into luminal A or luminal B (hormone-receptor-positive (HR+)), HER2-positive and basal-like subtypes.
  • Chromatin organization, mediated by DNA and histone post-translational modifications (PTMs), facilitates the acquisition of epigenetically distinct cellular states in genetically identical cells10,11,12.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that breast cancer, the most diagnosed cancer among women, is stratified by gene expression patterns into luminal and basal-like subtypes, and the latter is associated with worse prognosis1,2,3. Recent advances in single-cell technologies have underscored the presence of intratumour heterogeneity, which poses substantial challenges in cancer treatment and achieving long-term disease-free survival4,5,6,7. Here we extensively profile epigenetic heterogeneity in a cohort of treatment-naive human luminal tumours, which were obtained directly after surgical resection. By applying a single-cell epigenetic approach based on cytometry by time-of-flight, we identify a recurrent subpopulation of basal-like cells in luminal tumours with a conserved epigenetic signature across patients. These basal-like cells, also identified by deconvolution of whole-genome DNA methylation patterns, are characterized by high expression of aggressive oncogenic traits and downregulation of hormone receptor signalling. Direct comparison of single-cell proteomic and genomic profiling of monomethylation and trimethylation of histone 3 on lysine 4 revealed that these marks are key features associated with loss of luminal identity. Finally, we highlight the potential of concomitant single-molecule profiling of histone modifications on cell-free nucleosomes in blood as an epigenetic liquid biopsy approach for early diagnosis of breast cancer. Moreover, the epigenetic basal signature measured in blood is linked to prognosis, which enables the identification of patients at increased risk for disease relapse.

It has been revealed that gene expression profiles classify breast cancers into luminal A or luminal B (hormone-receptor-positive (HR+)), HER2-positive and basal-like subtypes. Among these, basal-like subtypes largely overlap with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC)2,3. These classifications guide treatment management and prognosis. Luminal HR+ breast cancer generally responds to endocrine therapy with favourable outcomes, yet many patients relapse8. Single-cell and spatial studies have revealed substantial intratumoural heterogeneity among subtypes, which potentially drive treatment resistance and recurrence4,5,6,7,9.

Chromatin organization, mediated by DNA and histone post-translational modifications (PTMs), facilitates the acquisition of epigenetically distinct cellular states in genetically identical cells10,11,12. Although single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell chromatin-accessibility sequencing (scATAC–seq) delineate intratumour heterogeneity13,14,15,16, the contribution of chromatin patterns remains unclear17. Single-cell profiling of histone marks, such as trimethylation of histone 3 on lysine 27 (H3K27me3), implicates chromatin states in breast tumour heterogeneity and treatment resistance18,19. However, these methods measure a limited number of chromatin marks, which hinders analyses of complex patterns and interactions. We developed a cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) method to systematically profile multiple histone PTMs and decode population-specific chromatin patterns to examine heterogeneity among cancer cells20,21,22,23.

Sources indicate that tumour epigenetic states are also reflected in blood. Cell-free, plasma-circulating nucleosomes, released mainly by dying normal and cancer cells, retain tissue-of-origin epigenetic patterns24,25,26,27. Our single-molecule imaging platform, epigenetics of plasma isolated nucleosomes (EPINUC), captures multiple epigenetic features on plasma nucleosomes28. This method detects colorectal cancer, including low-burden early-stage disease28, and enables minimally invasive molecular profiling and treatment monitoring of paediatric brain tumours29.

Sources indicate that here we present a holistic epigenetic analysis of primary treatment-naive breast tumours and blood cell-free nucleosomes. Linking recurrent intratumoural epigenetic patterns to circulating nucleosomes connects tumour epigenetic heterogeneity with its potential clinical implications. This work reveals epigenetic alterations as key mediators of intratumour heterogeneity and potential biomarkers for early diagnosis and prognosis.

According to recent reports, to assess heterogeneity in breast tumour histone modifications, we performed epigenetic focused CyTOF on fresh, surgically resected tumours from treatment-naive women and quantified histone modifications at single-cell resolution (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). The cohort included mainly luminal HR+ tumours and only one basal triple-negative (TN, HR–) tumour (n = 12; Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 1a,b), as standard neoadjuvant therapy excluded most TN cases from treatment-naive eligibility. Following batch correction and normalization, uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) analysis of all 12 tumours revealed that tumour cells largely occupied patient-specific regions, whereas stromal cells clustered together across patients. This result aligns with previous studies that measured single-cell genomic differences13,14 (Fig. 1b, Methods and Supplementary Fig. 2a). Partial overlap among luminal tumour cells from different patients probably reflects shared lineage-specific epigenetic programs. As expected, stromal cells expressed vimentin and αSMA, whereas tumour cells expressed the epithelial keratins, EpCAM and E-cadherin (Fig. 1b,c and Supplementary Fig. 2b,c). Notably, the basal TN tumour differed from HR+ tumours, showing low expression of the luminal marker GATA3 and high expression of the basal marker cytokeratin-5 (K5; also known as KRT5) and mesenchymal vimentin markers (Fig. 1b,c and Supplementary Fig. 2d). Stromal and tumour chromatin patterns also differed, a result that underscores their role in dictating cellular identity (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. 2e). CyTOF analysis of MCF7 (luminal) and four basal-like TN cell lines validated that GATA3 and K5 expression patterns can differentiate luminal and basal-like identities. Moreover, SHAP analysis30,31 identified these two markers as the strongest discriminators of tumour type (Fig. 1e,f). Using multiple cell-identity markers, we derived a PermCell luminal signature (Methods) that accurately distinguished the identities of the cell lines (Fig. 1g).

Sources indicate that we next examined intratumour heterogeneity, focusing on the cancer cells of each luminal breast tumour separately. UMAP clustering and density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) across all features revealed three subpopulations in each tumour, which we termed cycling, luminal and basal-like (Fig. 1h,i and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). These subpopulations were also conserved in two different luminal patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. This finding validates the observed heterogeneity as an inherent feature of luminal breast tumours and excludes contamination of normal cells (Fig. 1j and Extended Data Fig. 1c). MCF7 cells highlighted similar luminal and basal-like heterogeneity, although most cells were cycling, as expected for a cell line (Extended Data Fig. 1d). In tumours, only a luminal subset cycled and expressed high levels of Ki-67, a result consistent with previous immunohistochemistry (IHC) and scRNA-seq studies14,32. CyTOF Ki-67 levels correlated with pathology estimates (Fig. 1k). Cycling cells also showed high levels of multiple chromatin modifications, both in raw measurements and following normalization to core histones (Fig. 1i, Extended Data Fig. 1a–c and Supplementary Fig. 3). We validated this result by repeating CyTOF analyses of two tumours (14 and 18), adding the established cell cycle marker phospho-Rb (pRb). pRb-positive cells showed an increase in core histones, as expected from cycling cells, and a larger increase in histone PTMs (Supplementary Fig. 3). Accordingly, the epigenetically inferred cycling fraction strongly correlated with Ki-67 levels (Fig. 1l).

Most cancer cells strongly expressed GATA3 and scored highly for the luminal signature, consistent with clinical classification (Fig. 1h, Extended Data Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Fig. 4a). Moreover, in each tumour, the PDX samples and the MCF7 cells, we identified a minor recurrent subpopulation that acquired basal-like identity, with high K5 expression and a reduced luminal signature (Fig. 1h–j, Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 4a). This phenotypic diversity is consistent with previous single-cell studies of human and mouse breast tumours14,21,33,34. Notably, luminal and basal-like cells also had distinct histone PTM signatures (Fig. 1h–j and Extended Data Fig. 1). Accordingly, UMAP plots based solely on histone modifications revealed separation of the subpopulations, which validated the epigenetic basis of this phenotypic diversity (Supplementary Fig. 4b). In MCF7 cells, epigenetic UMAP and clustering similarly identified several clusters, including a K5hi basal-like population (Fig. 1m). These basal-like cells with reduced luminal signalling appeared closer in UMAP space to the TN cell lines, which provided further support for their basal-like identity (Supplementary Fig. 4c). Independent CyTOF experiments, additional MCF7 parental cell culture and populations derived from independent single-cell clones revealed similar subpopulation patterns, a result that argues against a genetic basis for these effects (Fig. 1n and Extended Data Fig. 2a–c). Moreover, individual PDX tumours derived from the same donor and grown independently in different mice showed similar subpopulation proportions, which provides support for a dynamic and plastic relationship between cell states (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Overall, our data revealed inherent intratumour heterogeneity in luminal tumours, with epigenetic variability between distinct subpopulations.

We further explored the characteristics of the cycling, luminal and basal-like subpopulations. Unsupervised clustering grouped corresponding subpopulations across patients, which confirmed their robustness and similarity (Fig. 2a). Across tumours, luminal cells expressed oestrogen receptor (ER), GATA3 and cytokeratin-8 and cytokeratin-18 (K8/18; also known as KRT8 and KRT18, respectively), whereas basal-like cells downregulated these luminal markers and highly expressed K5 (Fig. 2b). As these subpopulations also exhibited distinct and conserved chromatin patterns, we applied a machine-learning algorithm to predict intratumour classification35. In each tumour, a model trained on a random subset predicted the remaining cells with 94% accuracy, which confirmed the robust differences between subpopulations (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 3a). It also assigned 78% of unclustered ‘noise’ cells with >95% confidence, generating classifications that aligned with the original clustering and UMAP positions (Extended Data Fig. 3b). SHAP analysis identified the features driving each subpopulation. In detail, histone PTMs, particularly the four acetylation marks, were leading predictors of cycling cells despite overlap of individual marks with basal-like cells (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). Polycomb-associated H3K27me3 and H2Aub also contributed to the features, a finding consistent with previously observed Polycomb deregulation and pro-proliferative activity in breast cancer36,37,38.

Luminal and basal-like separation was similarly epigenetic driven, with H4K20me3, H3K36me3 and H3K9me2 marks having the highest SHAP scores (Fig. 2d). Across tumours, basal-like cells consistently had increased H3K9me2 and H3K4 monomethylation and trimethylation, whereas luminal cells had enhanced H4K20me3, H3K36me3, H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 marks (Fig. 2e). These results align with subtype-associated histone PTM signatures39 and reported roles for H3K4 demethylases, such as JARID1B, in luminal–basal transitions40. Both luminal and basal-like cells highlighted similar pRb distribution, which provide support for the conclusion that these results reflect distinct cell states rather than cell cycle differences (Extended Data Fig. 3e). Similar epigenetic signatures distinguished luminal and basal-like populations in PDX models (Extended Data Fig. 3f). Accordingly, epigenetic-only basal-like PermCell scores accurately captured basal-like cells in tumours, PDXs and MCF7 cells (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 4). Overall, our computational framework confirms that there is recurrent epigenetic heterogeneity in HR+ breast tumours and highlight chromatin patterns associated with basal-like K5hi cells.

Industry observers note that consistent with the CyTOF results, tumours with higher fractions of epigenetically defined basal-like cells had fewer ER-positive and progesterone receptor (PR)-positive cells, as measured by IHC (Extended Data Fig. 5a,b and Supplementary Table 2). Basal-like cells were also more abundant in worse-prognosis luminal B than luminal A tumours. This result is in agreement with studies showing that these tumours exhibit features shared with the basal-like subtype3,41,42,43 (Fig. 2g). Although tumour mutational burden was low across the cohort, it correlated positively with the CyTOF-defined basal-like fraction, which parallels the greater genomic instability typically associated with TNBC44,45 (Fig. 2h and Supplementary Table 2). TP53 mutant tumours likewise contained more basal-like cells (Extended Data Fig. 5c), a finding reminiscent of single-cell studies of glioblastoma showing that genetic mutations may affect balance between cellular states46. Overall, these associations between pathological and molecular characteristics link the epigenetically distinct basal-like subpopulation to a more aggressive disease phenotype.

To characterize these cells functionally, we performed FACS to sort cells from tumour 19 and then low-input mass spectrometry. After excluding stroma through pan-cytokeratin staining, cells were sorted according to K5 levels to enrich for basal-like cells compared with the luminal population. K5low cells highly expressed luminal markers and proteins associated with oestrogen signalling, whereas basal-like K5hi cells expressed proteins involved in oncogenic pathways, such as MYC–mTOR signalling (Fig. 2i–k). Moreover, multiple chromatin regulators differed between these subpopulations, including the H3K4me1 methyltransferase SETD7 and histone demethylase KDM4A, consistent with the histone PTM differences observed by CyTOF47,48 (Extended Data Fig. 5d). KDM4A, enriched in K5hi cells, targets H3K9me3 and H3K36me3, which potentially accounts for their reduced levels and H3K9me2 accumulation in the basal-like population49. Comparisons with a normal mammary single-cell atlas50 revealed hormone-sensing programs in K5low cells and an alveolar progenitor signature in K5hi cells (Fig. 2l), a result consistent with their enrichment in luminal and basal TN tumours, respectively50.

To gain a mechanistic understanding of these findings, we sorted MCF7 cells using K5-specific and GATA3-specific antibodies and performed transcriptomic profiling, comparing basal-like cells (K5hiGATA3low) to bulk MCF7 or extreme luminal cells (K5lowGATA3hi; Extended Data Fig. 5e,f). Notably, basal-like cells were enriched for epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) genes (P < 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 5f). We then focused on differentially expressed cell surface markers to enable live sorting, which revealed that CD74 was significantly upregulated in basal-like cells in both MCF7 and tumour 19 proteomic analyses (Fig. 2m and Extended Data Fig. 5g). Live-sorted CD74hi cells exhibited increased migratory capacity in migration and wound-healing assays, which provided further support for the more aggressive phenotypes of basal-like cells (Fig. 2n,o and Extended Data Fig. 5h). Together, these single-cell and bulk proteomics and functional assays identify epigenetically distinct K5hi basal-like cells in luminal tumours associated with aggressive traits such as reduced luminal signalling, elevated oncogenic signalling and increased migratory potential.

Industry observers note that the distinct chromatin and phenotypic states of the basal-like subpopulation led us to explore whether intratumour epigenetic heterogeneity is also apparent in DNA methylation patterns. Thus, we conducted deep whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) on three luminal tumours from our cohort. DNA methylation patterns accurately capture breast cancer subtyping, as shown by The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)51. We next jointly deconvoluted the TCGA and our WGBS data into functional archetypes (V1–V3), with each tumour positioned in the deconvolution space. Stratifying the data into three archetypes revealed the expected separation of basal (TN) tumours from luminal (HR+), with archetype V3 associated with basal tumours (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Tumours 18, 19 and 23 from our cohort clustered with the luminal tumours, as expected from their bulk clinical subtyping. Correlation of the archetype contribution with RNA expression confirmed the association of V1 and V2 with luminal transcriptional programs, whereas V3 was associated with EMT, a result consistent with previous studies of TN tumours52,53,54 (Extended Data Fig. 6b and Supplementary Fig. 5a). To improve resolution, we added a fourth archetype (V4). This analysis revealed another layer of diversity: basal TN tumours were strongly associated with V3, which corresponded with reduced oestrogen signalling and increased oncogenic signalling, whereas luminal tumours were more heterogeneous and spread across the V1 axis (Fig. 3a,b and Supplementary Fig. 5b). Notably, V1 was strongly enriched for EMT, thereby potentially capturing an intermediate-transitional state between luminal and basal-like programs. Moreover, the percentage of CyTOF-measured, vimentin-positive cells, indicative of EMT, in tumours 18 and 19 differed accordingly (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 5c). Tumour 19, with a higher V1 contribution, also comprised more vimentin-positive cells, as assessed by CyTOF. These results support the use of WGBS deconvolution to capture functionally distinct cellular states in tumours, such as luminal cells undergoing EMT.

Cells are represented by a scTransform-normalized gene activity matrix reflecting H3K4me1-associated regulatory activity per gene, with the read count excluded. Louvain clustering and cell numbers per tumour are indicated. f, Differentially H3K4me1-marked genes per cluster in e (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, log2 fold change > 1, adjusted P < 0.01) were analysed for enrichment against MSigDB Hallmark and breast-related collections (Supplementary Table 4). Shown are terms enriched among genes with increased H3K4me1 in cluster 2 in at least two out of three tumours (one-sided hypergeometric test, FDR < 0.05). Circle sizes indicate overlapping genes; colour, –log10[FDR]. g,h, UMAPs of H3K4me1 (g) and H3K4me3 (h) snCUT&Tag data, analysed as in e and f and coloured by UCell scores for signatures comprising genes contributing to the respective enrichments (Gaussian-smoothed). For H3K4me3 enrichment, see Extended Data Fig. 8h. i, Pearson’s correlations between snCUT&Tag read number and UCell scores for the indicated gene signatures per tumour and histone mark. Gene signatures shown in d,f,i are derived from previously published studies (refs. 13,59,85,86,87,88).

To directly link the CyTOF-defined subpopulations with DNA methylation patterns, we sorted K5hi and K5low cells from tumour 5 and tumour 23, followed by enzyme-mediated methylation sequencing (EM-seq). Functional enrichment of differentially methylated promoters revealed hypermethylation of oestrogen-response programs in K5hi cells, whereas genes associated with aggressive and oncogenic features, including KRAS signalling and mesenchymal or basal-state transitions, were hypomethylated (Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). We next derived a CpG island (CGI) methylation signature to distinguish the two states using CGIs that were concordantly differentially methylated across both tumours. In TCGA breast cancer data, this signature scored higher in basal-like tumours, which indicated that the K5hi methylation program resembles basal-like tumours (Extended Data Fig. 6e). K5hi samples also indicated higher contribution to the basal-associated and EMT-associated archetypes than K5low samples, in both the three-archetype and four-archetype models (Extended Data Fig. 6f,g). Thus, the CyTOF-defined basal-like population exhibits basal-like and EMT-related methylation programs, which reveals another layer of intratumoural epigenetic heterogeneity.

Having identified distinct DNA methylation programs associated with tumour cell states, we next assessed cell-to-cell variability by clustering read-level methylation patterns across 100-bp genomic bins and calculating empirical entropy as an estimation of cell-type heterogeneity55. Genes near high-entropy bins were associated with functional terms related to poor differentiation, tumour aggressiveness and basal compared with luminal identity (Supplementary Fig. 6a). This result suggests that empirical entropy, by capturing diverse DNA methylation states, can be used as a proxy for cell-to-cell heterogeneity and reveal functional differences between subpopulations. We next calculated the mean entropy for each CGI (Extended Data Fig. 7a). As expected, most CGIs were unmethylated across all cells56, thus showing zero entropy. The variable CGIs (entropy > 0) were functionally enriched for EMT and the related Hedgehog signalling pathways, which indicated that these are differentially regulated in tumours57 (Extended Data Fig. 7b). This analysis suggests that intratumour variability in methylation patterns may be associated with cell identity transitions.

To further explore intratumour entropy and its relation to cell identity, we leveraged a published multiomic study of luminal breast cancer that included single-cell expression and chromatin accessibility measurements13. Focusing on cancer cells, we observed intratumour heterogeneity in luminal and basal-like expression patterns, as previously described14,54 (Supplementary Fig. 6b). Using the ATAC–seq modality, we calculated the within-peak (WIP) fraction, a metric of epigenetic noise58, whereby a low-WIP fraction may indicate a destabilized or noisier epigenome, which supports cell plasticity. For each tumour, we correlated the WIP fraction with chromatin accessibility of basal-like and luminal gene signatures. Cells that scored high for EMT and basal-like identity demonstrated lower WIP fraction, a finding reminiscent of the higher DNA methylation entropy associated with these signatures (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 6c). Single-cell multiome analysis of a freshly resected independent luminal tumour reproduced the basal–luminal continuum and association between basal identity and reduced WIP fraction (Supplementary Fig. 6d,e). To explore whether the increased epigenetic noise is associated with higher transcriptional heterogeneity, we divided cells into quartiles according to a published basal–luminal index59 and basal-like and luminal gene sets (Methods). Indeed, across all tumours, cells with a high basal identity showed higher transcriptional heterogeneity (Extended Data Fig. 7c). In line with these observations, the CyTOF-defined basal-like subpopulation also showed higher epigenetic heterogeneity (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Moreover, read-level methylation entropy was higher in K5hi-sorted compared with K5low-sorted populations in both tumours analysed by EM-seq, with higher variability among the K5hi 200-cell replicates (Supplementary Fig. 6f,g). Together, our analyses across DNA methylation, chromatin accessibility and histone PTMs indicate that the basal-like subpopulation exhibts a noisy epigenetic landscape and increased transcriptional heterogeneity.

According to recent reports, our CyTOF analysis highlighted a global increase in several histone PTMs in the basal-like subpopulation, including H3K4 monomethylation and trimethylation (Fig. 2e). To explore the genomic distribution of these marks, we conducted single-nucleus CUT&Tag (snCUT&Tag) on three luminal tumours from our cohort60. Similar to the CyTOF data (Fig. 1b), stroma cells clustered together across patients, showing H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 deposition on fibroblast and endothelial markers. By contrast, tumours clustered separately, which indicated inter-patient variability (Extended Data Fig. 8a–d).

In a recent development, in each tumour, malignant cells clustered into distinct H3K4me1-defined or H3K4me3-defined states (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 8e,f). Differential analysis of H3K4me1 distribution between clusters highlighted a recurrent group of cells across tumours, annotated as ‘cluster 2’, with significant H3K4me1 enrichment at genes associated with basal-like identity and EMT (Fig. 3f,g and Extended Data Fig. 8g,i). In tumour 15, cluster 1 was also enriched for basal-like genes (adjusted P < 0.05), but not EMT. H3K4me3 similarly identified basal-like subpopulations in all tumours (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 8h,i). Accordingly, peaks associated with these clusters showed enrichment for transcription factor motifs linked to EMT and basal-like identity (Supplementary Fig. 7a). Next, we trained a classifier to identify H3K4me1-marked and H3K4me3-marked genes that contribute to variation between the clusters. For both histone methylations, these genes were enriched in terms related to breast cancer cellular identity, including oestrogen signalling, basal-like and mesenchymal identity (Supplementary Fig. 7b–e). Overall, our analysis provides support for chromatin-defined cell states in luminal tumour cells, including a basal-like state distinguished by H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 distributions.

Recent findings suggest that the above snCUT&Tag results aligned with the heterogeneity observed by CyTOF, which led us to compare the single-cell datasets and integrating both genomic and protein information. CyTOF-defined basal-like cells highlighted global increases in both H3K4 methylation marks. We reasoned that sequencing reads per nucleus may reflect global levels of the target modification. Single-cell epigenomic analyses generally assume similar global modification levels, discarding read-count information, as in our analysis above61 (Fig. 3e–h). Departing from this convention, we examined whether read counts capture additional aspects of epigenetic heterogeneity. Across all three tumours and both modifications, read counts negatively correlated with luminal identity signatures and positively with basal-like and mesenchymal signatures (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 9a,b). Consistently, cells with high read counts, potentially indicative of elevated global levels of H3K4me1 or H3K4me3, showed less enrichment of these active marks at luminal identity genes. Although requiring further validation, this direct comparison suggests that read counts may serve as proxy for global levels of histone modifications to capture additional aspects of epigenetic variation.

Industry observers note that to further integrate these datasets, we label-transferred the CyTOF classification (Figs. 1 and 2) onto the H3K4me1 snCUT&Tag dataset. CyTOF-predicted basal-like populations were enriched in the basal-like clusters identified by H3K4me1 genomic profiling (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 9b). For tumour 15, cluster 1 was also predicted to comprise basal-like cells, consistent with its higher H3K4me1 deposition on basal-like-associated genes (Fig. 3g and Extended Data Fig. 9c). CyTOF-predicted basal-like cells also revealed higher H3K4me1 deposition at EMT and basal-like gene signatures, which further confirmed their distinct epigenetic and functional features (Extended Data Fig. 9d). To validate these results, we sorted luminal PDX models and MCF7 cells by K5 expression, followed by H3K4me1 CUT&Tag. K5low-specific peaks were enriched near oestrogen signalling genes, whereas K5hi-specific peaks were associated with basal-like and mesenchymal programs, which confirmed the distinct H3K4me1 landscapes between subpopulations (Extended Data Fig. 9e). Together, the protein abundance and genomic distribution data implicate H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 as epigenetic determinants of the basal-like subpopulation in luminal tumours.

The repressive mark H3K9me2 was also identified as a strong contributor to the epigenetic basal-like signature (Fig. 2d,e). Thus, we conducted H3K9me2 snCUT&Tag on tumour 8, which was also profiled for H3K4me1. Given that H3K9me2 occupies large genomic regions, its distribution is not readily interpretable in relation to gene activity, especially in low-coverage single-cell datasets. We therefore leveraged the H3K4me1 data and trained a classifier, assuming opposing genomic distributions of enhancer-associated H3K4me1 and repressive H3K9me2 chromatin62,63, to identify malignant versus stromal cells (Extended Data Fig. 9f). We next clustered tumour cells by H3K9me2 genomic distribution and applied the same H3K4me1-based inference framework. This approach predicted strong enrichment of basal-like cells in cluster 4, consistent with elevated H3K9me2 deposition on oestrogen-related genes (Extended Data Fig. 9g–i). This cluster also showed the highest H3K9me2 read counts per nucleus, which provided support for its correspondence to the H3K9me2hi basal-like cells identified by CyTOF (Extended Data Fig. 9j). Overall, these analyses highlight an epigenetically distinct basal-like population with globally increased and redistributed active and repressive histone modifications over genes associated with luminal-basal identity and EMT.

Our multimodal analysis linked the chromatin landscape to intratumoural cell-state diversity. We next aimed to translate our tissue-level findings to a liquid biopsy test based on our single-molecule EPINUC technology, which profiles the epigenetics of plasma-isolated nucleosomes28,29. We tailored EPINUC for breast cancer by developing single-molecule systems to quantify the breast-tissue-related proteins K5, L1CAM and MUC1, and added the histone PTMs H4K16ac and H4K20me3 (refs. 64,65,66,67) (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Table 5 and Supplementary Fig. 8a–c). Nucleosomes from plasma were captured and their combinatorial modifications imaged by TIRF microscopy, whereas protein biomarkers were quantified in parallel single-molecule antibody-capture assays (Fig. 4a). The expanded 29-parameter panel was applied to a cohort of plasma from 77 women with luminal breast cancer and 30 healthy women, and the results revealed significant differences (Supplementary Table 6). For example, cancer samples contained more H3K9ac and H4K16ac nucleosomes (Fig. 4b). As PTMs were normalized to nucleosome abundance, these differences reflect the epigenetic state rather than tumour burden. We also used EPINUC to measure PTM ratios and co-occurrence, which revealed increased bivalent (H3K4me3 and H3K27me3) nucleosomes, as previously observed in colorectal cancer and pancreatic cancer28. Indeed, bivalency is altered across cancers68, and can prime drug-tolerant persister programs in breast cancer19.

It has been revealed that L1CAM and MST1 were also elevated in plasma from patients with breast cancer, a result in agreement with the association of high MST1 with poor prognosis in ER+ tumours69 (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 8d). Multiple parameters differed between healthy individuals and patients diagnosed with early-stage (T1) low-burden tumours, which demonstrated the early detection sensitivity of this method (Fig. 4b). Predictive power scores (PPS) revealed the contribution of the newly measured H4 PTMs, selected on the basis of the CyTOF analysis, which illustrates the value of matched tissue–plasma profiling (Fig. 4c). Principal component analysis (PCA) of predictive features separated healthy individuals from patients with breast cancer, which highlights the ability of EPINUC to capture differences between these groups (Fig. 4d).

We next applied machine-learning-based classifiers to diagnose luminal breast cancer from EPINUC data. SHAP analysis of XGBoost models trained on all patients, or only stage T1 cases, identified multiple histone PTMs and protein biomarkers as informative (Fig. 4e). Notably, both models emphasized combinatorial features, particularly H4K16ac and H4K20me3 co-occurrence, thereby highlighting the ability of EPINUC to quantify such combinations. In particular, H4K16ac activates transcription of transposable elements70, which reside in H4K20me3 heterochromatin71, and because transposable elements are often upregulated in cancer, elevated H4K16ac and H4K20me3 might be a cancer-associated phenomenon. Finally, we applied several classifiers to assess the diagnostic contribution of the expanded EPINUC panel in discriminating healthy individuals from patients with cancer. Use the original 20 EPINUC parameters28 produced an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.85 (Supplementary Fig. 9a), whereas the expanded 29-parameter panel achieved 0.95, including among patients with early-stage T1 cancer (Fig. 4f,g). Unlike mammography, the sensitivity of which declines with dense breast tissue72,73, the features and performance of EPINUC were unaffected by different BI-RADS breast density scores, including patients with heterogeneous and extremely dense breast scores (Supplementary Fig. 9b,c). To assess the robustness of the EPINUC-based classifier, we applied the model trained on the original cohort (MAYO-1; Fig. 4f) to an independent, separately processed set of plasma samples collected 6–12 months later (MAYO-2). Following batch correction (Methods), the pre-trained model accurately distinguished healthy from luminal breast cancer, achieving an AUC of 0.98 and high classification accuracy (Extended Data Fig. 10a,b).

It has been revealed that to generalize our findings, we analysed pretreatment plasma from patients with luminal breast cancer at two independent medical centres (Supplementary Table 6). EPINUC distinguished patients from healthy controls with high accuracy in both cohorts and highlighted comparable sensitivity and specificity in TNBC (Extended Data Fig. 10c–e). Pooling all luminal samples across centres (n = 188), a model trained on 75% of the data achieved an AUC of 0.96 and robustly classified the remaining 25% despite mixed sources and batches, a scenario that reflects real-world clinical settings (Fig. 4h, Extended Data Fig. 10f and Supplementary Fig. 10). Performance was similar for luminal A and luminal B tumours (Extended Data Fig. 10g). Although retrospective, these results support the use of high-resolution, multiparametric plasma epigenetic analyses for cancer diagnosis.

MAYO-1 comprised preoperative samples with at least 5 years of clinical follow-up, which enabled stratification by 5-year recurrence (Fig. 5a). Already at diagnosis, several EPINUC features differed between patients who were disease-free and patients who had relapsed disease. H3K4 monomethylation and trimethylation, associated with the aggressive basal-like subpopulation, were elevated in plasma of patients developing recurrent disease (Fig. 5b). H3K27me3 and H3K9ac were also elevated, perhaps reflecting other aggressive tumour or microenvironmental states, such as cycling cells that were particularly high for histone acetylations (Extended Data Fig. 1b). Nucleosomes modified with both H3K9ac and H3K4me1 were higher in the recurrence group, a result that further demonstrates the power of EPINUC in capturing these combinations (Fig. 5b). ER or PR status did not associate with relapse (Fisher’s exact test, P > 0.05), and the epigenetic signature persisted in tumours with the following characteristics: comparable ER and PR levels; only luminal A tumours; low-burden T1–T2 or grade 1–2 disease; and tumours without lymphovascular invasion (LVI). No EPINUC feature was significantly associated with histological grade, which indicates that there is prognostic information beyond known clinical parameters (Extended Data Fig. 11a–f).

Lines show Theil–Sen fit, shading indicates 95% CI. e, XGBoost classifier distinguishing disease-free (n = 44) and relapse (n = 33) groups using all EPINUC features. SHAP scores indicate the contribution of each epigenetic feature to classifier performance, ranked by importance. f–i, Recurrence prediction in patients with luminal breast cancer. f, ROC curve for the MAYO-1 cohort (disease-free, n = 44; relapse, n = 33; AUC = 0.81, 95% CI 0.71–0.90). g, AUC estimates for patients with complete clinical annotation (disease-free, n = 39; relapse, n = 28), using clinical prognostic variables (age, tumour stage, lymph-node stage, grade and luminal subtype), EPINUC features or both. h, ROC curve for the independent MAYO-2 cohort (disease-free, n = 20; relapse, n = 10; AUC = 0.92, 95% CI 0.79–1.00). i, ROC curves and AUC estimates using OncotypeDX score, EPINUC features, or both, among patients with available OncotypeDX measurements, comparing disease-free (n = 40) and relapse (n = 9). For ROC curves, shading indicates 95% CI; for AUC estimates, points and lines indicate AUC and 95% CI, respectively. Schematic in a created in BioRender; Furth, N. https://biorender.com/xg9gtix (2026).

To further explore the association between tumour and plasma epigenetic patterns, we analysed a small cohort of luminal tumours with histone PTM mass-spectrometry data39, which were similarly stratified by disease recurrence39. H3K4me1 and H3K9me2, which marked the basal-like cells in our CyTOF data, were significantly higher in patients who developed recurrence, a result that further links this subpopulation to aggressive tumour traits (Figs. 2e and 5c). Finally, for patients analysed in Figs. 1–3, we obtained preoperative blood samples, which enabled direct correlation of tumour (CyTOF) and blood (EPINUC) epigenetic patterns. Most histone PTMs correlated positively, with the recurrence-associated H3K4me1 and H3K9ac marks showing the strongest positive correlation, a result that provided further support for their prognostic value (Fig. 5d and Extended Data Fig. 11h). Although requiring larger validation, these data suggest that circulating nucleosomes report both the tumour presence and its epigenetic state, a finding with potentially vital implications for clinical management.

According to recent reports, to examine the prognostic power of EPINUC to predict disease recurrence, we applied machine-learning classifiers on the multiparametric data. The best model achieved an AUC of 0.81, and outperformed predictions based on classical prognostic parameters such as stage, grade and subtype (Fig. 5e–g and Extended Data Fig. 11i). To assess reproducibility and to benchmark established assays, MAYO-2 was focused on samples with available OncotypeDX scores74. Despite its smaller size, EPINUC predicted recurrence with an AUC of 0.92 (Fig. 5h). Across patients with OncotypeDX data from both cohorts, scores did not differ between disease-free and relapsed groups, whereas EPINUC retained discriminatory power (Fig. 5i, Extended Data Fig. 11j and Supplementary Fig. 11). Combining assays did not improve performance, which indicated limited added value from OncotypeDX in this setting. Overall, the data suggest that epigenetic signatures of tumour cell subpopulations, such as basal-like cells, may be captured in blood and provide insight into disease biology beyond the static tissue-based prognostic window. Pending larger prospective validation, these findings provide support for the use of EPINUC for early diagnosis and recurrence-risk stratification.

Sources indicate that single-cell studies have revealed clinically relevant phenotypic diversity across cancers, yet the epigenetic mechanisms fuelling this heterogeneity remain poorly understood75,76. Our analysis of luminal breast tumours uncovered tumour cell diversity consistent with previous transcriptomic and proteomic approaches14,21,33,34,54. Quantitative mass-spectrometry also revealed differences in global histone modification levels between breast cancer subtypes, which provides support for the idea that chromatin regulates cell identity39,77,78. Altered H3K4 demethylation can drive loss of luminal identity40, which suggests that changes in ER signalling, even without ESR1 mutations, may promote luminal-to-basal plasticity. Here we performed single-cell profiling of histone PTMs in luminal breast tumours. By measuring multiple global chromatin modifications at single-cell resolution, we identified a recurrent epigenetic signature of K5hi basal-like cells across tumours, supported across modalities by single-cell genomic profiling of H3K4 methylation.

Reconstitution of the full heterogeneity spectrum in single-cell-derived MCF7 clones and independently grown PDX tumours provides support for epigenetically driven, interconverting states rather than genetically distinct clones. Subpopulation frequencies varied among patients and may be influenced by mutations that bias state acquisition, as reported in glioblastoma46. This plasticity may enable adaptation to therapeutic pressures, which then promotes resistance and progression. Accordingly, proteomic intratumoural heterogeneity increases with tumour grade independently of genomic heterogeneity, thereby implicating epigenetic mechanisms7. Whether epigenetic therapies can limit plasticity and state transitions remains to be tested.

Sources indicate that breast cancer prognosis depends strongly on early detection, yet accurate screening while minimizing false positives remains challenging79,80,81,82. Detection of molecular changes before clinical progression could guide treatment adaptation and maximize first-line benefit83. Tumour-level histone PTM signatures distinguished luminal breast cancer cell states, whereas EPINUC analysis of pretreatment plasma samples provided proof-of-concept for outcome prediction. Notably, H3K4 methylation marks were elevated in both basal-like tumour cells and in plasma from patients with recurrent disease, which suggests that there is a link between this subpopulation and disease outcome.

According to recent reports, unlike CyTOF, which resolves tumour cell populations, plasma measurements integrate signals from damage of healthy tissue, the tumour microenvironment and local and systemic immune responses29,84. Nevertheless, patient-matched histone PTMs analyses in tumours and blood revealed a positive correlation for most marks, with the highest correlation observed for the recurrence-associated marks H3K4me1 and H3K9ac, which provides support for their prognostic value. Overall, our tissue and plasma chromatin dataset reveals epigenetically driven intratumoural heterogeneity in breast cancer and supports the use of EPINUC as a potential approach for breast cancer diagnosis and prognosis.
