Kevin De Bruyne responds to PSV Eindhoven transfer amid Napoli exit rumours

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Naim Beneddra | 15 Nov 2026 08:10.
  • Former Manchester City midfielder Kevin De Bruyne has refused to rule out a surprise January move to PSV Eindhoven, with the Dutch champions reportedly making contact over a potential deal to end his difficult spell at Napoli.
  • The 35-year-old Belgium international has emerged as an ambitious transfer target for PSV, who are exploring the possibility of bringing him back to the Netherlands after just 18 months in Italian football.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Naim Beneddra | 15 Nov 2026 08:10.

Former Manchester City midfielder Kevin De Bruyne has refused to rule out a surprise January move to PSV Eindhoven, with the Dutch champions reportedly making contact over a potential deal to end his difficult spell at Napoli.

The 35-year-old Belgium international has emerged as an ambitious transfer target for PSV, who are exploring the possibility of bringing him back to the Netherlands after just 18 months in Italian football.

According to Dutch publication Voetbal International, PSV have already approached De Bruyne's representatives, with preliminary discussions taking place over a potential winter transfer.

The former Premier League star addressed the speculation following Belgium's 2-1 Nations League victory over Turkey on Thursday, a match in which he scored.

While De Bruyne insisted that he remains happy with his current physical condition and performances, he stopped short of dismissing the possibility of leaving Napoli.

His response comes amid reports of growing uncertainty surrounding his future under Massimiliano Allegri, with PSV hoping to take advantage of his contractual situation.

Speaking to Belgian broadcaster VTM Nieuws after the Turkey match, De Bruyne was asked directly about reports linking him with a move to Eindhoven.

According to recent reports, "I can't say too much about it. At the moment I'm happy," the midfielder explained.

"I feel good, I'm playing every match at a good level. And what comes, comes. It's not the time to talk about it now.

"I know how it works. There are always lots of rumours. I stay calm about it – you know me. I'm happy with my level and how I feel physically. That's all that matters.".

Asked whether PSV's interest was mutual, De Bruyne offered a brief response: "We'll see.".

His comments followed reports in the Netherlands that PSV had begun assessing the financial conditions required to secure his signature.

Voetbal International confirmed that the Eredivisie club had made enquiries and established contact with the player, although the publication stressed that their interest remained at an early stage.

Italian newspaper Gazzetta dello Sport has subsequently reported that PSV also approached Napoli to clarify the club's intentions regarding De Bruyne's contract.

The Belgian's current agreement expires in June 2027, but Napoli hold an option to extend it by another season.

That clause could prove key to negotiations, with the Italian side yet to confirm whether they would consider allowing their experienced playmaker to leave midway through the campaign.

Belgium manager Mark van Bommel, who previously played for and managed PSV, believes the Dutch club could offer De Bruyne a suitable environment.

"He has to make the decision himself, but he doesn't live far away and Dutch football suits him," Van Bommel told VTM Nieuws.

"The attacking way of playing, always wanting to play football, that fits him.".

Current PSV manager Peter Bosz has also spoken highly of De Bruyne in the past, describing him as one of the greatest players in football history.

De Bruyne joined Napoli on a free transfer in the summer of 2025 following a decade at Manchester City, where he established himself as one of the Premier League's greatest midfielders.

However, his first season in Italy was disrupted by a hamstring injury that sidelined him for more than four months.

Napoli also failed to retain their Serie A title, while De Bruyne subsequently criticised former manager Antonio Conte's defensive approach.

The Belgian explained that he had struggled to operate in his preferred position and questioned the team's attacking ambition under the Italian.

Conte's replacement, Allegri, has not brought the improvement in results Napoli had hoped for.

The club sit 10th in Serie A after 11 matches and have lost three of their opening four Champions League fixtures, increasing scrutiny of their performances.

De Bruyne has also experienced reported disagreements with Allegri over his tactical role, although he remains an crucial member of the side.

Indeed, he has featured in all 15 of Napoli's competitive matches this season, contributing four goals and two assists.

His availability and productivity suggest that a January departure would not simply be the consequence of losing his place in the starting lineup.

There is also a personal dimension to the speculation.

De Bruyne's wife, Michele Lacroix, spoke in September about the family's difficulties adapting to life in Naples and their desire to return to Belgium.

In a recent development, "We want to live here, in Limburg. The sooner, the better," she told Belgian magazine NINA.

It has been revealed that "Kevin leads a very limited life in Naples. It's not much fun for him. Besides, we can't do anything together as a family in the city.".

Eindhoven's proximity to the Belgian border could make PSV an appealing destination, although De Bruyne has not publicly linked his family's circumstances to a possible transfer.

The midfielder has also been linked with a return to the Premier League through Everton, who were reportedly assessing their chances of securing his services earlier this month.

For PSV, the main obstacles remain Napoli's willingness to negotiate and the financial demands involved in signing a player of De Bruyne's stature.

With no agreement in place, his latest comments leave the possibility of a January move open without indicating that a departure has been decided.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ben Knapton | 15 Nov 2026 08:18.
  • Manchester City are reportedly on the verge of agreeing a upcoming deal with midfielder-turned-defender Matheus Nunes.
  • The former Wolverhampton Wanderers man is still on the same terms he agreed upon his arrival in 2023, and he is currently due to become a free agent in 2028.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 15 Nov 2026 08:18.

Manchester City are reportedly on the verge of agreeing a upcoming deal with midfielder-turned-defender Matheus Nunes.

The former Wolverhampton Wanderers man is still on the same terms he agreed upon his arrival in 2023, and he is currently due to become a free agent in 2028.

However, Nunes has become a key figure for the Sky Blues at right-back, managing a combined 13 assists across the last two Premier League campaigns after switching from a central midfield role.

Nunes started 32 Premier League matches in Pep Guardiola's farewell season last term, although he is yet to score or assist in 10 games across all competitions in the current season.

Nevertheless, the Portugal international's contributions have not gone unnoticed, and according to the Manchester Evening News, a renewal is close to being sealed.

Real Madrid manager Jose Mourinho is supposedly interested in signing Nunes, but City have no intention of letting the 28-year-old go and are in talks over a newly introduced three-year agreement.

Nunes is believed to be earning around £130,000 a week at the Etihad Stadium, but his fresh deal would include a £20k-a-week pay rise, taking him up to £150,000 a week.

The defender would subsequently be on the same salary as midfielders Mateo Kovacic and Ayyoub Bouaddi, and City are supposedly confident of retaining his services despite lingering uncertainty over their charges appeal.

Having been found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules, Man City - who have always vehemently denied the charges - could lose their Premier League status if their appeal against the charges outcome fails.

Nevertheless, the Sky Blues have supposedly stressed that their players remain content at the Etihad, and it should only be a matter of time before Nunes's new deal is announced.

The 28-year-old signed for Man City from Wolves for £51.7m in the summer of 2023, since when he has scored five goals and set up 25 more in 131 games for the club in all tournaments.

Nunes has won the Premier League, Club World Cup, FA Cup, EFL Cup and Community Shield at the Etihad Stadium and was also called up to Portugal's World Cup 2026 squad, but he played just one minute in North America.

Nunes is one of four City players who could depart for nothing in either 2027 or 2028; Kovacic and Marcus Bettinelli are due to become free agents next year, while backup goalkeeper Geronimo Rulli is out of contract at the end of next season.

Amid concerns over Gianluigi Donnarumma's form, Rulli may be in line for an extension if he earns a shot in between the sticks and manages to prove himself, although the Argentinian is already 34 years old.

Meanwhile, Ruben Dias and Vitor Reis both see their deals expire in 2029, but the former will likely be in line for at least a newly introduced short-term deal in the not-so-distant future.

Tech Report: Arsenal-linked Antonio Nusa channels 'inner Ronaldinho' as Norwegian media hail RB Leipzig star

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ben Knapton | 15 Nov 2026 09:45.
  • Arsenal-linked attacker Antonio Nusa sent tongues wagging once again with a standout performance in Norway's 3-1 UEFA Nations League victory over Wales on Saturday night.
  • The RB Leipzig protege has been linked with a £66m move to Arsenal in 2027, with sporting director Andrea Berta apparently accelerating his plans to bring Nusa to the Emirates Stadium.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 15 Nov 2026 09:45.

Arsenal-linked attacker Antonio Nusa sent tongues wagging once again with a standout performance in Norway's 3-1 UEFA Nations League victory over Wales on Saturday night.

The RB Leipzig protege has been linked with a £66m move to Arsenal in 2027, with sporting director Andrea Berta apparently accelerating his plans to bring Nusa to the Emirates Stadium.

The 21-year-old did his hopes of a marquee transfer no harm whatsoever in Norway's triumph against Wales, most notably opening the scoring on the stroke of the hour mark with a low strike from the edge of the area.

Nusa was a livewire all evening for Norway, having also registered four shots, drawn two fouls, completed nine progressive carries and created three chances at Ullevaal Stadium, triggering high praise from the Norwegian media in the process.

Nusa was awarded an 8/10 rating from Tipsbladet, who hailed the Leipzig winger for 'doing everything on his own' and being a 'constant moment of unrest' for Welsh defenders.

433 also gave Nusa an eight for being "Norway's biggest threat" on the night, as well as 'igniting the crowd' with his effervescent performance on the left-hand side.

VG, meanwhile, made an extremely bold claim, stating that Nusa brought out his 'inner Ronaldinho', reflecting on a moment when the Arsenal target took out several Wales players with a mazy dribble before being unable to find the target.

Aftenposten could not help but wax lyrical about Nusa either, labelling the 21-year-old the 'wizard' that fans came to see, and a player who strikes 'terror' into opposing defenders.

The Nusa love-in was not limited to Norwegian commentators, as Wales boss Craig Bellamy told the media after the game that he would put the Leipzig man in the top three or four players in the world in his position.

"If I was in one of the top three, four, five clubs in the world, I would have signed him," VG quotes Bellamy as saying. "If I had the money, of course, because he is going to be very expensive. But I would go all in for him.

According to recent reports, "I think he is a very special player. Difficult to control. Physically absolutely enormous. In terms of wingers, I would put him among the three or four best players in the world in that area.".

Norway's triumph leaves the Nordic nation third in League A Group 4 on six points from five games, three adrift of second-placed Denmark, whom they face in Tuesday's finale.

Victory for Norway in Copenhagen will guarantee a quarter-final place for Stale Solbakken's men, but failure to win will see them either qualify for the relegation playoffs or suffer an immediate demotion to League B.

Nusa now boasts 10 goals and 10 assists in 35 caps for Norway, while he has registered a striking six goals and eight assists in 15 matches for Leipzig in the 2026-27 season.

AC Milan’s former sporting director Igli Tare has explained that an injury most likely kept Niclas Füllkrug from taking off at AC Milan, scoring just one goal.

According to recent reports, it was at the start of January of this year that Milan decided to bring in Füllkrug to bolster the No.9 position for the second half of the season. While the start was encouraging on the pitch, with the winner against Lecce on January 18, he never really took off.

According to recent reports, actually, if you knew what was going on behind the scenes, the start wasn’t even that encouraging. Just over a week or so after joining, he broke his toe and it ended up having a huge effect on the entire loan spell.

Sources indicate that speaking to Sky Sport last night, Milan’s former sporting director Tare was asked about the signing of Füllkrug. This season, the German has scored 12 goals in 11 games for Werder Bremen and the director believes he could have had those numbers for the Rossoneri without the injury.

Recent findings suggest that füllkrug performed poorly in Milan, but in the Bundesliga he’s scoring a lot and is the top scorer. How do you explain that?

“It’s simple. He came to us after a tough time in England, with a lot of scepticism. And then, right away, he broke his toe. No one ever noted he’d been having injections on the bone for two months just to train, let alone to play.

“I knew he was a centre forward that the team was missing; given his characteristics and his interpretation of the game, his qualities were unquestionable. Just two years before coming to Milan, he’d played in the Champions League final, playing a key role in a competition with Borussia Dortmund,” he stated.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Jonathan O'Shea | 15 Nov 2026 10:02.
  • Austria have already wrapped up UEFA Nations League promotion before they face Israel in their final League B Group 3 fixture on Tuesday.
  • Set to meet in neutral Debrecen, Ralf Rangnick's men are confirmed in first place, while the Israelis are at risk of relegation to League C.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jonathan O'Shea | 15 Nov 2026 10:02.

Austria have already wrapped up UEFA Nations League promotion before they face Israel in their final League B Group 3 fixture on Tuesday.

Set to meet in neutral Debrecen, Ralf Rangnick's men are confirmed in first place, while the Israelis are at risk of relegation to League C.

Beaten by Serbia in the playoffs last time around - which cost them promotion to Europe's top tier - Austria have made no mistake in this season's Nations League.

With one game to go, they are already assured of a place in League A for the next edition, having built an unassailable five-point lead at the top of Group 3.

First place was confirmed at the Raiffeisen Arena on Saturday night, when substitute Sasa Kalajdzic poked home from close range to secure victory over the Republic of Ireland.

Heading towards the final 10 minutes, the LASK Linz striker finally ended a stubborn resistance from Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher, who had kept the hosts at bay with a string of sharp saves.

Having reached the knockout phase at the World Cup, Rangnick's side were always favourites to prevail in Group 3, and they never looked back after winning both of their first two fixtures.

In September, they kicked off by beating 10-man Israel 3-1, with Kalajdzic netting one of two late goals in Linz.

While their opponents are ranked 23rd by FIFA, Israel sit 76th in the global list and they lie rock-bottom of Group 3 as things stand.

After dropping down from League A in the previous edition, with only one win from six, the Israelis are on course for back-to-back relegations.

Ran Ben Shimon's side will either finish third and enter the demotion/promotion playoffs against a League C nation, or suffer automatic relegation once again.

It could be a complex conclusion to the group on Tuesday evening, but the best chance for Israel to avoid last place is by beating Austria and seeing Kosovo win in Dublin.

After holding the latter to a goalless draw at the weekend, the Sky Blue and Whites trail Ireland by two points and Kosovo by three, so their fate is out of their own hands.

Given they are guaranteed top spot, Austria may decide to rotate, as Rangnick continues to build for the future without some familiar faces.

Marko Arnautovic retired from international football after the World Cup, captain David Alaba has not been selected after struggling for fitness at Udinese, while Marcel Sabitzer is taking a break.

One of the new guard, Carney Chukwuemeka previously withdrew with a hamstring injury, while Werder Bremen winger Marco Grull pulled out because of a calf problem.

Israel will be missing key defender Raz Shlomo, who must serve a suspension for accumulated bookings; Barcelona teenager Orian Goren is also unavailable due to a muscular issue.

Dor Peretz - who scored in a Qatar 2022 qualifier against Austria - should join Ajax forward Oscar Gloukh in support of a lone striker.

With just two international goals between them, Idan Gorno and Dor Turgeman are the main contenders to feature up front.

Israel possible starting lineup:.

Da. Peretz; Dasa, Feingold, Nachimas, Stoinov, Revivo; Abada, Azoulay, Do. Peretz, Gloukh; Turgeman.

Austria possible starting lineup:.

Jungwirth; Posch, Svoboda, Affengruber, Prass; Seiwald, Laimer; Demir, Baumgartner, Schmid; Kalajdzic.

Though they might take their foot off the gas with promotion secured, Austria are a class above their final Group 3 opponents.

Rangnick's side remain unbeaten in five games so far - while scoring at a rate of two goals per game - and they can finish with a flourish in Hungary.

Published: 18:49 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:49 EST, 14 November 2026.

THE guy with the flyer was persistent.

In a recent development, ‘Mate, we are walking out in the 21st minute to protest 21 years of the Glazers. Will you join us?’ he asks earnestly, handing me a leaflet that announces: ‘Enough is Enough! Empty Old Trafford! Leave the stadium in the 21st minute. 21 years of failed ownership. Glazers OUT! Ineos OUT!’.

More than 70,000 spectators leaving their seat and walking out of the stadium in the 21st minute have been quite the statement, especially live on Sky Sports.

But as admirable as Saeed TV’s aim is (I discover later he is some sort of youtuber), it’s hard to see gain any traction.

Sources indicate that ‘Dad, we are not walking out of the match. It’s my first time in Old Trafford,’ I am told as we continue to meander up Matt Busby Way, a declaration from my 10-year-old that causes a fair bit of mirth among the crowd.

Mate, we are walking out in the 21st minute to protest 21 years of the Glazers. Will you join us?’.

‘What’s wrong with the owners anyway?’ Dan enquires innocently, which leads to a bind.

How deep down the rabbit-hole should I go with my ten-year-old on his first visit to the Theatre of Dreams.

According to recent reports, it’s probably not the time or place to try and explain leveraged buyouts and how much debt the Glazers have saddled the club with, £1.2 billion at the last count while taking millions out of it in dividends. Do I need to go further back and talk about Rock of Gibraltar’s unexpected success on the track and the concept of stud fees?

‘They are not putting enough money into the team and taking loads of money out of the club,’ is all I offer.

‘When Manchester City need a midfielder, they can buy Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez while United have to make do with someone who was sitting on Chelsea’s bench.’.

He doesn’t look convinced that’s much of a reason to walk out of a football but as the cathedral of consumerism that is the Manchester United megastore has appeared, he forgets about United’s disastrous ownership model – for now, at least.

During his doomed attempt to coax Jurgen Klopp to Old Trafford around 2014, Ed Woodward apparently told him that United was the sporting version of Disneyland.

And to be sardined inside the megastore in the couple of hours before kick-off, you have to accept that the much-maligned former CEO may have been right about one thing.

Sources indicate that think Arnott’s a couple of days before Christmas, just with a lot more people. You even need to pass through airport-like security before even entering and spend your dosh.

One of the common refrains among United supporters is why are the Glazers holding onto the club when they don’t even seem to care.

Thirty seconds inside the megastore on match-day and you realise why the Americans are so keen to hold onto the asset they’re bleeding dry – and they probably care a great deal.

Dan gets obligatory photo at statue of United's holy trinity, a moment he will look back on.

Even with the team languishing in the relegation zone, having won a single league game all season, people are keen to spend, spend, spend.

I see people wandering around with five or six different shirts, from different eras (I did succumb and bought Dan the black shirt from 95-96 season, because it reminds me of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and better times!).

It has been revealed that you can get a photo with a replica of a Premier League trophy. That’s just £10. Or Lego sets of Old Trafford or the Munich clock.

In a recent development, that will just set you back £25. For many in this shop, it seems allowing the club to empty their wallet is as much a part of the day as the actual football.

There are other parts of the ritual, which remain and have yet to be infected by the poisonous atmosphere around the club – and remind the three dads bringing their kids to Old Trafford for the first time of better days.

Such as curry chips and battered sausage from Lou Macari’s chipper. And the customary photo in front of the statue of the holy trinity of Best, Law and Charlton.

The megastore was the one place that seemed immune to the toxicity in the air. Once outside again and all that could be heard was the moans and groans, mainly because Shea Lacey wasn’t starting.

Industry observers note that coming here since the 1990s, we have seen the skyline of Manchester transformed as it became a sleek, modern city. It seems the one place that hasn’t changed is Old Trafford. It has remained the same.

Stuck in time. It looked sleek and modern in 1999, but now there is a tired, decrepit feel to the stadium – and not just because of the leaking roof. It could do with a lick or two of paint.

Stuck in time. It looked sleek and modern in 1999, but now there is a tired, decrepit feel to the stadium.

No wonder Massive Sir Jim is determined to plough ahead with his prepares to make a crudely-designed circus tent ‘the Wembley of the North.’ Not that there is anyone inside Old Trafford of the same mind.

Senne Lammens has just trotted onto the field with Tom Heaton and Karl Darlow to do their pre-match warm-up when the chants start, telling Jim Ratcliffe he can stick his newly introduced stadium up his posterior.

It is a weird atmosphere, with all the chanting against the owners – both Glazers and Ineos – and nothing being sung in support of the players.

As my friend points out it must be so difficult for the team to show the best of themselves when things are this toxic in the stadium.

Dan has been to the Jodi Stand enough times on a Friday night to know there is plenty of choice and crude language at football matches, but still I nearly felt at covering his ears at some of the stuff being sung in Old Trafford last Sunday, especially that directed at CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

We had hoped that things might have been different when the game kicked off, but within a minute, Aston Villa had scored.

And three minutes later, they had scored again when Lammens fumbled Alysson’s shot into Nicolas Jackson’s path. Maybe walking out in the 21st minute wasn’t such a bad idea.

Industry observers note that the crowd’s ire had gone from the owners to the players now, with a sustained chant of ‘You are not fit to wear the shirt.’ United did rally and by half-time, it was 2-2. But the mood was still dismal as we queued for a quick beer.

Recent findings suggest that the 1958 Group had asked fans not to buy booze, another protest against the owners. But it seemed nobody was paying much attention to that.

One of the issues at United is that there seem to be too many splintered fan groups – there is also ClaimBackUnited and Fan Coalition ’58 – as well as Saeed TV, who seemed to be on his own solo run.

Industry observers note that we didn’t feel bad about ignoring the booze ban, as everyone was doing it. And within a couple of minutes of the second-half, we saw the reason why. You need to fortify yourself to watch Diogo Dalot try to defend.

For much of the second-half, it seemed like Michael Carrick’s brief tenure was going to peter out in a forgettable defeat, as Villa seemed to manage the game perfectly.

Dan and his friends were growing frustrated, pointing out the players weren’t doing what their coaches tell them to do on a weekly basis, leading me to conclude that maybe my son’s under-11 side are better-coached than United.

The last on-pitch act of Carrick's tenure.

And then there was the chaotic and crazy final few minutes in stoppage-time. And a draw that came out of nowhere and was celebrated like a victory.

That was the thing. Even though the mood inside the stadium was toxic for most of the game, even though the team were two down inside four minutes and the season has been a disaster, everyone still came away from Old Trafford, happy and with a smile on their face.

Sources indicate that only football can do that. More than that, perhaps only Manchester United – despite everything – can do that.

There have been some dark days in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era but this was up there with the very worst of them: the kind of performance that gets a manager sacked, the kind of display that points to a fundamental disconnect, the kind of occasion that leaves you thinking Manchester United are as far away as they have ever been.

When players seem so averse to doing the very basics, such as running, and the club habitually have such trouble attracting the right profiles and personalities, it is hard to escape the feeling that saying goodbye to another manager is going to do little more than paper over the many cracks at Old Trafford.

But, watching this, you had to think Michael Carrick will do well to limp on as far as Sunday, when United face Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

Recent findings suggest that and that was before we had heard the United captain, Bruno Fernandes, appearing to call out the manager’s tactics just a week on from the last show of public dissent from a player, when Lisandro Martínez attacked the Old Trafford board. If only these players were as good at talking on the pitch.

At the final whistle, Carrick walked over to the 700-strong group of United supporters, held up both hands in apology on no fewer than seven occasions and then walked off down the tunnel without looking in the direction of any of his players.

There were shades of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer at Watford in November 2021, when he also held up his hands in apology before being sacked 24 hours later.

According to recent reports, in that instance, United fans booed Solskjaer. Carrick at least received some polite applause from the fans, who are a smart bunch and know the club’s problems extend far beyond the man in the dugout. Still, it is always the manager who pays the price. Solskjaer said he knew at half-time he was toast and Carrick is now under real threat himself – and seemingly at loggerheads with his captain.

Fernandes’s criticism of United’s set-up and approach was cutting and a direct attack on his manager and backroom team. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” the United captain said.

It has been revealed that carrick has been telling us for weeks that he and his squad are together, that the team are not too far away, that it is all about small margins. He even described Sunday’s 1-1 draw at Leeds as a “fresh start”. But Como blew the lid off any pretence of that being the case. Even by the standards of this season to date, though, what unfolded here in the rain in Lombardy was shocking to witness.

Como, inspired by the outstanding Nico Paz, were every bit as good as United – who have won just two of 11 games this season – were a pitiful mess.

According to recent reports, having conceded after just 47 seconds to Atlético Madrid last week, United were behind after only 118 seconds this time. That in itself told you a lot about these players and this team and it set the tone for what was to follow: a masterclass in incompetence and indifference. There have only been four worse results in United’s European history, although you will struggle to find a poorer performance than this.

Michael Carrick has insisted there is not a “toxic culture” at Manchester United in the wake of scathing criticism from former manager Erik ten Hag of the Old Trafford hierarchy and player power at the club.

The current United manager – who is under pressure after the club’s worst start to a season for 40 years – also believes he has the backing of the United board, despite Ten Hag accusing Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos regime of a series of “broken promises”.

In an interview with The Athletic, Ten Hag blamed Ratcliffe and his executives for fuelling a “toxic culture” by giving power to players and failing to back him on disciplinary matters relating to Marcus Rashford, Jadon Sancho and other first-teamers.

But Carrick remarked he had not encountered any toxicity since taking over from Ruben Amorim in January and suggested United’s last two outings, a 1-1 draw against Leeds United and a 2-0 defeat to Atlético Madrid, underlined the camaraderie in the group.

“Since I came back, the players and the staff have given us everything that they could give,” Carrick mentioned before Wednesday’s Champions League clash against Cesc Fàbregas’s Como in northern Italy, where he is battling an injury and illness crisis.

“We’ve had some good performances. We’ve had some performances that we want to do better and we can improve on. We’ve made some mistakes.

“But I have to say, the type of performance put into the weekend and for large parts against Atlético, there’s a lot of togetherness there. There’s a lot of will and determination to do better and wanting to do it for each other, which is notable.”.

Two wins – against Ipswich Town and Sabah – in United’s first 10 matches of the season, a public outburst from Lisandro Martínez and accusations of a “toxic culture” at the club have piled pressure on Carrick. And an uninspiring draw at Elland Road on Sunday did little to settle the rising tide of discontent within the United fanbase.

When asked for his team news, the first words that came from the United head coach’s mouth were: “Right, bit of mixed bag to be honest.” That was not a great sign, and Carrick will be without Martínez, Kobbie Mainoo, Luke Shaw, Ayden Heaven, Marcus Rashford, Benjamin Sesko and Patrick Dorgu, who are injured, while Leny Yoro serves a suspension following his red card against Atlético Madrid.

Like United, the hosts are without a handful of key players, with Moise Kean, Trevoh Chalobah, Assane Diao and Jesus Rodriguez missing from the match-day squad. The abundantly talented Argentine No 10 Nico Paz will feature, however, and he will be keen to showcase his talents in the Champions League.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Ahead of Sunday's UEFA Nations League battle between Spain and England, Sports Mole site coordinator Ben Knapton explains why the Three Lions only have a "10-15%" chance of topping the group and makes an intriguing claim over Ben White and Cole Palmer.
  • According to recent reports, I'd give them a very slim chance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 15 Nov 2026 10:43.

Ahead of Sunday's UEFA Nations League battle between Spain and England, Sports Mole site coordinator Ben Knapton explains why the Three Lions only have a "10-15%" chance of topping the group and makes an intriguing claim over Ben White and Cole Palmer.

According to recent reports, I'd give them a very slim chance. We know that any win will do because in the Nations League, head-to-head results take precedence over goal difference.

If England win by one goal, they're level with Spain on head-to-head points, head-to-head goal difference and head-to-head goals scored, so then overall goal difference takes precedence, where England are superior to Spain.

If they win by two or three goals, then they top the group as well.

It's quite hard to judge based on what we've seen in one game, especially because I think we're now at that point in the season where fatigue is building and domestic and European commitments are really ramping up, especially for Premier League players.

Recent findings suggest that I think we saw a bit of that in England's performance against Croatia. Quite a few standout names, I wouldn't say they had off nights, but they were just OK.

Lewis Hall was a standout, and Morgan Rogers too, but there was no one I really thought, "Wow, that was a magnificent individual display.".

A win against Croatia is still nothing really to be scoffed at, even if they're not the Croatia side that they used to be. But facing world champions Spain, it's not impossible, of course. Nothing is impossible in football, but it'd be a very slim chance for me.

There is one thing that England are better at than Spain recently; they've scored two or more goals in each of their last six games, while Spain have done it in each of their last five.

Although the last time Spain scored just the one goal was in the World Cup final, so I can't really get too big-headed on that front.

Spain are now unbeaten in 43 matches, they haven't lost in 32 months, so I'd be pretty shocked if England could get the job done.

It's going to be really interesting to see what Tuchel does team news wise, because we're hoping that he'll be boosted by as many as three returns for this game.

Lewis-Skelly was banned against Croatia, and he'll return here. Ezri Konsa and Djed Spence just trained individually before the Croatia game, but there's hope that they'll return. I would absolutely start Konsa over Quansah for this game.

It's going to be fascinating to see whether Ben White comes in at right-back. He was booed again last night when he came off the bench.

He previously came out and said that if people knew the full story, then they wouldn't boo him. Now I'm just thinking, if Cole Palmer comes back into the squad, is he going to get the same level of treatment?

It is not an identical situation to Ben White, pulling out for load management versus personal reasons, but that's one I'll be fascinated to see if he gets called up in March.

Interestingly, I have seen some criticism of Declan Rice in an England kit. With Arsenal, Arteta really plays to his strengths, dropping him in between the centre-backs, where he can play those line-breaking passes.

We don't really see that so often for England, so I've seen quite a few people saying if Alex Scott was in the squad, they would start him alongside Elliot Anderson.

In a recent development, lewis-Skelly is another option now that he's back from his ban, but I think it'll be Rice and Anderson in the middle. It'll be the same front four, but I would give them maybe a 10 to 15% chance of getting the win they need to top the group.

Cardinale says pre-season is ‘up to Amorim’ as Milan will not chase ‘extra two million’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gerry Cardinale has provided some refreshing comments on Milan’s pre-season plans for the future, confirming that money will no longer dictate where they go.
  • In a recent development, over the last ten years or so, it has become far more common for significant clubs to travel across the world for their pre-season campaigns.
  • While it’s great to connect with local fan bases, the travel is demanding for the players.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gerry Cardinale has provided some refreshing comments on Milan’s pre-season plans for the future, confirming that money will no longer dictate where they go.

In a recent development, over the last ten years or so, it has become far more common for significant clubs to travel across the world for their pre-season campaigns. For example, Milan have been in Australia for two consecutive pre-seasons now, taking on Perth Glory and most recently Inter.

While it’s great to connect with local fan bases, the travel is demanding for the players. This summer, Milan played games in Glasgow (Scotland), Perth (Australia), Jakarta (Indonesia), and Wroclaw (Poland). resulting in a lot of travel.

Speaking about the pre-season in his long interview with Gazzetta dello Sport, Cardinale noted that the upcoming pre-season planning will be decided by Ruben Amorim. Money will no longer dictate where they go. Instead, the best initiative for preparing the players will be chosen.

In an effort to generate newly introduced revenue, are you also considering a tour for AC Milan next summer? Will that still be Australia or the United States?

Industry observers note that “We have already discussed it with Amorim, and I will just tell you that if we play friendlies abroad, they will be in the United States next summer. If we do… We haven’t decided yet, and the decision will be up to Ruben.

Sources indicate that “It will depend on what’s best for the team: playing friendlies abroad must add value to the group, not bring in a couple of million for the club. Those extra two million will no longer be our goal, as they were under the previous management. That won’t happen again under this ownership.

Recent findings suggest that “Everything we organise in terms of friendlies will be carefully considered with our coach. Every move. And we won’t participate in tours organised by others. We put our players first. We want to help them prepare well to win. That’s our goal, and we aim to achieve it as soon as possible.”.

Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 94 min read (18879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~94 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that brown adipocytes (BAs) are thermogenic cells that regulate energy homeostasis, and age-related declines in thermogenesis contribute to cold sensitivity1,2,3,4,5.
  • Sources indicate that functional cellular heterogeneity is well documented in hepatocytes, driven by liver zonation7, and in muscle fibres, shaped by local environmental cues, particularly motor neuron activity8.
  • Thermogenic adipose tissue undergoes adaptive thermogenesis and is crucial for energy expenditure and thermoregulation1,2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that brown adipocytes (BAs) are thermogenic cells that regulate energy homeostasis, and age-related declines in thermogenesis contribute to cold sensitivity1,2,3,4,5. We previously identified a BA subpopulation with low UCP1 expression (hereafter, BA-L cells) that coexists with the classical, high-UCP1-expressing BAs (hereafter, BA-H cells)6. Here we show that IL-1β secreted by neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby BAs in the BA-L state. Specifically, IL-1β stabilizes hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (H6PD) protein from degradation to ensure the generation of active glucocorticoids, which activate the glucocorticoid receptor (GR, encoded by Nr3c1) and increase the expression of its target gene, regulator of G-protein signalling 2 (Rgs2), thereby suppressing UCP1 expression. Cold exposure reduces IL-1β levels, depending on sympathetic innervation, leading to H6PD degradation and the conversion of BA-L cells to BA-H cells, thereby enhancing UCP1-dependent thermogenesis. Rising environmental temperatures trigger the opposite events. BA-specific inducible deletion of Nr3c1 during cold exposure locks these cells in the BA-H state, leading to persistent thermogenesis and increased energy expenditure days after the mice return to room temperature. Notably, IL-1β is elevated in aged brown adipose tissue, resulting in a locked low BA-H/BA-L ratio and cold intolerance. Suppressing GR in aged mice restores the BA-H/BA-L ratio, resumes thermogenesis and increases energy expenditure. Our findings reveal a spatiotemporal neuronal–immune regulation of BA heterogeneity that governs thermogenesis and offers a fundamental understanding of the mechanisms underlying increased cold sensitivity in older individuals.

Sources indicate that functional cellular heterogeneity is well documented in hepatocytes, driven by liver zonation7, and in muscle fibres, shaped by local environmental cues, particularly motor neuron activity8. Single-cell technologies have revealed extensive new patterns of heterogeneity of specific cell types within the same tissue9, yet their biological importance remains largely undetermined.

Thermogenic adipose tissue undergoes adaptive thermogenesis and is crucial for energy expenditure and thermoregulation1,2. Its specialized metabolism and precise responses to environmental and physiological stimuli make it an ideal model for studying functional cellular heterogeneity. Thermogenic capacity declines substantially with age in rodents and humans, leading to age-related cold sensitivity and metabolic disorders3,4,5, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.

According to recent reports, BAs and beige adipocytes mediate UCP1-dependent non-shivering thermogenesis10. Although substantial progress has been made in identifying the key pathways that activate thermogenesis, most studies have been conducted at the whole-tissue level, leaving the mechanisms governing its activation, maintenance and deactivation incompletely understood.

The heterogeneity of BAs within the same brown adipose tissue (BAT) and beige adipocyte cluster within inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) has been characterized by our group6 and others5,11,12,13,14. We found that BAs heterogeneously express UCP1 and classified those with low expression as BA-L cells and those with high expression as BA-H cells6. At room temperature, BA-H cells constitute 30–50% of all BAs; BA-H cells predominate after cold exposure, whereas BA-L cells predominate under thermoneutral conditions6. This raises questions of why BA heterogeneity exists, and whether it reflects random variation along a thermogenic continuum or spatially organized, tightly regulated states within the tissue.

Here we identify dynamic bistable regulation of BA heterogeneity controlled by the spatial proximity of BAs to IL-1β puncta through a neuronal–immune regulatory mechanism. This regulation becomes dysfunctional during ageing, leading to cold intolerance in older adults. These findings highlight how different cell types collectively control cellular heterogeneity in a spatiotemporal manner, integrating environmental and internal cues to regulate tissue metabolism and function.

Reanalysis of our previous single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) dataset6 revealed enrichment of glucocorticoid signalling and GR-target genes in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). Top BA-L-cell-enriched genes include H6pd, Rgs2 and thioredoxin-interacting protein (Txnip), whereas BA-H cells were enriched for thermogenesis-related genes, including Ucp1 and cytochrome c oxidase 6B1 (Cox6b1) (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b,d–f). Nr3c1 was similarly expressed in BA-H and BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f).

We generated Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice for inducible labelling of Ucp1+ cells by crossing the Ucp1-rtTA, TRE-cre and Rosa-stop-mT/mG mouse lines (Extended Data Fig. 2a). After 1 week of feeding on a doxycycline diet at room temperature (24 °C), GFP+ and GFP− BAs revealed a patchy distribution (Fig. 1a), consistent with BA heterogeneity in AdipoChaser mice6. The Ucp1-rtTA mice used a relatively weak 5 kb Ucp1 promoter15 so GFP is only expressed in UCP1high-expressing BAs (BA-H cells), while Ucp1-cre mice have a strong bacterial artificial chromosome-based Ucp1 promoter that drives Cre expression in all BAs16. Immunofluorescence (IF) staining confirmed selective H6PD expression in BA-L cells (Fig. 1a); 50% of BAs were UCP1+(GFP+)H6PD−, 45% were UCP1−(GFP−)H6PD+ and 5% were UCP1+(GFP+)H6PD+ (Fig. 1b). Similar heterogeneity was observed in iWAT after 1 week of cold exposure (6 °C) (Fig. 1c), with 45% of these beige adipocytes being UCP1+H6PD−, 49% UCP1−H6PD+ and 6% UCP1+H6PD+ (Fig. 1d). Human BAT showed a similar reciprocal UCP1 and H6PD pattern in multilocular brown–beige adipocytes (Fig. 1e), 45% of BAs were UCP1+H6PD−, 47% were UCP1−H6PD+ and 8% were UCP1+H6PD+ (Fig. 1f). Western blotting confirmed more than twofold higher H6PD in BA-L cells than in BA-H cells and more than fourfold higher UCP1 in BA-H cells than in BA-L cells, while H6PD was enriched in mature BAs relative to in the stromal vascular fractions (SVFs) (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). Together, these data identify H6PD as a BA-L marker.

It has been revealed that to enable real-time labelling of BA-H cells, we generated Ucp1-mGFP knock-in mice by inserting a P2A-mGFP cassette after Ucp1 exon 6, immediately upstream of the stop codon (Extended Data Fig. 2d). These mice displayed robust BAT GFP fluorescence without altered UCP1 expression (Extended Data Fig. 2e,f). GFP IF staining revealed a heterogeneous distribution of GFP+ and GFP− BAs (Extended Data Fig. 2g). In vitro-cultured BAs and beige adipocytes demonstrated selective H6PD expression in GFP− BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 2h), validating our in vivo findings.

We next investigated UCP1-independent thermogenesis through the futile creatine cycle17,18,19,20,21. Tissue-non-specific alkaline phosphatase (TNAP) and creatine kinase B (CKB) protein levels increased 4.8-fold and 2.5-fold, respectively, in BAT during cold exposure and were enriched 2.9-fold and 2.0-fold in BA-L cells versus in BA-H cells (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b), consistent with higher Ckb mRNA in BA-L cells6. IF staining further showed TNAP enrichment in BA-L cells (H6PDhigh BAs) in BAT and H6PDhigh beige adipocytes in cold-exposed iWAT (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). In vitro-differentiated BAs also displayed selective TNAP expression in BA-L cells (GFP− BAs) (Extended Data Fig. 3e), indicating that the futile creatine cycle is more active in BA-L cells.

Industry observers note that regarding the metabolic differences between BA-L cells and BA-H cells, BA-L cells have half the basal respiration, but similar maximal respiration compared to BA-H cells, indicating similarly high mitochondrial potential6. Using in vivo [U-13C]glucose tracing22, we recently highlighted that BAT has the most active glucose oxidation among metabolically active tissues, while in vitro tracing confirmed active glucose oxidation in differentiated BAs23. To characterize BA-L metabolism, we performed [U-13C] glucose and [U-13C] palmitate tracing in freshly isolated BA-H cells and BA-L cells, followed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) analysis (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Fully labelled (m+16) free palmitate (C16:0) was about twofold higher in BA-L cells, indicating greater fatty acid uptake (Extended Data Fig. 4b), while fully labelled total palmitate was sixfold higher, suggesting preferential fatty acids storage in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 4c). BA-L cells also showed lower citrate enrichment from both tracers, indicating lower glucose and fatty acid oxidation (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Thus, BA-L cells exhibit greater fatty acid uptake and accumulation but lower fatty acid and glucose oxidation, consistent with their lower basal respiration6.

Industry observers note that we next examined whether H6PD is a functional marker of BA-L cells. H6PD depletion in BAs differentiated from BAT SVFs of Ucp1-mGFP mice increased Ucp1 expression sixfold (Fig. 1g), indicating that H6PD negatively regulates Ucp1. Conversely, H6pd overexpression by lentiviral injection into BAT of Ucp1-mGFP mice (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 4e,f) significantly reduced the proportion of BA-H cells (Fig. 1i,j). Thus, H6PD is a functional marker of BA-L that regulates UCP1 expression and BA heterogeneity.

H6PD localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum lumen and generates endoplasmic reticulum-resident NADPH, distinct from cytosolic glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)24. H6PD primarily determines the reductase activity of endoplasmic reticulum-localized 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSD11B1), which converts inactive cortisone to active cortisol25. GR protein levels were similar between BA-H cells and BA-L cells, indicating that GR signalling is not regulated by receptor abundance (Extended Data Fig. 3b). We next investigated whether GR signalling regulates UCP1 expression. Simultaneous treatment of BAs differentiated from the SVFs of wild-type (WT) mice with 11-dehydrocorticosterone (11-DHC), a natural substrate for active glucocorticoid biosynthesis25, and noradrenaline (NA) substantially increased UCP1 protein (Fig. 2a). However, 24 h 11-DHC pretreatment blunted NA-induced UCP1 expression (Fig. 2b). Thus, prolonged activation of GR signalling suppresses BA responsiveness to NA, maintaining BA-L cells in a stable, low-thermogenic status.

NS, not significant. For a–g, i–k and m, data are mean ± s.e.m. Scale bar, 50 μm (h).

It has been revealed that forskolin activates adenylyl cyclase (AC) to generate cAMP26. 11-DHC pretreatment also blocked forskolin-induced UCP1 expression (Fig. 2c), suggesting inhibition of AC activity or downstream cAMP signalling. To determine where GR signalling acts within the canonical β-adrenergic receptor–cAMP–PKA pathway that controls UCP1 expression27, we measured PKA activity in in vitro-differentiated BAs after 24 h of 11-DHC pretreatment, followed by NA, forskolin or 8-BrcAMP (a cAMP derivative). 11-DHC pretreatment markedly reduced NA- or forskolin-induced PKA activity (Fig. 2d,e), but not the response to 8-BrcAMP (Fig. 2f), indicating that downstream cAMP signalling is not affected by GR activation. Thus, GR signalling potentially suppresses UCP1 expression by inhibiting AC-mediated cAMP production.

It has been revealed that whereas 11-DHC requires conversion to active glucocorticoids, dexamethasone (DEX) directly activates GR. In contrast to the delayed effect of 11-DHC, DEX suppressed NA-induced UCP1 expression after co-treatment (Fig. 2g), an effect that was abrogated by the GR antagonist mifepristone (RU-486) (Fig. 2g). Similarly, in the in vitro-differentiated BAs, CL-316,243 increased Ucp1 expression about 3-fold, whereas DEX pretreatment reduced this induction to about 1.6-fold (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Together, these data support the conclusion that GR activation maintains BA-L cells in a low-UCP1-expressing state by suppressing cAMP production.

We next investigated how GR signalling regulates BA heterogeneity. DEX is commonly used in adipogenic differentiation cocktails; its withdrawal increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 2.8-fold in BAs differentiated from BAT SVF of Ucp1-mGFP mice (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c). Conversely, 11-DHC and the active glucocorticoid corticosterone decreased the BA-H/BA-L ratio compared with in the DEX-free control, independent of differentiation efficiency (Extended Data Fig. 5b–d). In WT mice, DEX induced BAT whitening and reduced the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 74% (Extended Data Fig. 5e,f). Thus, manipulating GR signalling alters BA heterogeneity both in vitro and in vivo.

To determine how GR signalling inhibits cAMP production, we examined other BA-L-enriched genes. Rgs2 was highly expressed in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b,e,f). RGS2 binds to the C1 domain of AC III, V and VI, attenuating Gαs-dependent cAMP accumulation28. IF staining confirmed selective RGS2 expression in BA-L cells, with 40% of BAs being UCP1+(GFP+)RGS2−, 55% UCP1−(GFP−)RGS2+ and 5% UCP1+(GFP+)RGS2+ (Fig. 2h). RGS2 was also selectively expressed in GFP− BA-L cells in in vitro-differentiated BAs (brown and beige) (Extended Data Fig. 5g,h). Analysis of published GR chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) followed by sequencing datasets29 identified GR occupancy within the promoter and intronic regions of Rgs2 (Extended Data Fig. 5i). ChIP–quantitative PCR (qPCR) in in vitro-differentiated BAs confirmed GR binding at the Rgs2 promoter, which was enhanced by DEX (Fig. 2i). Lastly, DEX increased Rgs2 mRNA 2.2-fold in freshly isolated BAs (Fig. 2j), supporting Rgs2 as a GR target. Thus, RGS2 is a GR target in the BAs that inhibits cAMP production. Knocking down Rgs2 in in vitro-differentiated BAs (Fig. 2k) did not affect PKA activity in response to NA alone (Extended Data Fig. 5j,k). However, Rgs2 knockdown abrogated the inhibitory effect of 11-DHC pretreatment on NA-induced PKA substrate phosphorylation (Fig. 2l,m). Rgs2 is therefore a GR target in BAs that suppresses Ucp1 expression by inhibiting AC activity, and BA-L cells are stabilized in the low-thermogenic state through the GR–RGS2–AC signalling axis.

Sources indicate that H6PD protein levels in BAT changed inversely with UCP1 across environmental temperatures, while GR protein was only slightly elevated at thermoneutrality (30 °C) (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Cold exposure reduced H6PD protein by 1.8-fold in iWAT, but not in gonadal white adipose tissue (gWAT) (Extended Data Fig. 6b,c), suggesting thermogenic-depot-specific regulation. CL-316,243 similarly decreased H6PD and increased UCP1 protein levels in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6d). H6pd mRNA decreased rather than increased with rising temperature in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6e), indicating post-transcriptional regulation. Thus, H6PD protein levels, but not mRNA levels, change dynamically in BAT in response to fluctuating environmental temperatures, which may be essential for altering the BA-H/BA-L ratio in response to thermogenic demand.

Sources indicate that sympathetic neurons secrete NA to activate BA thermogenesis. We next tested whether sympathetic innervation mediates cold-induced H6PD protein reduction using unilateral BAT denervation, validated by reduced tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) protein (Fig. 3a). Cold exposure increased BA-H cells from 31.1% to 85.6% (Fig. 3b), as previously reported6. Denervation prevented the cold-induced reduction of H6PD (Fig. 3a), and although there was an increase in the BA-H/BA-L ratio, the proportion of BA-H cells was 66% lower than the sham group during cold exposure (29.1% versus 85.6%) (Fig. 3b). The low BA-H/BA-L ratio was accompanied by BA whitening (Extended Data Fig. 6f), a feature associated with impaired thermogenesis30. Notably, H6PD consistently labelled BA-L cells regardless of the variable BA-H/BA-L ratio at different environmental temperatures (Fig. 3b). Thus, sympathetic innervation is required to reduce H6PD protein and raise the BA-H/BA-L ratio after cold exposure.

Cold exposure also downregulated GR target genes, including Rasd1, Fkbp5, Pik3r1, Tsc22d3 and Rgs2 in BAT, whereas denervation blunted these effects (Extended Data Fig. 6g), supporting the involvement of GR signalling in raising the BA-H/BA-L ratio. We next tested whether the opposite occurred when shifting mice from cold to thermoneutrality. H6PD protein increased 2.1-fold in BAT, while GR protein remained unchanged (Fig. 3c). Transitioning cold-exposed mice to 30 °C also restored GR target gene expression in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6h), indicating that H6PD and GR signalling dynamically respond to temperature fluctuations to regulate BA heterogeneity.

We next tested whether blocking GR during the transition from cold to warmer temperatures prevents BA-H cells from switching to BA-L cells. We generated a BA-H-specific, inducible Nr3c1-knockout model by crossing Ucp1-rtTA, TRE-cre and Nr3c1flox/flox mice (Fig. 3d). Mice were first exposed to 6 °C for 1 week to raise the BA-H/BA-L ratio, followed by 1 week of doxycycline diet under cold conditions to induce Nr3c1 deletion in BA-H cells (Ucp1-Nr3c1flox/flox turning into Ucp1-Nr3c1−/−), and were then returned to room temperature with the doxycycline diet for another week. One week is long enough for the mice to reduce thermogenesis according to the rise in environmental temperature. IF staining confirmed Nr3c1 deletion in most BAs (Fig. 3e), consistent with 86% of BAs being BA-H cells during cold exposure (Fig. 3b), and western blotting showed reduced GR and RGS2 in isolated BAs (Fig. 3f). We previously showed that BA-H cells contain smaller lipid droplets and therefore have higher density, whereas BA-L cells have larger lipid droplets, lower density and float after mild centrifugation (like white adipocytes)6. Notably, BAT from Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice sank in PBS, whereas control BAT floated (Fig. 3g), suggesting a higher density and a higher BA-H/BA-L ratio. Consistently, Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice showed browner BAT with smaller lipid droplets, increased iWAT beiging (Fig. 3h) and a higher proportion of BA-H cells (Fig. 3i). Metabolic cage studies further showed increased energy expenditure and oxygen consumption in Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice, without changes in body weight (Fig. 3j,k and Extended Data Fig. 6i), body composition, food intake, respiratory exchange ratio or locomotor activity (Extended Data Fig. 6j–n). As the controls were metabolically healthy young adults, Ucp1-Nr3c1−/− mice showed no further improvements in glucose tolerance or insulin sensitivity (Extended Data Fig. 6o,p). These data highlight stage- and cell-subtype-specific requirements for GR signalling to regulate bistable BA states and thermogenesis. Inhibition of GR reactivation during the transition from cold to room temperature preserved a high BA-H/BA-L ratio and persistent thermogenesis despite reduced environmental thermogenic demand. These data not only confirm that we can block the BA-H-to-BA-L switch by inhibiting GR signalling, but also indicate that manipulating BA heterogeneity can increase thermogenesis and significantly boost whole-body energy expenditure.

It has been revealed that to elucidate the sympathetic regulation of H6PD protein, we treated in vitro-differentiated BAs with NA but observed no change in H6PD protein (Fig. 4a), suggesting that other cell types and factors are involved in sympathetic regulation of H6PD. We next assessed cytokine expression in BAT and found that Il1b exhibited the greatest reduction (by 53%) after cold exposure (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 7a), and the greatest induction (by 3.3-fold) when mice were shifted from cold to thermoneutrality (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 7b). Cold-induced Il1b suppression was blunted by BAT sympathetic denervation (Fig. 4b), while NA reduced Il1b expression in BAT explants (Extended Data Fig. 7c). Il1b was predominantly expressed in SVFs rather than in mature adipocytes (Fig. 4d) and its expression changed with environmental temperature (Fig. 4d). qPCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR) analysis further confirmed the predominant expression of Il1b in CD45+ SVFs (Fig. 4e), indicating an immune cell source. By contrast, systemic IL-1β levels remained unchanged across environmental temperatures, suggesting local regulation of IL-1β levels in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 7d).

Notably, IF staining revealed that BA-L cells clustered around IL-1β puncta, whereas BA-H cells formed clusters further away (Fig. 4f and Extended Data Fig. 7e), a pattern that was observed across room temperature, during cold exposure and after denervation (Extended Data Fig. 7e). Quantification indicated that IL-1β puncta and GFP+ cells (BA-H cells) show a significant negative Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC = −0.5 ± 0.1), suggesting a mutually exclusive pattern between these two factors at room temperature (Extended Data Fig. 7f). During cold exposure, this pattern persisted but was weaker (PCC = −0.2 ± 0.1), as fewer IL-1β puncta were available for quantification (Extended Data Fig. 7f). BAT denervation prevented the reduction in IL-1β puncta, maintained a low BA-H/BA-L ratio and preserved a strong negative correlation with GFP+ cells (BA-H cells) (PCC = −0.45 ± 0.1). Thus, across all three conditions, BA-L cells were consistently close to IL-1β puncta, indicating a strong correlation between IL-1β and BA heterogeneity.

Recent findings suggest that we next tested whether IL-1β regulates H6PD protein levels in BAs. Among the proinflammatory cytokines tested, TNF and IL-1β increased H6PD protein levels by 1.8- and 3.5-fold, respectively (Fig. 4g), without increasing H6pd mRNA (Extended Data Fig. 7g), confirming a post-transcriptional regulation of H6PD. Combined IL-1β, TNF and IFNγ treatment did not further increase H6PD protein beyond the effect of IL-1β alone (Fig. 4g). IL-1β increased H6PD protein in a time-dependent manner (Fig. 4h). During cycloheximide (CHX) treatment, H6PD abundance decreased by 30% and 50% at 6 and 12 h, respectively, whereas IL-1β prevented this decline (Fig. 4i), indicating increased H6PD protein stability from degradation. IL-1β is known to activate multiple downstream pathways, including JNK, MEK–ERK, p38–MAPK and IKK–NF-κB. Among inhibitors targeting these pathways, only the MEK and ERK inhibitor U0126 attenuated IL-1β-induced H6PD upregulation (Extended Data Fig. 7h,i), indicating that MEK–ERK mediates IL-1β-induced H6PD stability.

It has been revealed that we next examined whether IL-1β regulates UCP1 expression. IL-1β did not alter UCP1 expression in the in vitro-differentiated BAs in the absence of 11-DHC, but reduced UCP1 protein levels by 53% in the presence of 11-DHC (Extended Data Fig. 7j,k), indicating that IL-1β suppresses UCP1 through GR signalling.

Adipose-tissue-resident immune cells can regulate sympathetic innervation31,32,33. However, TH and synaptophysin staining showed similar sympathetic innervation of BA-H cells and BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 7l,m), indicating that IL-1β regulates BA heterogeneity independently of differential sympathetic innervation.

To identify the immune cells that secrete IL-1β in BAT, we integrated multiple published BAT scRNA-seq datasets14,34,35,36,37 (Extended Data Fig. 8a). β-Adrenergic receptors were expressed in CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b), suggesting potential sympathetic regulation. Subclustering analysis revealed that Il1b was enriched in neutrophils (CD45+CD11b+F4/80−CXCR2+), monocytes (CD45+CD11b+F4/80−Ly6C+), and macrophages (CD45+CD11b+F4/80+) (Extended Data Fig. 8c–e). Flow cytometry confirmed that IL-1β was mainly produced by CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 9a,b), with IL-1β+ cells predominantly comprising neutrophils and macrophages, but not monocytes (Extended Data Fig. 9c–e). IL-1β+ cells represented 10% of neutrophils and 1% of macrophages, indicating that IL-1β production is restricted to specific subsets (Extended Data Fig. 9d). Despite the low frequency, the greater abundance of macrophages resulted in substantial numbers of IL-1β+ macrophages, with IL-1β+ neutrophils only 1.7-fold more abundant (Extended Data Fig. 9e), indicating that both cell types are major IL-1β sources. IF staining further confirmed IL-1β colocalization with subsets of CXCR2+ neutrophils and F4/80+ macrophages in BAT (Extended Data Fig. 9f,g).

It has been revealed that depletion of CD45+ immune cells from BAT SVFs increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 2.7-fold without affecting overall differentiation efficiency (Extended Data Fig. 9h–j), supporting a role for immune cells in regulating BA heterogeneity. To further confirm the role of local IL-1β in thermogenic regulation, we injected lentivirus encoding Il1rn (encoding IL-1RA), a naturally occurring inhibitor of IL-1 receptor signalling, or an mCherry control directly into BAT (Extended Data Fig. 10a). IL-1RA increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio twofold in mice housed at room temperature (Fig. 4j,k). In in vitro-differentiated BAs, Il1r knockdown attenuated IL-1β-mediated suppression of UCP1 expression, indicating a direct effect of IL-1β on BAs (Extended Data Fig. 10b). Moreover, in vivo pharmacological inhibition of IL-1β production using the caspase-1 inhibitor VX-765 increased the BA-H/BA-L ratio by 2.2-fold (Extended Data Fig. 10c,d), further demonstrating a functional role for IL-1β in regulating BA heterogeneity.

We next investigated how temperature fluctuations regulate IL-1β in BAT. Il1b expression in primary BAT SVFs was temperature-dependent (Fig. 4d), whereas IL-1β+ immune cell numbers remained unchanged across housing temperatures (Extended Data Fig. 10e–h), indicating regulation independent of immune cell recruitment. NA directly suppressed Il1b expression in BAT-derived CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 10i), suggesting adrenergic regulation of IL-1β production. Consistent with adrenergic receptor expression in CD45+ immune cells (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b), scRNA-seq analysis revealed selective expression of Adrb1 and Adrb2, but not α-adrenergic receptor genes, in Il1b-expressing immune cell populations (Extended Data Fig. 11a). We further examined adrenergic regulation of Il1b using bone marrow-derived neutrophils. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induced Il1b expression dose dependently (Extended Data Fig. 11b), whereas NA pretreatment suppressed this induction in a dose- and time-dependent manner (Extended Data Fig. 11c,d). This effect was reversed by the non-selective β-adrenergic receptor antagonist propranolol, but not by the non-selective α-adrenergic receptor antagonist phenoxybenzamine (Extended Data Fig. 11e,f). Consistently, propranolol administration, but not phenoxybenzamine, increased Il1b expression in BAT in vivo (Extended Data Fig. 11g,h), supporting β-adrenergic suppression of IL-1β production.

Recent findings suggest that decreased BA thermogenesis has been reported with obesity38 and ageing3. However, high fat diet- (HFD)-induced obese mice were completely cold-tolerant, with 100% survival after 7 days of cold exposure (Fig. 5a,b). HFD feeding decreased H6PD and increased UCP1 protein levels (Fig. 5c), indicating preserved BAT thermogenic potential. By contrast, aged mice exhibited cold intolerance, with reduced body temperature and a 25% mortality within the first 2 days (Fig. 5d,e), suggesting impaired thermogenesis. Aged mice showed a 2.3-fold increase in H6PD and a 40% decrease in UCP1 (Fig. 5f), suggesting a reduced BA-H/BA-L ratio. GR was modestly reduced by HFD feeding but unchanged with ageing. These differences suggest that cold-induced thermogenesis is more severely impaired with ageing than with obesity at a young age, and that the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying impaired thermogenesis may differ substantially.
