Sources indicate that in young Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice, BA-H cells increased from 28.8% at 24 °C to 61.7% and 89.7% after 1 and 3 days of cold exposure, respectively. In aged mice, the baseline BA-H/BA-L ratio at 24 °C was extremely low (0.31%), and BA-H cells increased to 15% and 50.9% after 1 and 3 days of cold exposure, respectively (Fig. 5g,h), suggesting delayed BA bistable regulation in response to cold stimulation. H6PD progressively decreased during cold exposure in both young and aged mice (Fig. 5i and Extended Data Fig. 11i), but its level at cold exposure in aged mice was comparable to that in young mice at 24 °C (Extended Data Fig. 11i). UCP1 was also reduced in aged mice, consistent with the lower BA-H/BA-L ratio (Extended Data Fig. 11i). Despite increased BA-L abundance, cold-induced TNAP expression was also blunted with age, although TNAP remained enriched in BA-L cells (Extended Data Fig. 11j), suggesting impaired futile creatine cycle activation. Aged mice also exhibited a 1.8-fold increase in BAT corticosterone (the active form of glucocorticoid in mice) in BAT, but not serum corticosterone (Extended Data Fig. 11k,l), and a sixfold increase in BAT Il1b expression arising from SVFs (Extended Data Fig. 11m,n). Together, these results suggest that elevated local IL-1β and H6PD-mediated overactivation of the GR–RGS2–AC axis lower the BA-H/BA-L ratio, therefore impairing cold-induced thermogenesis in aged mice.

Recent findings suggest that lastly, we investigated whether GR inhibition could restore BA bistable regulation and thermogenesis in aged mice. One week of RU-486 treatment increased the proportion of BA-H cells in aged mice from 0.5% to 8.3% at room temperature and from 10.6% to 32.8% after 1 day of cold exposure (Fig. 5j–m). RU-486 also reduced lipid droplet accumulation within BAs and improved BAT whitening (Fig. 5n), increased rectal temperature during the cold tolerance test and reduced body weight in the first few days of cold exposure (Extended Data Fig. 11o,p). Metabolic cage studies revealed that RU-486 treatment increased energy expenditure and oxygen consumption across the day–night cycle, without changes in respiratory exchange ratio, locomotor activity or food intake (Extended Data Fig. 11q–u). Thus, GR antagonism increases energy expenditure in aged mice, potentially due to elevated UCP1-dependent thermogenesis in BAT.

It has been revealed that we found that the two BA subtypes are spatially organized and tightly regulated. IL-1β stabilizes surrounding BAs in the low-thermogenic state (BA-L cells) by extending H6PD protein half-life. H6PD facilitates active glucocorticoid production, which suppresses UCP1 expression through the GR–RGS2–AC axis (Extended Data Fig. 12a). BAs further from IL-1β puncta are stabilized in the high-thermogenic state (BA-H cells) with low H6PD protein levels (Extended Data Fig. 12b). During cold stimulation, activated sympathetic neurons secrete NA, which suppresses IL-1β production by immune cells. Low IL-1β levels promote H6PD degradation and switch BA-L cells into BA-H cells (Extended Data Fig. 12a,b). After cold stimulation, this process is reversed, restoring a lower BA-H/BA-L ratio. Age impairs the flexibility to alter BA heterogeneity due to IL-1β overload in BAT, which significantly contributes to the age-related decline in thermogenesis (Extended Data Fig. 12b).

Recent findings suggest that the advantages of this spatiotemporal neuronal–immune regulation of BA heterogeneity are multifaceted. First, it enables a dual-layered response: an immediate, acute response through readily active BA-H cells, and a longer-term, chronic response that involves shifting cellular heterogeneity. Second, it facilitates communication between different cell types through spatial proximity, thereby integrating stimuli from multiple systems, combining environmental and internal cues, and enabling precise regulation of cell states. Third, shifting between BA-H and BA-L states preserves BAs from oxidative damage associated with sustained high thermogenesis.

In a recent development, although this study primarily focused on UCP1-dependent thermogenesis, UCP1-independent mechanisms are also critical for thermogenic adipose tissue function and whole-body metabolic homeostasis39,40,41. We observed that TNAP, a key component of the futile creatine cycle, is enriched in BA-L cells. Cold exposure increased the proportion of BA-H cells while inducing CKB and TNAP expression in BAT42, reflecting enhanced futile creatine cycle activity either specifically in BA-L cells or across all BAs, with BA-L cells retaining higher activity. Importantly, cold-induced TNAP expression was compromised with age, while remaining enriched in BA-L cells. These results suggest that both UCP1- and futile creatine cycle-dependent thermogenesis are impaired with age.

Recent findings suggest that BAT has long been recognized as a target organ for glucocorticoids, but their precise role remains unclear. Some studies indicate that glucocorticoids suppress UCP1 expression and/or BAT activity43,44,45,46, whereas others reach the opposite conclusions47,48,49. Glucocorticoids have also been implicated in warm-induced beige adipocyte whitening50. This study reveals that GR signalling in BAT regulates BA heterogeneity by locking BAs in the BA-L state and reducing their responsiveness to NA. Active glucocorticoid levels are regulated locally, independent of systemic levels25. Thus, systemic glucocorticoid treatments may not alter active glucocorticoid levels in individual BAs, potentially explaining previous conflicting observations. Importantly, inducible GR deletion in BAs during the transition from cold to room temperature sustained the high BA-H/BA-L ratio and thermogenesis. The stage- and cell-subtype-specific requirement of GR signalling explains why Nr3c1-knockout mice do not exhibit altered BAT development or thermogenesis51,52, and indicates that targeting GR at selective timing could profoundly manipulate thermogenic activity.

According to recent reports, our study highlighted that BA heterogeneity is determined by communication from sympathetic neurons to immune cells, rather than by direct communication from sympathetic neurons to BAs. NA, the primary neurotransmitter from sympathetic nerves, has been shown to modulate immune cell response by regulating cytokine production by immune cells in the liver and adipose tissue53,54. We found that NA directly suppresses Il1b production in immune cells through β-adrenergic signalling, thereby modulating BA heterogeneity. Notably, a recent study showed that cold-induced β3-adrenergic activation transiently recruits neutrophils predominantly to white adipose tissue (WAT), particularly the visceral depot55. These infiltrating neutrophils produce IL-1β, which suppresses local lipolysis by attenuating cAMP-dependent signalling, thereby limiting excessive lipid mobilization. Based on our findings in BAT, IL-1β may similarly suppress lipolysis through the H6PD–GR–RGS2–AC axis in white adipocytes. Notably, Il1b expression in WAT exhibits transient kinetics, peaking at 12 h after stimulation and returning to basal levels at 24 h. Given that NA suppresses Il1b expression in BAT, it may similarly suppress Il1b expression in newly infiltrated neutrophils in WAT.

It has been revealed that it remains unclear why in vitro-differentiated BAs exhibit heterogeneity. BAs may intrinsically differentiate into cells with varying UCP1 levels to preserve thermogenic flexibility or maintain metabolic balance. Cross-talk between BAs and IL-1β+ immune cells in vivo may further reinforce and spatially organize this heterogeneity. Alternatively, IL-1β+ immune cells in SVFs during differentiation may influence the local environment. Indeed, depletion of CD45+ immune cells from SVFs before differentiation substantially increased the proportion of BA-H cells, suggesting that SVF immune cells reduce the BA-H/BA-L ratio. Future efforts with cell type-specific receptor knockout mouse models will help to validate and further elucidate how sympathetic innervation regulates IL-1β secretion and how IL-1β regulates H6PD protein stability.

Decline of thermogenesis and age-related adiposity56 contribute to age-related metabolic disorders. Previous studies suggest that reduction in thermogenic activity may be due to impaired beige adipogenesis5,57, declined mitochondrial fuel oxidation3, reduced adrenergic receptors, altered other master regulators of thermogenesis58 and compromised sympathetic innervation due to infiltration of senescent immune cells59. Our study revealed that Il1b is increased in aged BAT, consistent with previous studies reporting increased immune cell infiltration and upregulated cytokines in aged BAT59. Increased IL-1β stabilized large amounts of BAs in the BA-L state and suppressed thermogenesis in aged mice. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of GR signalling by a GR antagonist raised the BA-H/BA-L ratio and improved cold-induced thermogenesis in aged mice, indicating that BA-specific GR signalling could be targeted to correct age-related cold intolerance and significantly increase basal metabolism. However, given the systemic effects of RU-486 (ref. 60), other tissues and cell types may also contribute. Future efforts will focus on the effects of targeted inhibition of GR signalling specifically in thermogenic cells.

Recent findings suggest that all animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees of City of Hope (protocol 17014). Mice were maintained under a 12 h–12 h dark–light cycle in a temperature-controlled facility with ad libitum access to water and food. The diets included a standard chow diet (5053, Lab diet), an HFD (D12492, Research Diets) and a chow diet supplemented with 600 mg per kg doxycycline (S4107, Bio-Serv), as described for individual experiments. The Ucp1-rtTA mouse line was generated as previously described15,61. The Ucp1-mGFP knock-in mouse line was created by Biocytogen through microinjection of CRISPR components and a donor vector into C57BL/6J zygotes. The single guide RNA targeted the junction of the exon 6 coding region and 3′ untranslated region (UTR) (CTTCCTCCAAGTTGCTTATG + TGG) of the Ucp1 gene, and a P2A-mGFP cassette was inserted at the 5′ end of the 3′ UTR, immediately upstream of the Ucp1 gene stop codon. TRE-Cre (B6.Cg-Tg(tetO-cre)1Jaw/J, 006234), Rosa26-loxp-STOP-loxp-mT/mG (B6.129(Cg)-Gt (ROSA)26Sortm4(ACTB-tdTomato,-eGFP) Luo/J, 007676) and Nr3c1-floxed (B6.Cg-Nr3c1tm1.1Jda/J, 021021) mouse lines were purchased from the Jackson Laboratories. To generate mice lacking GR proteins selectively in BAs, Ucp1-rtTA and TRE-Cre mice were crossed with Nr3c1-floxed mice. Littermates lacking TRE-Cre were used as control mice. All mice were maintained on a pure C57BL/6J background. The sample sizes for animal experiments were determined based on previous studies. Experimental groups were randomly assigned. Investigators were blinded to group allocation during rectal temperature measurement, but blinding was not feasible for other experiments.

Sources indicate that unilateral denervation of BAT was performed as previously described62. In brief, 8-week-old male mice were anaesthetized with 5% isoflurane and placed onto a warm surgical platform. The interscapular surgical region was shaved and sterilized with 70% isopropyl rubbing alcohol and iodine. A 1 cm lateral incision was made from the scapula to the neck, and the interscapular BAT depot was carefully detached from the underlying muscle layer and retracted cranially over the head using toothed forceps. Five branches of the intercostal sympathetic nerve bundles innervating the left and right BAT lobes were exposed. Unilateral denervation was achieved by cutting the nerve bundles on the left side, while the right nerve bundles were exposed and touched as a sham-operated control. The BAT lobes were repositioned, and the incision was closed using absorbable 5.0 sutures. Mice were allowed to recover for 2 weeks before undergoing further experimental procedures.

To construct the H6pd-expressing lentiviral vector, the mouse H6pd complementary DNA (cDNA) (NM_173371.4) was amplified using primers with 5′ BamH I and 3′ Sal I restriction sites. To construct the Il1rn-expressing lentiviral vector, the mouse Il1rn cDNA (NM_031167.5) was amplified using primers with 5′ BamH I and 3′ Sal I restriction sites. The PCR products were cleaved with BamH I and Sal I and ligated into the pLenti-mCherry vector (36084, Addgene) to generate the pLenti-mH6pd lentiviral vector or pLenti-mIl1rn lentiviral vector. Lentiviral particles were produced by co-transfecting HEK293T (ATCC) cells with the pLenti-mCherry, pLenti-mH6pd, or pLenti-mIl1rn transfer plasmids, along with the packaging psPAX2 (12260, Addgene) and envelope plasmids pMD2.G (12259, Addgene) at a 1:1:1 ratio, using PEI (1 μg DNA to 3 µl PEI). HEK293T cells were not independently authenticated but were regularly tested for mycoplasma contamination, with negative results. After 72 h, the supernatant containing lentiviral particles was collected, filtered through a 0.45-μm PES filter and concentrated using the Lenti-X concentrator (631232, Takara Bio). The concentrated lentivirus was resuspended in PBS, stored at −80 °C and titrated using an RT-PCR Titration kit (631235, Takara Bio). Lentivirus administration in BAT was performed as described previously63. In brief, 10-week-old male Ucp1-mGFP or Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice were anaesthetized with 5% isoflurane. A small lateral incision (~0.5–0.8 cm) was made in the interscapular area to expose BAT. Then 10–20 μl of either pLenti-mH6pd lentivirus, pLenti-mIl1rn lentiviral or a negative control lentivirus (109 IFU ml−1) was directly injected at three distinct sites into each interscapular BAT lobe.

For three-dimensional fluorescence imaging of BAT, we used the Adipo-Clear method as described previously64. In brief, 8-week-old male Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice were fed a doxycycline diet for 3 days at 24 °C. Mice were anaesthetized and perfused with cold PBS containing 100 U ml−1 heparin (H3149, Sigma-Aldrich), followed by ice-cold 4% PFA. The BAT was then dissected and post-fixed in 4% PFA at 4 °C overnight. After fixation, the tissue was washed with PBS, trimmed and delipidated using a graded series of methanol–B1n buffer, followed by 100% dichloromethane. After delipidation, the BAT was washed with a graded series of methanol–B1n buffer, followed by PTwH buffer. The sample was then incubated with primary rabbit anti-TH polyclonal antibody (1:200, ab152, Abcam) or rabbit anti-synaptophysin antibody (1:200, ab32127, Abcam) along with chicken anti-GFP antibody (1:200, ab13970, Abcam), diluted in PTxwH buffer at room temperature for 3 days. After incubation with primary antibodies, the sample was washed with PTxwH buffer and then incubated with secondary antibodies: Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit IgG(H+L) (A31573, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Cy3 AffiniPure F(ab′)2 fragment donkey anti-chicken IgY (IgG) (H+L) (703-166-155, Jackson Immuno Research) secondary antibodies at room temperature for 3 days. The sample was dehydrated through a series of methanol and 100% dichloromethane and then cleared with dibenzyl ether. Three-dimensional imaging of the cleared BAT was performed using tile scanning with a confocal laser-scanning microscope (LSM 880, Zeiss) at ×10 and ×20 magnifications, with image acquisition and analysis conducted using the Zeiss Zen black software.

It has been revealed that the SVF of BAT was isolated from the interscapular BAT of mice on postnatal day 7, while the SVF from iWAT was obtained from 5-week-old male mice. In brief, dissected BAT or iWAT was minced and digested for 45 min at 37 °C in a digestion buffer containing 1.5 mg ml−1 collagenase D (11088882001, Sigma-Aldrich) in an isolation buffer (0.123 M NaCl, 5 mM KCl, 1.3 mM CaCl2, 5 mM glucose, 100 mM HEPES and 4% BSA). The cell–tissue mixture was filtered through a 70-μm cell strainer (08-771-2, Thermo Fisher Scientific) to remove undigested fragments, then centrifuged for 5 min at 300g at 4 °C. The resulting cell pellet was resuspended in growth medium (DMEM, 10566016 Life Technologies; 1% penicillin–streptomycin, SV30010 Hyclone; 0.1% gentamicin, 1855724 Life Technologies and 20 mM HEPES, Sigma-Aldrich, H3537) containing 20% FBS (16H328, Sigma-Aldrich) and filtered again through a 40-μm cell strainer (08-771-1, Thermo Fisher Scientific) to remove clumps and adipocytes. The flow-through was centrifuged for 5 min at 300g at 4 °C, and the SVF pellet was resuspended in SVF growth medium and plated onto a 12-well tissue culture plate for RNA and protein extraction or onto a 35 mm glass-bottom tissue culture dish for IF staining. For differentiation into brown and beige adipocytes, SVF cells were switched to fresh induction medium (DMEM plus DEX (1 μM), insulin (0.12 μg ml−1), isobutylmethylxanthine (0.5 mM), T3 (1 nM), indomethacin (0.125 mM), 20 mM HEPES, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 0.1% gentamicin) containing 10% FBS on day 0 (2 days after reaching confluence). After 2 days, the medium was replaced with maintenance medium (DMEM with insulin (0.12 μg ml−1), T3 (1 nM), 20 mM HEPES, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 0.1% gentamicin) containing 10% FBS, and this maintenance medium was changed every 2 days until further use.

For glucocorticoid treatment, SVF cells from the BAT of Ucp1-mGFP mice were cultured and differentiated as described. During differentiation, cells were treated with or without 1 μM corticosterone (16063, Cayman Chemical), 1 μM DEX (D4902, Sigma-Aldrich) or 1 μM 11-DHC (32907, Cayman Chemical) in the induction medium. On differentiation day 6, the density of GFP fluorescence was assessed under a microscope (BZ-X710, Keyence) to quantify the BA-H/BA-L ratio. For the PKA activity assay, on differentiation day 6, primary BAs differentiated were pretreated with 1 μM 11-DHC or vehicle for 48 h, followed by incubation with 1 μM NA (A0937, Sigma-Aldrich), 10 μM forskolin (F6886, Sigma-Aldrich) or 500 μM 8-Br-cAMP (B7880, Sigma-Aldrich) for 30 min. PKA activity was measured by western blot analysis using antibodies specific to phosphorylated PKA substrates. For the H6PD half-life assay, BAs differentiated from primary BAT SVFs were pretreated with 10 ng ml−1 IL-1β (401-ML-005, R&D Systems) or vehicle for 4 h, followed by exposure to 50 µg ml−1 CHX (C1988, Sigma-Aldrich) with IL-1β or saline for various timepoints (0, 3, 6 and 12 h) at 37 °C, with H6PD quantified by western blot analysis. For cytokine treatment, on differentiation day 6, primary BAs were treated with saline, 10 ng ml−1 IL-1β, 20 ng ml−1 TNF (410-MT-010, R&D Systems) and 10 ng ml−1 IFNγ (485-MI-100, R&D Systems) alone or in combination for 48 h. For IL-1β signalling inhibition, BAs were treated with saline, 10 ng ml−1 IL-1β or IL-1β in combination with 10 μM p38 kinase inhibitor SB203580 (559395, Sigma-Aldrich), 5 μM NF-κB inhibitor BAY11-7082 (196871, Sigma-Aldrich), 10 μM JNK inhibitor SP600125 (420119, Sigma-Aldrich), 10 μM ERK inhibitor U0126 (662005, Sigma-Aldrich) or 5 mM IKKβ inhibitor aspirin (A5376, Sigma-Aldrich) for 48 h, with inhibitors administered 1 h before IL-1β treatment. To test the effect of IL-1β on UCP1 expression, BAs on day 6 were switched to culture medium containing charcoal-stripped FBS and then treated with vehicle or 10 ng ml−1 IL-1β for 48 h in the absence or presence of 1 μM 11-DHC. For DEX and RU-486 treatment, the BAs on day 6 were pretreated with vehicle or 10 μM RU-486 for 1 h, followed by treatment with 1 μM NA in the presence or absence of 1 μM DEX for 24 h. The concentrations of UCP1, H6PD and β-actin were quantified by western blot analysis. To assess the effect of immune cells on BAs heterogeneity, SVF cells from the BAT of Ucp1-mGFP mice were cultured and differentiated as described, with or without CD45+ immune cells. CD45+ immune cells were depleted from SVFs using PE-anti-CD45 antibody (103106, BioLegend) and EasySep Reagents (17656, StemCell Technologies).

It has been revealed that mature BAs from the interscapular BAT of 10-week-old male mice were obtained as described before. In brief, BATs were dissected, cleaned of contaminating muscle and WAT, minced into small pieces, and digested in collagenase-dispase buffer (17703034, Gibco) for 1 h at 37 °C with shaking at 110 r.p.m. The cell suspension was filtered through 100-μm cell strainers (08-771-19, Thermo Fisher Scientific) to remove undigested tissues, washed with 3 volumes of DMEM/F12 medium (10565018, Life Technologies) containing 10% FBS and centrifuged at 100g for 5 min at room temperature. The floating BAs were transferred and resuspended in PBS wash buffer three times. After quantification, 5 × 105 BAs were suspended in Matrigel (Corning, CB-40234C) at a 1:1 volume ratio and seeded into 6-well tissue culture dishes. The plates were incubated at 37 °C for 15 min to induce gel formation. Maintenance medium (DMEM with insulin (0.12 μg ml−1), T3 (1 nM), 20 mM HEPES, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 0.1% gentamicin) containing 10% FBS was then added to the wells with either vehicle, 1 μM DEX, 10 μM CL-316,243 (C5976, Sigma-Aldrich) or 1 μM DEX combined with 10 μM CL-316,243 for 24 h. For the separation of BA-H and BA-L cells, we modified our previous protocol6 by adding additional steps to further deplete contaminating SVFs in BA-L cells. In brief, floating BAs were collected as BA-L cells, and the pellet containing BA-H cells and SVF was further separated using the EasyPlate magnet-based method. The cell suspension was incubated with PE-conjugated antibodies against immune cells (PE-anti-CD45, 103106, BioLegend), endothelial cells (PE-anti-CD31, 102408, BioLegend), fibroblasts (PE-anti-CD140a, 135905, BioLegend) and pericytes (PE-anti-CD146, 134704, BioLegend) and processed using EasySep reagents (17656, StemCell Technologies) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Freshly isolated BA-H and BA-L cells (1 × 105 per condition) were incubated in tracing medium (D5030, Sigma-Aldrich) containing either 5 mM [U-13C]glucose or 0.5 mM [U-13C]palmitate for 2 h and 6 h. After incubation, cells were washed with NaCl and collected with cold 50% methanol as before22,23. Metabolites were extracted and analysed by GC–MS.

Mice were anaesthetized and perfused with PBS, followed by 10% formalin fixative buffer. The interscapular BAT, iWAT and gWAT were carefully dissected and post-fixed in 10% formalin buffer overnight at 4 °C. After dehydration, paraffin embedding and sectioning, tissue sections were stained with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E).

According to recent reports, for human samples, adipose tissue was collected during thyroid surgery. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients. Supraclavicular adipose tissue was removed as waste biological material from subjects undergoing surgery at the General Hospital (AOU; Ancona, Italy) for thyroid diseases. Ethical approval was obtained from the specific Commission within the Azienda Ospedaliero Universitaria delle Marche (University Hospital of the Marche Region). The ethical approval protocol code is 208156. Immediately after removal, tissue pieces were fixed overnight at 4 °C by immersion in 4% paraformaldehyde in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 7.4). They were then dehydrated, cleared and paraffin embedded. Sections from three levels (100 μm apart) were stained with H&E to assess morphology and BAT presence for UCP1-immunohistochemistry.

For IF staining of mouse and human tissues, paraffin-embedded sections of Ucp1-mGFP and Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice and human BAT slides were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated using a graded ethanol series to double-distilled H2O. The slides were immersed in 10 mM sodium citrate buffer (C9999, Sigma-Aldrich) and boiled for 30 min for antigen retrieval, then blocked in PBST containing 0.3% Triton X-100 and 5% BSA. Primary antibodies used were as follows: perilipin (1:500, NB100-60554, Novus and ab61682, Abcam), UCP1 (1:200, ab23841, Abcam and MAB6158, R&D Systems), GFP (1:200, ab13970, Abcam; and 2956S, Cell Signaling Technology), mCherry (1:200, ab167453, Abcam), H6PD (1:200, ab170895, Abcam; and 15255-1-AP, Proteintech), TNAP (1:200, AF2910, R&D Systems), GR (1:200, 12041S, Cell Signaling Technology), RGS2 (1:200, NBP1-32284, Novus), IL-1RA (1:100, MA5-35068, Thermo Fisher Scientific), IL-1β (1:50, AF-401-NA, R&D Systems), F4/80 (1:100, ab6640, Abcam) and CXCR2 (1:100, 20634-1-AP, Proteintech). Secondary antibodies (1:200 dilution) used were Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated donkey anti-mouse IgG (H+L) (A31571, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 555-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit IgG(H+L) (A31572, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit IgG(H+L) (A31573, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated donkey anti-goat IgG (H+L) (A32814, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 555-conjugated donkey anti-rat IgG (H+L) (A48270, Thermo Fisher Scientific), Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated donkey anti-goat IgG (H+L) (A21447, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and Cy3 AffiniPure F(ab′)2 fragment donkey anti-chicken IgY (IgG) (H+L) (703-166-155, Jackson Immuno Research). Slides were counterstained with 1 μg ml−1 DAPI (D9542, Sigma-Aldrich) and mounted with prolonged Anti-Fade mounting medium (P36931, Invitrogen). Bright-field and fluorescence images were acquired using an inverted fluorescence phase-contrast microscope (BZ-X710, Keyence).

Fluorescence microscopy images were acquired for three experimental conditions: room temperature, cold exposure and cold exposure with denervation. For each condition, dual-channel fluorescence images were collected with UCP1 labelled in the green channel and IL-1β labelled in the magenta channel, along with corresponding autofluorescence reference images for cellular region identification. All image analysis was performed using custom Python scripts using the tifffile, numpy, scipy and pandas libraries. To restrict analysis to cellular regions and exclude background artifacts, autofluorescence images were Gaussian-smoothed and used to generate binary masks with a threshold of 50 arbitrary units applied to autofluorescence intensity values65, ensuring that correlation analysis was performed exclusively on biologically relevant areas. To eliminate low-intensity noise and focus analysis on meaningful fluorescence signals, intensity-based thresholds were applied to both channels: UCP1 (green channel) at 70 arbitrary units and IL-1β (magenta channel) at 20 arbitrary units. Pixels were retained for analysis if they exceeded the threshold in either channel, using a logical OR to preserve regions with specific labelling while maintaining sensitivity to differential expression patterns. Co-localization between UCP1 and IL-1β was quantified using the Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC), calculated pixel-wise across filtered cellular regions66. After masking and thresholding, images were vectorized by flattening two-dimensional pixel arrays into one-dimensional arrays. The PCC was computed using scipy.stats, providing both the correlation coefficient and associated P value for each image pair. Statistical comparisons between experimental conditions were performed using Welch’s t-tests for independent samples with unequal variances. This approach accounts for potential differences in variance between experimental groups while providing robust statistical inference. Results were compiled into structured data frames and visualized using bar plots with error bars.

Total RNA was extracted from tissues or cultured cells using either TRIzol reagent (15596026, Thermo Fisher Scientific) or RNAqueous-Micro Total RNA Isolation Kit (AM1931, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The first-strand cDNA was synthesized using the iScript cDNA synthesis kit (1708891, Bio-Rad) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. qPCR was performed using the SYBR Green PCR system (A25742, Applied Biosystems) with Tbp as the internal control. A list of all of the primer sequences is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Sources indicate that adipose tissues, cultured adipocytes and isolated mature BAs were collected and lysed in radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) buffer (20-188, Sigma-Aldrich) containing protease inhibitor cocktails (11836170001, Sigma-Aldrich) and phosphatase inhibitor cocktails (P5726, P0044, Sigma-Aldrich). The extracted protein samples were loaded onto and separated on a 4–15% gradient SDS–PAGE TGX stain-free gel (4568086, Bio-Rad) and transferred to a PVDF membrane (1620177, Bio-Rad). The membranes were incubated with specific primary antibodies against H6PD (ab170895, Abcam and 15255-1-AP, Proteintech), UCP1 (ab23841, Abcam), GFP (2956S, Cell Signaling Technology), phosphorylated PKA substrates (RRXS*/T*) (9624S, Cell Signaling Technology), TH (ab152, Abcam), TNAP (AF2910, R&D Systems), CKB (18713-1-AP, Proteintech), GR (12041S, Cell Signaling Technology), IL-1R1 (PA5-97866, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and β-actin (4970 and 58169, Cell Signaling Technology). HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (1706515, Bio-Rad) and HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (1706516, Bio-Rad) were used as secondary antibodies. The immunoreactive signals were detected using the Pierce ECL Western Blotting Substrate (32209, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and SuperSignal West Pico PLUS Chemiluminescent substrate (34577, Thermo Fisher Scientific).

It has been revealed that mature BAs were reverse-transfected with dsiRNA as described previously67. In brief, on differentiation day 5, BAT-derived primary BAs were trypsinized using 0.25% trypsin (25200, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 15 min. The cells were then resuspended in culture medium and seeded onto gelatin-coated cell culture plates that had been pre-incubated with a pool of 50 nM H6pd dsiRNAs, 50 nM Rgs2 dsiRNAs, 50 nM Il1r1 dsiRNAs or relevant control dsiRNAs (Integrated DNA Technologies), mixed with 5 μl ml−1 of Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (13778075, Thermo Fisher Scientific) diluted in Opti-MEM medium (31985070, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The final density of BAs was 2.5 × 105 cells per cm2 of culture plate. Mature BAs were treated or collected 2 days after transfection. A list of all of the dsiRNA sequences is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Mice were housed individually in temperature- and light-controlled rodent incubators (Powers Scientific) set to either thermoneutrality (30 °C) or cold (6 °C), with ad libitum access to food and water. For the β3-adrenoceptor agonist treatment experiment, mice were maintained at thermoneutrality for 1 week, followed by daily intraperitoneal injections of CL-316,243 in PBS at 1 mg per kg body weight for an additional 7 days. For adrenoceptor antagonist treatment, mice were exposed at 6 °C for 16 h, followed by intraperitoneal injections of propranolol (10 mg per kg; P0884, Sigma-Aldrich) or phenoxybenzamine hydrochloride (5 mg per kg; HY-B043A, MedChemExpress) in PBS for 4 h.

For flow cytometry analysis, SVF cells were blocked with anti-mouse-CD16/32 (1:500, 101302, BioLegend) for 10 min, and then stained with anti-mouse-CD45-BV605 (1:400, 103155, BioLegend), anti-mouse-CD11b-APC (1:100, 101212, BioLegend), anti-mouse-F4/80-488 (1:100, 123120, BioLegend), anti-mouse-Ly6C-PE/Cy7 (1:400, 128018, BioLegend), anti-mouse-CXCR2-PE (1:20, 149304, BioLegend), anti-mouse-CD3-488 (1:100, 100210, BioLegend) and anti-mouse-CD19-PE (1:200, 152408, BioLegend) for individual experiments for 20 min on ice. After antibody incubation, the cells were washed once with 2% FBS–PBS. For intracellular staining, cells were stained with LIVE–DEAD fixable dead cell stain (65-0868-14, Invitrogen) for 30 min on ice. After washing with PBS, cells were fixed and permeabilized using a fixation/permeabilization kit (554714, BD bioscience) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, cells were fixed with fixation–permeabilization solution for 15 min on ice, followed by a wash with PBS and 1× perm–wash buffer. Cells were stained with anti-mouse-IL-1β-APC/eFluor 780 (1:80, 47-7114-82, Invitrogen) in 1× perm–wash buffer for 30 min on ice. After staining, cells were washed once with 1× perm–wash buffer and analysed by BD Fortessa cytometer. The flow plots were analysed by FlowJo (v.10).

Eight-week-old male C57BL/6J mice were subcutaneously (s.c.) injected with either vehicle or 5 mg per kg per day water-soluble DEX (D2915, Sigma-Aldrich) dissolved in PBS for 2 weeks. Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG mice aged 10 weeks were maintained on doxycycline chow diet and administered vehicle or VX-765 (HY-13205, MedChemExpress, 50 mg per kg per day), dissolved in 20% (v/v) Cremophor EL, through daily intraperitoneal injection for 1 week. Ucp1-Chaser-mT/mG or WT mice aged 70–75 weeks were injected s.c. with 60 mg per kg mifepristone (RU-486) (HY-13683, MedChemExpress) dissolved in DMSO–corn oil or with DMSO–corn oil alone daily as controls for 1 week. Body temperature was recorded daily throughout the treatment period. After the final RU-486 or vehicle injection, mice were individually housed and exposed to a cold environment (6 °C). Rectal temperatures were measured at the indicated timepoints using a rodent thermometer (Bioseb, TK8851). For metabolic phenotyping, 72-week-old male WT mice were s.c. injected with either vehicle or RU-486 (60 mg per kg per day) for 1 week, followed by metabolic phenotyping with continuing daily vehicle or RU-486 injection for an additional 3 days. During the metabolic cage study, energy expenditure, oxygen consumption, RER, locomotor activity and food intake were recorded. At the end point, the mice were perfused with PBS and 10% formalin and processed for H&E and IF staining as described above.

Sources indicate that male Ucp1-rtTA;TRE-cre;Nr3c1flox/flox or control littermates aged 10 weeks were fed a doxycycline diet at 6 °C for 1 week, then continued for an additional week after being moved back to 24 °C, followed by glucose tolerance tests and insulin tolerance tests. For the glucose tolerance test, mice were fasted for 12 h before intraperitoneal injection of glucose (2 g per kg body weight). For the insulin tolerance test, mice were fasted for 6 h before intraperitoneal injection of insulin (0.75 U kg−1, Eli Lilly). Tail vein blood samples were collected at 0, 15, 30, 60, 90 and 120 min after injection, and blood glucose levels were measured using a Contour glucometer (Bayer).

Sources indicate that BAT depots were dissected from the interscapular BAT of male C57BL/6J mice exposed to 30 °C for 1 week and minced into 1–2 mm3 explants. The explants were washed three times with PBS and transferred to a six-well plate containing DMEM with 10% FBS. BAT SVFs were isolated as described above, and CD45+ immune cells were enriched using PE-anti-CD45 antibody (103106, BioLegend) and EasySep Reagents (17656, StemCell Technologies). Explants were incubated in saline or 10 mM NA (A0937, Sigma-Aldrich) for 24 h and CD45+ immune cells were treated with saline or NA (1 μM) for 4 h. After incubation, explants and CD45+ cells were collected for RNA extraction.

In a recent development, bone marrow neutrophils were isolated from 10-week-old male WT mice. In brief, femurs and tibias were flushed with PBS containing 2 mM EDTA and 2% FBS using a 23-gauge needle, and the cell suspension was filtered through a 70-μm strainer. Cells were centrifuged at 400g for 5 min, and the pellet was resuspended in red blood cell lysis buffer (R7757, Sigma-Aldrich) for 1 min at room temperature, followed by neutralization with PBS containing 2% FBS. Neutrophils were enriched using PE-anti-Ly6G antibody (127608, BioLegend) and EasySep Reagents (17656, StemCell Technologies). Neutrophils were cultured in RPMI 1640 supplemented with 2% FBS. Neutrophils were stimulated with LPS (0–1,000 ng ml−1; L4391, Sigma-Aldrich) for 6 h or pretreated with NA (0–10 μM) for 30 min before 100 ng ml−1 LPS stimulation. For time-dependent experiments, neutrophils were treated with LPS with or without 1 μM NA pretreatment for 1–9 h. For adrenergic blockade experiments, neutrophils were pretreated with 1 μM propranolol (P0884, Sigma-Aldrich) or 1 μM phenoxybenzamine (HY-B0431A, MedChemExpress) for 60 min, followed by 1 μM NA and 100 ng ml−1 LPS stimulation. For IL-1β measurement, 10 μM nigericin (HY-100381, MedChemExpress) was added 30 min before sample collection. Neutrophils were collected for RNA extraction, and the supernatants were collected for enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) analysis.

Blood samples were collected between 08:00 and 10:00, then centrifuged at 2,000g and 4 °C for 20 min to separate the serum. BAT was homogenized in a TissueLyser with 1 ml of 80% methanol on ice. The samples were then subjected to 3–5 freeze–thaw cycles and centrifuged at 4 °C and 13,000 r.p.m. for 15 min. The supernatant, which contains sterols, was collected, evaporated and dissolved in an assay buffer. Serum and tissue corticosterone levels were measured using a corticosterone ELISA kit (ADI-900-097, Enzo Biochem). Serum IL-1β levels were measured using an IL-1β ELISA kit (ab197742, Abcam). Neutrophil supernatant IL-1β was measured using an IL-1β ELISA kit (MLB00C-1, R&D Systems).

According to recent reports, scRNA-seq data from the non-adipocyte fraction of BAT of C57BL/6J mice maintained at room temperature were obtained and selected from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database under accessions GSE207707, GSE177635, GSE160585 and GSE161447. Data processing and analysis were conducted using Seurat v.4.0.6 in R v.4.1.2. Each dataset was imported, converted to Seurat objects, normalized and then variable features were identified. Integration anchors were computed to merge the datasets into a unified Seurat object. Quality control involved filtering out cells with fewer than 200 detected features and those with mitochondrial gene content exceeding 10%. The integrated data were scaled, and principal component analysis was performed. Clustering was performed using the Louvain algorithm with a resolution of 1.0. For visualization, t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding was used to depict cell clusters. Identification of each cell type was determined by comparing cell cluster-specific marker genes with known cell type-specific markers from the literature. Immune cell clusters were further identified and subclustered based on the expression of Ptprc, and non-immune cell types, including erythrocytes (Hba-a1 and Hba-a2), capillary endothelial cells (Pecam1 and Gpibp1), smooth muscle cells (Acta2) and adipose progenitor cells (Pdgfra and Col3a1), were excluded from the analysis.

Sources indicate that to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and enriched pathways between BA-L and BA-H cells, scRNA-seq data deposited in the NCBI GEO database under accession number GSE125269 were analysed. Adipocyte clusters were selected based on Plin1 expression, while contaminating endothelial cells (Pecam1) were excluded from the analysis. BA-L and BA-H cell populations were identified as described previously6. These populations were further compared to identify DEGs using the FindMarker function, which applied the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, with a log-transformed fold change threshold of 0.25 and a minimum detection fraction (min.pct) of 25%. To control the false discovery rate, P values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg method, and genes with an adjusted P of <0.05 were considered statistically significant. Visualization of the top 50 upregulated DEGs in both BA-L and BA-H cells was generated using the DoHeatmap function. Pathway enrichment analysis was performed on the top 75 upregulated and downregulated DEGs in BA-L cells using Gene Ontology Biological Processes. The analysis used Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P values to identify significantly enriched pathways. Pathways with an adjusted P of <0.05 and containing at least three enriched genes were considered significantly enriched. The top 20 enriched pathways were determined based on adjusted P values. Dot plots of these pathways were generated to visualize the enrichment results, with specific pathways of interest highlighted for enhanced interpretability.

In a recent development, after the vehicle and DEX treatment, in vitro-differentiated BAs were cross-linked with 1% formaldehyde (15714-S, Electron Microscopy Sciences) for 10 min at room temperature and quenched with 125 mM glycine for 10 min. Cells were then incubated with ice-cold nucleus preparation buffer (10 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 10 mM KCl, 250 mM sucrose, 0.1% NP-40, 0.2 mM DTT, protease inhibitor cocktails) and homogenized using a KIMBLE Dounce tissue grinder (D8938, Sigma-Aldrich). The nuclei were collected by centrifugation at 1,000g for 10 min, washed with PBS containing protease inhibitor cocktails (11836170001, Sigma-Aldrich) and then resuspended in 250 μl nuclear lysis buffer (10 mM Tris, pH 8, 1 mM EDTA and 0.1% SDS). The chromatin was fragmented using the Bioruptor sonicator (Diagenode) for 30 cycles, 30 s on–30 s off with the maximum power setting to generate DNA fragments of 200–500 bp. The sheared chromatin was centrifuged at 13,000 r.p.m. for 10 min at 4 °C to remove debris and diluted tenfold with ChIP dilution buffer (16.7 mM Tris (pH 8), 1.2 mM EDTA, 167 mM NaCl, 1.1% Triton X-100, 0.01% SDS, protease inhibitor cocktail), with 10 μg chromatin for each ChIP. An aliquot of 10% was used for the input control. Then, 5 μg anti-GR antibody (NBP2-42221, Novus Biologicals) or normal rabbit IgG (2729S, Cell Signaling Technology) was added for overnight rocking at 4 °C. Next, 40 μl protein A/G Dynabeads (26162, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was added to the ChIP samples and rotated for 2 h at 4 °C. The Dynabeads were washed in low-salt wash buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 2 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS), high-salt wash buffer (20 mM Tris (pH 8), 2 mM EDTA, 500 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS), LiCl wash buffer (10 mM Tris (pH 8), 1 mM EDTA, 1% NP-40, 1% sodium deoxycholate, 250 mM LiCl) and TE buffer (10 mM Tris (pH 8), 1 mM EDTA) twice at each step. The antibody–chromatin complex was eluted and reverse-cross-linked in 200 μl elution buffer (10 mM Tris (pH 8), 50 mM EDTA, 0.1% SDS, 300 mM NaCl, 0.8 mg ml−1 proteinase K and 10 μg ml−1 RNase A) by incubating at 50 °C for 2 h and subsequently at 65 °C for 8 h. The immunoprecipitated DNA fragments were purified using the MiniElute PCR Purification Kit (28004, Qiagen). ChIP–qPCR was performed using the primers listed in Supplementary Table 1. ChIP enrichments were calculated relative to the input DNA control.

Sources indicate that statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism v.10. Results are presented as mean ± s.e.m. All measurements were obtained from individual samples. For each two-group comparison, equality of variances was first assessed using the F test. An unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test was used when the F test indicated equal variances, whereas Welch’s t-tests were used when the assumption of equal variances was not met. For one-way ANOVA, Tukey’s multiple-comparison test was used when variances were equal, whereas Dunnett’s T3 multiple-comparison test was used when variances were unequal. For two-way ANOVA, Tukey’s or Šídák’s multiple-comparison test was selected according to the experimental design. The statistical tests used are specified in the corresponding figure legends. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Exact P values for all statistical comparisons are provided in Supplementary Table 2.

a, Heatmap of genes differentially expressed in BA-L cells and BA-H cells in BAT, with H6pd, Rgs2, and Ucp1 highlighted with a red asterisk. Data were obtained from the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) (accession GSE125269). b, Heatmap of genes related to thermogenesis and GR signalling that are differentially expressed in BA-L cells and BA-H cells, with Ucp1 and H6pd highlighted in red. c, Top pathway enrichment analysis for BA-L cells compared with BA-H cells, including upregulated and downregulated biological processes, with glucocorticoid-related pathways highlighted in red. The “Gene Ratio” represents the ratio of the number of input (differentially expressed) genes associated with a given pathway to the total number of input genes. p-values are shown in standard scientific notation; dot colour indicates the adjusted p-values (the brighter red indicating greater significance), and the dot size reflects the number of enriched genes. d, UMAP plots of the adipocyte fraction from BAT of WT mice maintained at room temperature. e, Distribution of the expression of Ucp1, Cox6b1, H6pd, Rgs2, Txnip and Nr3c1 within UMAP plots. f, Violin plots showing the expression and distribution of Ucp1, Cox6b1, H6pd, Rgs2, Txnip and Nr3c1.

According to recent reports, a, The Ucp1-Chaser-mTmG mouse model is generated by crossing Ucp1-rtTA transgenic mice with TRE-Cre and Rosa26-loxP-STOP-loxP-mT/mG transgenic mice. In Ucp1-Chaser-mTmG mice, all cells express tdTomato. When mice are put on a doxycycline diet, UCP1-high-expressing cells will start rtTA expression; rtTA will then bind to the TRE promoter, inducing Cre expression. Cre will specifically excise the floxed membrane-localizing Tomato (mTomato) sequence, initiating expression of membrane-localizing GFP (mGFP). b, BA-L cells and BA-H cells were freshly isolated from the BAT of WT mice. H6PD and UCP1 immunoblots and quantification normalized to Ponceau S staining. Representative Ponceau S-stained membrane as shown as loading controls. n = 4 per group. c, SVFs and BAs were freshly isolated from the BAT of WT mice. PDGFRα, UCP1, H6PD, and β-actin immunoblots and quantification. n = 4 per group. d, Ucp1-mGFP knock-in (KI) generation strategy: A P2A-mGFP cassette was inserted into the 5′ end of 3′UTR, immediately upstream of the STOP codon of Ucp1 gene. e, Representative GFP fluorescent images of whole BAT from 10-week-old male Ucp1-mGFP (left) and WT (right) littermates, demonstrating GFP expression exclusively in Ucp1-mGFP mice. f, GFP, UCP1, and β-actin immunoblots and quantification in whole BAT from 10-week-old male Ucp1-mGFP mice and WT littermates. n = 6 per group. g, IF staining showing the pattern of GFP (green) expression in the BAT of 10-week-old male Ucp1-mGFP mice. h, IF staining for GFP (green), H6PD (red), perilipin (white), and DAPI (blue) in vitro-differentiated brown adipocytes and beige adipocytes derived from Ucp1-mGFP mice BAT SVFs and iWAT SVFs. Statistics were computed by unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test [b, f (UCP1)] or unpaired two-tailed Welch’s t-test [c, f (GFP)]. **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001. For b, c, and f, data are mean ± s.e.m.

According to recent reports, a, Molecular mechanism for the maintenance of the BA-L state. BA has two stable states, low and high thermogenesis, based on UCP1 expression. BA states are governed by their spatial proximity to IL-1β+ immune cells (mainly neutrophils and macrophages), which integrate signals from sympathetic neurons and immune cells to determine whether H6PD protein levels should be stabilized or degraded. Green arrows illustrate how BA-L cells are stabilized in a low-thermogenic state: IL-1β enhances the protein stability of H6PD in thermogenic adipocytes, thereby boosting the production of active glucocorticoids. Glucocorticoid activates the expression of its target RGS2, which inhibits adenylyl cyclase and reduces cAMP production, thereby reducing UCP1 expression. Red arrows illustrate how BA-L cells switch into BA-H cells upon cold exposure: cold stimulation activates sympathetic neurons, which decrease local BAT IL-1β levels; lower IL-1β levels lead to H6PD protein degradation, turning BA-L into BA-H. The purple arrow illustrates that in aged individuals, IL-1β is elevated in BAT. High IL-1β levels persistently prevent H6PD degradation, desensitizing BAs’ cold response by locking them in BA-L states. Illustration created with BioRender; Wang, Q. https://BioRender.com/basqx8x (2026). b, Bistable regulation of BA heterogeneity in a spatiotemporal manner governs thermogenic activity. We report that IL-1β-secreting immune cells, mainly neutrophils and macrophages, stabilize the surrounding BAs in a low-thermogenic state by preventing H6PD degradation; BAs farther from IL-1β+ cells are stabilized in a high-thermogenic state. Specifically, H6PD is a functional marker of BA-L cells and boosts the production of active GC. GC then activates the expression of its target, RGS2, which inhibits adenylyl cyclase, reducing cAMP production and, in turn, UCP1 expression. This bistable regulation dynamically and precisely controls cellular heterogeneity in response to signalling from sympathetic nerves and the immune system, managing thermogenesis at the tissue level. Increased IL-1β levels in the BAT of aged individuals lock BAs in a low-thermogenic state, thereby lowering thermogenic activity and leading to cold intolerance. Illustration created with BioRender; Wang, Q. https://BioRender.com/mj195m9 (2026).

#2137. Tech Report: Jorge Jesus responds after Cristiano Ronaldo tribute ends in Portugal record defeat

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (905 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Jorge Jesus responds after Cristiano Ronaldo tribute ends in Portugal record defeat

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (905 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Naim Beneddra | 15 Nov 2026 10:52.
  • Sources indicate that portugal's first home match since Cristiano Ronaldo's international retirement was supposed to celebrate the end of an extraordinary era.
  • The Portuguese players walked onto the pitch in Braga wearing Ronaldo's iconic number seven shirt, while supporters unveiled a giant banner reading "Obrigado, Capitão" — "Thank you, Captain".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Naim Beneddra | 15 Nov 2026 10:52.

Sources indicate that portugal's first home match since Cristiano Ronaldo's international retirement was supposed to celebrate the end of an extraordinary era. Instead, a 4-1 defeat to Denmark produced the country's heaviest-ever home loss in competitive football and prompted a remarkably blunt response from Jorge Jesus about his former captain.

The Portuguese players walked onto the pitch in Braga wearing Ronaldo's iconic number seven shirt, while supporters unveiled a giant banner reading "Obrigado, Capitão" — "Thank you, Captain".

An additional tribute followed in the seventh minute, with Ronaldo's image appearing on the stadium screens as fans applauded the 41-year-old, who declared his international retirement on November 5.

By the final whistle, however, the atmosphere had changed dramatically. Some supporters had left the stadium, while others chanted Ronaldo's name as Denmark inflicted a humiliating defeat on the reigning Nations League champions.

Asked afterwards whether Portugal were missing their former captain, Jesus delivered a pointed response.

"How can I miss him when he's no longer with the national team? What is there to miss? Maybe just his company," the 72-year-old told reporters.

"He doesn't play anymore, he's not here and he's already decided his future.".

The comments added another chapter to the strained relationship between Ronaldo and Jesus, whose disagreement over the forward's international role preceded his retirement.

The scale of Saturday's defeat becomes even more striking when placed alongside Portugal's history.

According to Portuguese statistics outlet Zerozero, the national team had never previously lost a competitive home fixture by three goals or more.

Portugal's last defeat by such a margin on home soil came on September 6, 2003, when Spain secured a 3-0 friendly victory in Guimaraes.

Ronaldo had made his senior international debut against Kazakhstan just 17 days earlier, at the age of 18.

It means Portugal's first home match following his retirement produced a result not seen on Portuguese soil since the opening weeks of his international career.

The last time Portugal had lost 4-1 at home was even earlier, against Finland in a friendly on March 27, 2002.

There is an vital distinction: those previous defeats came in friendlies, whereas Denmark's victory was achieved in a competitive Nations League fixture.

The timing was particularly painful given the elaborate tribute organised by the Portuguese Football Federation to recognise Ronaldo's 23 years of international service.

The former Manchester United and Real Madrid forward ended his international career with 146 goals in 234 appearances, leaving behind records that underline the significance of his departure.

Saturday's celebrations were intended to recognise those achievements, but the match also exposed problems that Portugal must address without their former captain.

Rasmus Hojlund, another former Manchester United forward, scored twice for Denmark, while Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg and Joachim Andersen were also on target.

Bernardo Silva's stoppage-time goal merely reduced the margin of defeat.

Portugal had won their previous four Nations League matches under Jesus, including a 4-2 victory over Denmark in Copenhagen on October 1.

Six weeks later, the same opponents exposed serious weaknesses in the Portuguese defensive organisation.

Jesus refused to connect Ronaldo's absence directly with Saturday's result, insisting that the former captain had already made his decision regarding international football.

The Portuguese manager nevertheless acknowledged the significance of Ronaldo's contribution and understood why supporters were chanting his name.

He explained that fans would naturally remember everything Ronaldo had achieved over 23 years with the national team, while recognising that some had left the stadium because of their disappointment with the scoreline.

On the pitch, Jesus identified a more immediate explanation for the collapse.

Speaking at his post-match press conference, as reported by A Bola, the former Benfica manager admitted that his side had been unable to contain Denmark's attacking movements, particularly after half-time.

He pointed to failures throughout Portugal's defensive structure rather than blaming the back four alone.

The pressing, usually a defining feature of his teams, had been especially ineffective.

Jesus acknowledged that Portugal's players repeatedly arrived too late to challenge the Danish ball-carrier, allowing the visitors to move possession forward before pressure could be applied.

That failure left the defensive line exposed, with Denmark exploiting spaces between Portugal's defenders.

The manager also admitted that the result had forced him to reconsider his intends for Tuesday's final group fixture against Wales.

He had initially intended to give opportunities to several players in Cardiff, but Saturday's performance means he may now rely more heavily on those who helped Portugal win their opening four matches.

Despite the historic nature of the defeat, Jesus rejected the suggestion that his previous work should be called into question.

He reminded his players that Portugal remained top of Nations League Group A4 and still controlled their own position.

The Portuguese have 12 points, three more than Denmark, and have already secured their place in the quarter-finals.

However, the Danes now hold the head-to-head advantage following Saturday's result and could overtake Portugal if they defeat Norway and Jesus's side lose to Wales.

A draw in Cardiff would be enough for Portugal to finish first.

Jesus therefore faces an immediate challenge: restoring the defensive discipline that disappeared against Denmark while preparing a team beginning life without its most influential international figure.

Portugal make the trip to Cardiff to face Wales on Tuesday night needing to avoid defeat to guarantee top spot of Group A4 in the UEFA Nations League.

Although Wales will finish bottom of the group, the Dragons need a point to ensure that they feature in the relegation playoffs.

While there were positives to take from Wales' performance against Norway on Saturday night, Craig Bellamy's side succumbed to a 3-1 defeat in Oslo.

From knowing that a draw in Scandinavia would have kept them in third place, Wales have now gone from being certain to finish behind Portugal, Denmark and Norway.

However, despite losing four of their five matches, Wales are in a strong position to secure a relegation playoff tie in March.

Unless two of Serbia, Turkey and Czech Republic win their respective final games of the group, that consolation will be secured.

Bellamy takes his team into this contest with just one victory from nine matches, Wales having posted three draws and five defeats since March.

Meanwhile, Portugal travel to Cardiff on the back of a surprise 4-1 defeat at home to Denmark on Saturday.

After Cristiano Ronaldo's recent international retirement, Jorge Jesus would have been hoping for a fifth win in succession, but he and his players were given a reality check having fallen four goals behind come the 75th minute.

Although they have already secured a spot in the quarter-finals, Portugal must avoid defeat to leave Denmark unable to overtake them for first place on the final matchday.

The only clean sheet of Jesus's reign so far was in the 1-0 victory over Wales on matchday one.

Portugal form (all competitions):.

With Ethan Ampadu serving a suspension, Josh Sheehan could be drafted into the Wales midfield.

Connor Roberts is expected to replace the injured Neco Williams at right-back, while Bellamy may try to find a role for David Brooks after his goal in Norway.

Meanwhile, Antonio Silva is in line to deputise for Ruben Dias in the Portugal defence, a consequence of the Manchester City centre-back serving a suspension.

Nazinho is an alternative at full-back if Jesus wants to withdraw Alberto Costa or Diogo Dalot from his backline.

Joao Neves and Bernardo Silva could be brought into the midfield, with Ruben Neves and Pedro Neto potentially dropping out.

Darlow; Roberts, Rodon, Davies, Dasilva; Cullen, Sheehan; Johnson, Brooks, Wilson; Koumas.

Portugal possible starting lineup:.

D Costa; A Costa, A Silva, Veiga, Dalot; J Neves, Vitinha; B Silva, Felix, Fernandes; Ramos.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jonathan O'Shea | 15 Nov 2026 11:44, Last updated: 16 Nov 2026 14:05.

Facing off for a UEFA Nations League playoff spot, the Republic of Ireland and Kosovo will clash at Dublin's Aviva Stadium on Tuesday night.

With the hosts trailing their visitors by one point in League B Group 3, the pair are vying for second place behind confirmed winners Austria.

Any hope of securing automatic promotion to Europe's top level was ended when Ireland lost in Austria on Saturday night, leaving them six points adrift of their hosts.

Ending the stubborn resistance of goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher, who produced a string of sharp saves throughout the match, substitute Sasa Kalajdzic notched a late winner in Linz.

As a result, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side sit third in Group 3, one point behind Kosovo, who they must now beat on the final matchday.

The stakes are quite high, as victory would ensure both a Nations League promotion playoff and entry to pot two for next month's Euro 2028 qualifying draw.

At the outset, Hallgrimsson highlighted how positive results in this campaign would aid Ireland's aim of reaching a Euros that will be partly played on home soil.

Another set of circumstances could instead send them into a relegation playoff against League C opponents - if they lose again and Israel defeat Austria, the Boys in Green will finish fourth.

Yet, having kicked off with a 1-0 loss in Pristina earlier this season, Ireland will welcome Kosovo to Dublin with an historic promotion still up for grabs.

After both sides endured agony in the World Cup playoffs, Kosovo came out on top in September's Group 3 opener, as Vedat Muriqi finally broke through with a late winner.

Franco Foda's team have made rapid progress in the Nations League, previously finishing second in their League C section, before winning both legs of a playoff against Iceland.

Now in Europe's second tier for the first time, Kosovo could soon ascend straight up to League A.

If they avoid defeat on Tuesday evening, the Balkan nation will guarantee entry to the promotion playoffs, which are set to take place in March.

Second spot would have been even more firmly within their grasp but for failing to beat Israel last time out, when Veldin Hodza was sent off in a 0-0 home draw.

Even so, having picked up a single point from three consecutive fixtures, one more will be enough to keep Kosovo's campaign alive.

Republic of Ireland Nations League form:.

Despite Ireland's loss in Linz, Hallgrimsson is likely to keep a settled side, although captain Nathan Collins has been ruled out by a knee injury.

John Egan, Jake O'Brien and Jimmy Dunne will all compete to replace the Brentford centre-back in a three-man defence.

After forming an attacking trident in recent games, Jack Moylan and Adam Idah should continue to support Troy Parrott up front.

The latter may have endured a dry spell with Real Betis, but he has scored 10 goals in his last eight competitive appearances for Ireland.

Meanwhile, Muriqi is set to spearhead Kosovo's front line, as their captain and all-time top scorer with 33 international goals - including one in the reverse fixture.

Como winger Mergim Vojvoda should feature in Muriqi's supporting cast, but Juventus forward Edon Zhegrova has just withdrawn due to injury.

Ermal Krasniqi and Lumbardh Dellova - both of Turkish Super Lig surprise package Amedspor - were already ruled out, while Hodza must serve a suspension.

Republic of Ireland possible starting lineup:.

Kelleher; O'Shea, Egan, Scales; Abankwah, Molumby, Azaz, Manning; Moylan; Idah, Parrott.

Kosovo possible starting lineup:.

Saipi; Kamberi, I. Krasniqi, Raci, Gallapeni; Emerllahu, Avdullahu; Vojvoda, Rashica, Zabergja; Muriqi.

September's loss in Pristina was one of only two in Ireland's last 13 matches, and the Boys in Green generally raise their game on home turf.

As Kosovo are missing some key men from a thin squad, they may suffer defeat in Dublin and slip down to third place.

James Fontanella-Khan is up and running with his latest position at AC Milan, following an interesting background which includes the former Rossoneri man Alberto Gilardino.

Industry observers note that it was in the middle of September that various outlets reported that Fontanella-Khan was joining Milan’s management as the upcoming Chief Corporate Affairs Officer. Two months have passed since and the 43-year-old is now up and running with his new gig.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

He has been spotted among the top brass in the stands of San Siro during the most recent games and he was also present at the dinner Gerry Cardinale hosted before the derby. In other words, he’s not exactly working remotely, instead expected to spend most of his time in Milan.

In a recent development, today’s edition of Corriere dello Sport (via MilanNews) has taken a closer look at Fontanella-Khan, who has various valuable experiences to rely on in his new gig. Most recently, he was the US Financial Editor for the Financial Times, even moderating some conferences that Cardinale spoke at.

Sources indicate that before making waves in the US, however, he actually grew up in Italy and even played football himself. He was a goalkeeper in Piacenza’s youth team, reaching the Primavera of the club, and he was even a teammate of Alberto Gilardino (the former Milan striker) at one point.

After deciding that football wasn’t his path in life, he left Italy to start an internship for the Financial Times in London. He worked his way up and remained at the newspaper for over 20 years before accepting the Milan gig.

As for his role with Milan, according to Corriere dello Sport, he could be described as a General Manager. He handles communications, politics (he will be present at the League assemblies), and represents the club at various events.

Part of his goal is to connect the US mentality of the Rossoneri ownership with the Italian identity of the club, partly relying on his background as a footballer and Milan fan.

#2128. Breaking: England's Euro 2028 mission starts NOW! Thomas Tuchel's men must beat Spain to prove they can compete with the best - or risk their 'DNA' cursing them yet again, writes OLIVER HOLT

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1334 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Dailymail ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: England's Euro 2028 mission starts NOW! Thomas Tuchel's men must beat Spain to prove they can compete with the best - or risk their 'DNA' cursing them yet again, writes OLIVER HOLT

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1334 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 16:10 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 14 November 2026.
  • It is four months, almost to the day, since England shrank from the call of history and lost their World Cup semi-final to Argentina in Atlanta but Thomas Tuchel may not believe that the Nations League tie against Spain in the Metropolitano on Sunday evening represents his best shot at redemption for the way things played out that afternoon in America’s South.
  • In a recent development, that is largely because Tuchel does not appear to believe he has anything to redeem himself for.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By OLIVER HOLT, CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 16:10 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 14 November 2026.

It is four months, almost to the day, since England shrank from the call of history and lost their World Cup semi-final to Argentina in Atlanta but Thomas Tuchel may not believe that the Nations League tie against Spain in the Metropolitano on Sunday evening represents his best shot at redemption for the way things played out that afternoon in America’s South.

In a recent development, that is largely because Tuchel does not appear to believe he has anything to redeem himself for. The manner of his side’s capitulation - and the substitutions he made - in the Mercedes-Benz Stadium last July enraged the nation, but Tuchel mentioned the fault was in the damned DNA of the English, that we were underlings, and that our players found it constitutionally impossible to keep hold of the ball.

Whatever Tuchel thinks, the fact remains that the tie against Lamine Yamal, Fabian Ruiz, Pedri and Mikel Oyarzabal and the rest of the world champions at the home of Atletico Madrid offers Tuchel and his players the opportunity to encourage themselves and their fans that they are not destined to be also-rans wired to fall at the final hurdle for evermore.

It has been revealed that spain are formidable opposition. They are on a record-breaking run of 43 matches unbeaten and have won their last 12 in succession. They haven't drawn a game since their June 15 game against Cape Verde in the World Cup. Their last defeat was on March 22, 2024, when they lost 1-0 to Colombia in a friendly. Some ask whether they are the best international side the world has ever seen.

‘Spain seem unbeatable,’ Tuchel noted, when he walked into the press room at the Metropolitano on Saturday night and heard hymns of praise being lavished upon the opponents he is about to face.

Sources indicate that ‘They have a very strong identity and a very strong mentality. We are trying to take it away from them. We are up for it. We are up for the fight. We are up for a spectacular match. We can see how far we can push the limits with the world champions in Madrid. The group is full of self-belief and rightly so.’.

England must beat Spain to prove they can compete with the best - even if they have flaws.

Thomas Tuchel must show he can find a way around the limitations presented by the 'DNA' he has complained about.

In a recent development, this may be the toughest game that Tuchel’s England side play until the European Championships in 2028, where the final will be contested at Wembley, and they will play all their games at home. They need to go into that tournament with the belief that they can beat the best when the pressure is at its highest.

It has been revealed that beating Spain away in the final game of the group phase of the Nations League is not quite the same as a critical match at a major tournament but it is as stiff a challenge as Tuchel is going to face until then. Beating Croatia 7-0 in front of gangs of schoolkids in Rijeka last month was hailed as the best England performance of the Tuchel era. Which says it all, really.

Industry observers note that it was a great performance in a relatively meaningless match. Now it is time for him to show that he can marshal an England side to succeed against the very best, not fall apart when the prize is in sight. His protestations of powerlessness in the aftermath of the Argentina defeat were not a good look for a coach who was hired with the idea that his coaching prowess and his game management could get England over the line.

Has he learned anything from the manner of the Argentina defeat? ‘This game against Spain will be proof of concept at the highest level,’ he mentioned, ‘but we are up for it. I think we have taken the next step after the World Cup. The best thing is to trust our process and trust ourselves. We need to be clear about how we want to impose ourselves and I think that is all visible.’.

Now it is time for him to show that he can find a way past the limitations of England’s footballing DNA, find a way to compete with Spain and France when it really matters, and find a way to end the culture of near misses that has come to be England’s lot in the last decade of appearances in semi-finals and finals.

England have played six matches since that day of crushing disappointment in Atlanta and scored 22 goals. But in the only one of those matches that really mattered, they lost 3-2 to Spain at Wembley in the opening tie of their Nations League campaign at the end of September, a game in which they were largely outclassed by Luis de la Fuente’s team.

In a recent development, spain are what England have to aim for. Tuchel mentioned their example and their ability and their mindset straight after the semi-final loss to Argentina. ‘Ball possession plays a crucial role,’ he said at his post-match press conference in Atlanta. ‘It’s maybe not in our DNA like it is in our Spanish DNA or in our Argentinian-Brazilian DNA, to take the ball and control the game with the ball.’.

This may well be their toughest game until the final of the 2028 European Championships, if they get that far.

The England coach stated more recently that England need to go back to trusting a traditional style that emphasises direct, high-intensity physicality rather than trying to copy Spanish patience in ball-retention. England, though, were taught a lesson in sophistication by the Spanish in September.

It has been revealed that and for all the attention lavished on Yamal, Spain’s defence is the best in the world. Rodri, the shield for that defence and also the world’s best in the role, is not fit for this game but even without him, Spain’s back-line inspires an awful lot more confidence than England’s.

‘They were the best in the World Cup at the back,’ Declan Rice, England’s central midfielder, mentioned on Saturday. ‘Defence wins you titles. Everyone talks about their attacking talent but you look at their central defenders, their full backs and the way their midfielders contribute to the defence, too.’.

That defence will have to stop England’s resurgent front line, led by Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane, who could be flanked by Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers and backed up by the supreme talent of Jude Bellingham just behind them.

Industry observers note that bellingham’s improving relationship with Tuchel, which cannot have been harmed by the inclusion of Bellingham’s brother, Jobe, in this squad, is another reason to hope that England still retain the capacity to improve after the World Cup. The elder Bellingham has become England’s most influential player.

England at their best would be one of the few teams capable of extending them. Rice mentioned on Saturday that the game between the two sides was ‘massive’. England need to prove they can find a way to get closer to the world champions. To beat them, Rice said, would be a ‘massive statement’.

It has been revealed that ‘Playing against them is a great incentive to win. It will show where we are as a group. We are trying to attack teams full throttle and with players like Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham and Morgan Rogers in our attack, it feels as if it is going to take off one night and maybe tomorrow night will be the night. We can beat Spain. For sure, we can.’.

Tuchel needs to prove England can win, not just be noble contenders. They need to prove that their DNA need not be a curse.

With Jamaica having finished second behind Guatemala in their group, Mexico would have been confident of earning an advantage from Saturday's first leg in Kingston.

Instead, Mexico are fortunate to still be competitive in the tie having found themselves 3-0 down by the 63rd minute.

Two goals in the closing 20 minutes kept the World Cup last-16 representatives in the tie, yet Rafael Marquez remains without a win as manager.

The former defender has now overseen two draws and three draws, with El Tri having lost 3-0 and 2-0 to USA and Chile respectively prior to their latest fixture.

As defending champions, it would be a major knock on Marquez should he fail to guide Mexico to at least the last four of the competition.

Meanwhile, Jamaica are attempting to move closer to a second semi-final appearance in three Nations League campaigns.

Having lost out to DR Congo in the World Cup playoffs earlier in the year, Rudolph Speid's side have delivered a strong response.

Although two defeats have been posted in seven games, they defeated El Salvador and earned a draw with Honduras on away territory before Saturday's five-goal thriller.

Jamaica had failed to win their previous six games against Mexico before that contest, emphasising the magnitude of the result.

Despite his role as captain, Cesar Montes could be among those to drop down to the substitutes' bench, along with forward Santiago Gimenez.

Eighteen-year-old Gilberto Mora should keep his spot in a creative midfield role.

As for Jamaica, Denzel Hall may be handed a start over Kyle Ming at right wing-back.

However, Speid could be against making further changes to his side, unless he highlights preference towards introducing fresh legs.

Javon East has started the last three games down the middle of the attack.

That’s the view of former QPR and Charlton striker Conor Washington as he has his say on Crawley Town’s next managerial appointment.

Reds owners have yet to name a permanent successor for Colin Kazim-Richards, who was sacked on October 21 following a poor start to the season which has sees them rock bottom of League Two.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Kevin Blackwell has been in charge on an interim basis but Reds fans are eagerly anticipating who will be the next permanent boss as they look to climb the table.

But Washington, in his latest exclusive EFL column for BestBettingBonuses.co.uk, claims there is a bigger picture at play.

“I think the bigger question for me is around the overall football strategy at the club,” he noted. “With the structure they've got, they either need to decide on a clear way they want the club to play, recruit players who fit that and then appoint managers who can implement it, or they need to appoint a manager with a really clear playing style and back him with recruitment that suits what he's trying to do. Both approaches can work, but you can't really keep moving between the two.

"Otherwise you end up with players recruited for one manager being asked to play a completely different way under the next one.

“From what Colin Kazim-Richards said in the summer, there was clearly an attempt to recruit players specifically for his ideas, but now they're potentially looking for another manager just a few months later. That's where the problems can start.”.

And he added that it’s a massive job for whoever comes in. He mentioned: “I think whoever comes in needs to be really clear about what they've inherited, what the players are actually capable of and how they can get the best out of them.

"There's no point appointing someone because you like their philosophy if the squad isn't equipped to carry it out, particularly when you're fighting to stay in the league.”.

Reds face Fleetwood Town at home on Saturday following their international break.
